extra_data.title: Tulips

headings.text: The economy during the Golden Age

paragraphs.text: In the 17th century, Amsterdam was a prosperous city in the Netherlands. Besides, the Netherlands experienced a period of immense wealth and cultural development. Trade, science, and the arts flourished, creating a thriving middle class with disposable income. This prosperity led to a growing interest in luxury items, including rare flowers such as tulips. The booming economy encouraged speculative investments, and tulips quickly became a symbol of wealth and social status. Their rising popularity was not merely about beauty but about prestige—owning exotic tulips was a way to showcase one's success in this golden era.

Tulips first gained popularity in the Ottoman Empire and later spread to Western Europe. When they arrived in the Netherlands, they became an instant sensation. Their bold colors and unique shapes captivated people, and soon tulips were planted in aristocratic gardens and depicted in still-life paintings. The flower’s visual appeal made it highly desirable among the wealthy and artistic communities. By the early 1600s, tulips had become one of the most fashionable items in Dutch society, and their fame began to outshine other plants traditionally valued in Europe.

As their popularity increased, tulips transitioned from decorative items to commodities. They began to be sold in markets, sometimes even before they had bloomed. Merchants treated tulip bulbs like valuable assets, often purchasing them based on future availability. Buyers and sellers exchanged contracts instead of the actual flowers, betting on future prices. This speculative behavior turned the tulip into more than just a flower—it became a financial instrument, with its value fluctuating daily based on market trends and demand.

There are hundreds of tulip varieties, differing in color, shape, and pattern. Some of the most prized tulips during the 17th century were those with unique stripes or flame-like markings on their petals. These effects were later discovered to be caused by a virus affecting the flower, but at the time they were considered extremely rare and beautiful. Breeders carefully cultivated new hybrids, and collectors paid large sums for bulbs with unusual appearances. This diversity in types helped fuel the tulip craze, as people competed to own the most exotic specimens.

The tulip trade operated on a complex system of contracts, options, and informal agreements. Because bulbs bloom only once a year, buyers often agreed on future purchases, sometimes without even seeing the flower. Specialized markets were established where traders could buy and sell tulip futures. Prices were agreed upon months in advance, and payments were made when the bulbs were delivered. This abstract trading model made it easier for speculators to participate, but it also disconnected the trade from the real value of the product itself.

Tulip trading wasn’t limited to the Netherlands. As demand grew, bulbs were shipped across Europe—from France to England and beyond. Traders carried these rare goods by land and sea, navigating a web of routes and tariffs. Each region had its own preferences, and what was fashionable in Amsterdam might not be as popular in Paris. Nonetheless, tulips remained a desirable item among European elites, and international trade routes helped spread both the flower and its financial influence across the continent.

The tulip market collapsed suddenly in 1637. After years of increasing prices and wild speculation, confidence disappeared overnight. Buyers stopped showing up to auctions, and contracts became worthless. Panic spread, and traders who had invested heavily were left with massive debts and unsellable bulbs. This event, often referred to as the first economic bubble in history, highlighted the dangers of speculative markets. The tulip crash left a deep impact on the Dutch economy and became a cautionary tale still taught in economics courses today.

extra_data.title: Meatless

headings.text: Factory farming - it is a harmful thing

paragraphs.text: Vegetarianism is not a single dietary choice but includes many different forms. Some vegetarians avoid meat but still eat dairy and eggs—these are called lacto-ovo vegetarians. Others, like vegans, avoid all animal-derived products, including honey and gelatin. There are also pescatarians, who exclude meat but still consume fish. Flexitarians mostly eat plant-based foods but occasionally include meat or fish. These variations show that a meatless diet can be adapted to individual needs and beliefs, making it a flexible and increasingly popular choice for people around the world.

People adopt meatless diets for many different reasons. For some, religious beliefs guide their eating habits, while others avoid meat out of concern for animal welfare. Some are motivated by environmental issues, believing that reducing meat consumption lowers their carbon footprint. Health is also a major factor, as some studies link vegetarian diets to lower risks of heart disease and diabetes. The motivations are as varied as the people who choose them, and it's not uncommon for individuals to follow a plant-based lifestyle for a combination of reasons.

Many people wonder if it's truly possible to live without eating meat. The answer is yes, as proven by millions of vegetarians and vegans worldwide. While it requires some planning to ensure a balanced intake of protein, iron, and vitamin B12, plant-based diets can be nutritionally complete. In fact, major health organizations have stated that well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets are suitable for all stages of life, including childhood and pregnancy. With a variety of plant-based options now available, choosing a meatless lifestyle is more practical than ever.

Factory farming—the industrialized method of raising animals for food—has been criticized for its negative effects on both animals and the environment. Animals are often kept in cramped, stressful conditions, and the use of antibiotics to promote growth raises concerns about resistance. Additionally, factory farms contribute to pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. These harmful impacts are among the key reasons why some people choose to reduce or eliminate meat from their diet. Supporting ethical and sustainable food sources is becoming a growing priority for many consumers.

At the core of many vegetarian beliefs is the idea of respecting all forms of life. For some, avoiding meat is a moral decision rooted in the belief that animals have the right to live without suffering. This perspective emphasizes empathy, compassion, and non-violence. It is also reflected in certain spiritual or religious practices where harming living beings is discouraged. Choosing a meatless diet becomes more than just a personal choice—it represents a commitment to treating all creatures with dignity and care.

A common benefit reported by people who switch to a plant-based diet is improved health. Many experience lower cholesterol levels, better digestion, and increased energy. Vegetarian diets are often rich in fiber, antioxidants, and healthy fats. Studies show that people who consume more fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes tend to have lower risks of heart disease and obesity. However, balance is key—a diet full of processed plant foods can still be unhealthy. When done right, a meatless diet can be a strong foundation for a healthy lifestyle.

Reducing meat consumption can also be seen as a global responsibility. Livestock farming is a major contributor to climate change, water usage, and deforestation. By choosing plant-based options, individuals can lower their environmental impact and support a more sustainable food system. Small changes made by many people can have a big collective effect. From conserving water to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, a meatless diet can be a meaningful step toward addressing some of the planet’s most urgent environmental challenges.

extra_data.title: Frozen land

headings.text: The hidden landscape beneath the ice
Where is the end of the Earth?

paragraphs.text: Although Antarctica is not claimed as a country, several nations have laid territorial claims over parts of the continent. However, under the Antarctic Treaty System signed in 1959, no single country has full ownership. Instead, the region is governed collectively by over 50 countries that have agreed to preserve it for peaceful and scientific purposes. No military activity is allowed, and scientific cooperation is encouraged. This unique model of international governance helps protect the fragile environment of the frozen land and ensures that its resources are not exploited for commercial gain.

The first known landing on Antarctica took place in the early 19th century when a group of seal hunters unintentionally arrived at the icy coastline. Later, exploratory missions were organized specifically to set foot on the continent. In 1895, a Norwegian expedition became the first officially recognized landing. These early steps were dangerous and uncertain, with little knowledge of the terrain or weather. Still, the achievement marked a turning point in human exploration, showing that even the most remote and inhospitable places on Earth could be reached with courage and persistence.

Antarctica has often been described as the end of the Earth. Located at the southernmost point of the planet, it remains one of the most mysterious and least accessible places for humans. It's surrounded by the Southern Ocean and sits opposite the Arctic in the global geography. For centuries, explorers speculated whether such a place existed at all. Today, while satellite images and scientific missions provide more data, the continent still retains an aura of the unknown, attracting adventurers and scientists who want to experience the planet's final frontier.

Despite being covered in thick sheets of ice, Antarctica has a surprisingly diverse and dramatic landscape hidden beneath its surface. Using ground-penetrating radar and satellite imaging, scientists have discovered vast mountain ranges, deep valleys, and even ancient lakes buried under kilometers of ice. These findings suggest that Antarctica was once a very different environment. Studying this hidden geography helps researchers understand the Earth's geological past, as well as how changes in climate may affect the region's ice coverage in the future.

The early 20th century saw a dramatic competition between nations to reach the South Pole. Most famously, British explorer Robert Falcon Scott and Norwegian Roald Amundsen led rival expeditions. Amundsen reached the Pole first in 1911, using dog sleds and careful planning. Scott arrived weeks later, only to perish on the return journey with his team. The race to the pole was one of the most extreme tests of human endurance and remains one of the most iconic chapters in the history of polar exploration.

Travel across Antarctica remains one of the most difficult journeys on Earth. However, modern technology has significantly reduced the physical effort required. In the past, explorers dragged heavy sleds by hand or used animals, often in dangerous and freezing conditions. Today, snowmobiles, tracked vehicles, and even aircraft allow researchers to move equipment and people more easily. While the environment is still harsh, advances in transportation and survival gear make scientific missions more efficient and less life-threatening than those of early explorers.

Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth, with temperatures regularly dropping below –60°C in winter. The continent's high altitude, its position near the South Pole, and the fact that sunlight is absent for months all contribute to its extreme chill. Its white ice surface also reflects most of the sun's heat back into the atmosphere. These unique features make it difficult for heat to accumulate, and as a result, the region remains frozen even in summer. Understanding these conditions helps scientists study global weather patterns and climate change.

extra_data.title: Wellness Trends.

paragraphs.text: In recent years, the concept of health has expanded to include more than just physical well-being. Holistic approaches emphasize the interconnectedness of the body, mind, and environment, encouraging individuals to consider emotional balance, mental clarity, nutrition, and lifestyle habits all together. This broader perspective helps people achieve deeper and more sustainable wellness by addressing multiple aspects of their lives rather than isolated symptoms.

Mental health has increasingly become a priority in public health discussions. Awareness campaigns aim to reduce the stigma around mental illnesses and encourage people to talk openly about their struggles. Providing education on recognizing early signs of anxiety, depression, and stress empowers individuals to seek help sooner. Many organizations also offer support networks and resources to foster a more compassionate and understanding society.

Community-based fitness initiatives are gaining popularity as a way to make exercise more enjoyable and accessible. By participating in group activities like yoga classes, walking clubs, or sports leagues, people not only improve their physical health but also build meaningful social connections. These programs create a sense of belonging and motivate individuals to stick with their fitness goals over time, contributing to healthier and happier communities.

Although fad diets often promise rapid weight loss or improved health, relying too heavily on these trends can be problematic. Many popular diets lack scientific backing and may exclude important nutrients, leading to imbalanced nutrition. Nutrition experts stress that sustainable eating should focus on balanced meals, moderation, and personal needs rather than quick fixes. Developing a healthy relationship with food is more beneficial than following the latest diet craze.

The rise of social media and online platforms has led to widespread sharing of health information, but not all of it is accurate or safe. Misinformation about supplements, treatments, and health practices can cause confusion or even harm. It is important for individuals to critically evaluate sources, consult healthcare professionals, and rely on evidence-based guidance when making decisions about their wellness routines.

Supportive groups focused on wellness play a crucial role in helping people maintain healthy lifestyles. Whether online forums or local meetups, these communities offer encouragement, share tips, and provide accountability. Members can exchange experiences, celebrate successes, and find motivation during challenges, creating an environment where individuals feel empowered to achieve their health goals.

Achieving long-term health requires more than temporary diets or exercise bursts. Sustainable wellness involves adopting gradual changes that can be maintained over time, such as improving sleep habits, managing stress, and incorporating regular physical activity. By setting realistic goals and making incremental adjustments, individuals are more likely to enjoy lasting benefits and improve their overall quality of life.

extra_data.title: Tulips

headings.text: The economy during the Golden Age

paragraphs.text: During the Dutch Golden Age in the 17th century, the Netherlands experienced a period of immense wealth and cultural development. Trade, science, and the arts flourished, creating a thriving middle class with disposable income. This prosperity led to a growing interest in luxury items, including rare flowers such as tulips. The booming economy encouraged speculative investments, and tulips quickly became a symbol of wealth and social status. Their rising popularity was not merely about beauty but about prestige-owning exotic tulips was a way to showcase one's success in this golden era.

Tulips first gained popularity in the Ottoman Empire and later spread to Western Europe. When they arrived in the Netherlands, they became an instant sensation. Their bold colors and unique shapes captivated people, and soon tulips were planted in aristocratic gardens and depicted in still-life paintings. The flower’s visual appeal made it highly desirable among the wealthy and artistic communities. By the early 1600s, tulips had become one of the most fashionable items in Dutch society, and their fame began to outshine other plants traditionally valued in Europe.

As their popularity increased, tulips transitioned from decorative items to commodities. They began to be sold in markets, sometimes even before they had bloomed. Merchants treated tulip bulbs like valuable assets, often purchasing them based on future availability. Buyers and sellers exchanged contracts instead of the actual flowers, betting on future prices. This speculative behavior turned the tulip into more than just a flower-it became a financial instrument, with its value fluctuating daily based on market trends and demand.

There are hundreds of tulip varieties, differing in color, shape, and pattern. Some of the most prized tulips during the 17th century were those with unique stripes or flame-like markings on their petals. These effects were later discovered to be caused by a virus affecting the flower, but at the time they were considered extremely rare and beautiful. Breeders carefully cultivated new hybrids, and collectors paid large sums for bulbs with unusual appearances. This diversity in types helped fuel the tulip craze, as people competed to own the most exotic specimens.

The tulip trade operated on a complex system of contracts, options, and informal agreements. Because bulbs bloom only once a year, buyers often agreed on future purchases, sometimes without even seeing the flower. Specialized markets were established where traders could buy and sell tulip futures. Prices were agreed upon months in advance, and payments were made when the bulbs were delivered. This abstract trading model made it easier for speculators to participate, but it also disconnected the trade from the real value of the product itself.

Tulip trading wasn’t limited to the Netherlands. As demand grew, bulbs were shipped across Europe-from France to England and beyond. Traders carried these rare goods by land and sea, navigating a web of routes and tariffs. Each region had its own preferences, and what was fashionable in Amsterdam might not be as popular in Paris. Nonetheless, tulips remained a desirable item among European elites, and international trade routes helped spread both the flower and its financial influence across the continent.

The tulip market collapsed suddenly in 1637. After years of increasing prices and wild speculation, confidence disappeared overnight. Buyers stopped showing up to auctions, and contracts became worthless. Panic spread, and traders who had invested heavily were left with massive debts and unsellable bulbs. This event, often referred to as the first economic bubble in history, highlighted the dangers of speculative markets. The tulip crash left a deep impact on the Dutch economy and became a cautionary tale still taught in economics courses today.

extra_data.title: Women Mathematicians.

headings.text: Attempting to create a gender balance
Labels can change perspective on people
A long career showing exceptional ability

paragraphs.text: For centuries, the achievements of women in mathematics were either omitted from historical records or attributed to male colleagues. Hypatia of Alexandria, one of the earliest known female mathematicians, was respected in her time, yet many of her contributions were later credited to male scholars. Such erasure has been a recurring theme in the history of women in this field.

Emmy Noether, often described as the most important woman in the history of mathematics, revolutionized abstract algebra and theoretical physics. Albert Einstein referred to her work as "the very expression of the spirit of modern algebra." Only recently has her legacy gained the widespread recognition it deserves, demonstrating a growing effort to acknowledge those once overlooked.

In many historical accounts, the success of male mathematicians has overshadowed the collaborative efforts of their female peers. For example, the development of chaos theory often credits Edward Lorenz, yet contributions by female mathematicians working in the same field are frequently omitted from textbooks and academic narratives.

Mary Cartwright had a mathematical career spanning over six decades. Her work in nonlinear differential equations laid the groundwork for chaos theory, influencing both mathematics and engineering. Despite the challenges faced by women in academia during her time, she maintained a consistent output of high-quality research throughout her life.

When female mathematicians are described as "women geniuses" or "female prodigies," the gender label, while well-intended, often implies that excellence is rare among women. Such terms, though celebratory, can unintentionally reinforce the idea that women's success in mathematics is unusual, rather than simply the result of talent and hard work.

To address the gender imbalance in mathematics, many universities and organizations now run outreach programs, offer scholarships specifically for women, and encourage female mentorship in STEM fields. These efforts aim not to give unfair advantage, but to create equal opportunities in a domain where women have historically been underrepresented.

In efforts to level the playing field, some institutions have implemented standardized criteria for admissions or research evaluation. However, such uniform methods can sometimes ignore the diverse paths and challenges faced by individuals, particularly women balancing academic and societal expectations. A one-size-fits-all approach may not always foster true equity.

Language changes with technology, culture, and daily life, so it is understandable that people create new expressions to describe modern experiences.

In formal education and professional writing, uncontrolled changes may also create misunderstandings.
In my opinion, we should not reject all new words, but we should use them carefully. Useful and widely understood expressions can be accepted, while clear rules should still be kept for academic and official contexts. In this way, language can remain both flexible and understandable.

Dear Club President,
I am writing to share some suggestions on how our Home Living Club can support young families who are looking for a home. Nowadays, many people find it difficult to buy or rent a house because of high prices and limited information.
Firstly, I suggest that the club organize workshops with experts who can provide advice on budgeting, home loans, and affordable housing options. This would help families better understand the process and make smarter decisions.
Secondly, we could create a list of reliable real estate agents and useful online resources. This would save time and help families avoid risks when searching for a home.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to your response.
Best regards,
Nam

formalEmail.sampleAnswer:
Dear Manager,

Thank you for your email about helping young families find suitable homes. I am very glad that the club wants to support them, as I know several young couples who have struggled with this problem, and I would like to offer two suggestions.

Firstly, the club could organise a monthly information evening with a local estate agent and a bank adviser. Many young families do not understand mortgages, contracts or their rights as tenants, so clear advice from experts would save them time and money.

Secondly, we could create a simple online noticeboard on the club website where members share flats and houses they know are available. Personal recommendations are often more reliable than commercial adverts, and this would cost the club almost nothing.

I would be happy to help set up either of these ideas. Please let me know what you think.

Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]

Dear Manager,

Thank you for your email about the suggestion to introduce an entrance fee. I appreciate being asked for my opinion.

I understand that maintenance costs are rising, and I am concerned about the museum's future. However, I believe that charging a fee would be a mistake. Free entry is the main reason why students, families and elderly people visit so often, and many of them simply could not afford regular tickets. If visitor numbers fall, the museum would lose its role as a place for the whole community.

Instead, I would suggest two alternatives. First, the museum could place donation boxes at the entrance and encourage visitors to give what they can. Second, it could charge a small fee only for special exhibitions and evening events, while keeping the main collection free.

I hope these ideas are helpful.

Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]

explanation:
1. Đoạn mở đầu nói ăn chay không phải một luật cứng mà là sự chuyển dịch dần dần, có nhiều mức độ khác nhau — thay đổi từ từ chứ không phải quy tắc nghiêm ngặt.
2. Đoạn giải quyết nỗi lo đạm: đậu lăng, đậu gà, đậu phụ, hạt, bánh mì và cơm đều góp đạm, ăn đa dạng trong ngày là đủ — tìm nguyên liệu xây dựng cơ thể từ nguồn khác.
3. Đoạn chỉ ra vài chất cần để mắt: B12 hầu như chỉ có trong sản phẩm động vật nên phải bổ sung, sắt từ thực vật hấp thu kém hơn — những lỗ hổng cần theo dõi.
4. Đoạn cảnh báo bỏ thịt không tự động thành ăn lành mạnh: đồ chay đông lạnh và đồ ăn sẵn nhiều muối, nhiều dầu, sống bằng khoai chiên và bánh mì trắng cũng không tốt — không phải lựa chọn nào cũng lành mạnh.
5. Đoạn bàn chuyện tiền: đậu khô, rau theo mùa, yến mạch, đậu Hà Lan đông lạnh thuộc nhóm rẻ nhất, nhưng đồ chay chế biến sẵn lại đắt — ảnh hưởng tới ngân sách hằng tuần.
6. Đoạn nói kỹ năng nấu quyết định nhiều hơn ta tưởng: rau luộc nhạt thì không ai thích, cũng rau đó đem nướng vàng, nêm tỏi, thảo mộc, chanh thì khác hẳn — làm nguyên liệu đơn giản trở nên ngon.
7. Đoạn kết khuyên bắt đầu nhẹ nhàng: chọn một hai ngày mỗi tuần, sửa lại món quen thay vì học món mới phức tạp, thủ sẵn vài món tin cậy cho tối bận — bắt đầu mà không tạo áp lực.

extra_data.title: A Plant-Based Plate

headings.text: The effect on a weekly budget
A gradual shift rather than a strict rule
Not every option is a healthy one

paragraphs.text: The most common change in eating habits today is not a dramatic one. Instead of announcing that they will never touch meat again, many people simply cook it less often, replacing it two or three evenings a week with beans, vegetables or eggs. This slower approach is easier to keep up, causes fewer arguments at family meals, and lets someone test unfamiliar dishes before deciding how far they really want to go.

The first worry people mention is protein, although it is easier to solve than they expect. Lentils, chickpeas, tofu, nuts, seeds and even ordinary bread and rice all make a contribution, and eating a variety of them across the day supplies what the body needs. A bowl of rice with beans, or hummus with wholemeal bread, gives a good mixture without any careful calculation at every single meal.

A few nutrients do deserve closer attention. Vitamin B12 occurs naturally almost only in animal products, so anyone avoiding those completely should take a supplement or choose foods that have it added. Iron from plants is absorbed less easily, though eating peppers or citrus fruit at the same time improves the situation. Those who give up milk and cheese also need another regular source of calcium.

It is a mistake to assume that leaving meat out automatically improves a diet. Shop shelves are now full of frozen substitutes and ready meals that are heavily processed and high in salt and fat, and living on chips, white bread and biscuits technically meets the definition as well. The advantages reported in research, such as more fibre and lower cholesterol, come from vegetables, pulses and whole grains rather than from the label on a packet.

Money is another practical consideration, and the answer depends on what goes into the basket. Dried pulses, seasonal vegetables, oats and frozen peas are among the cheapest items in any shop, and households that build their meals around them usually spend less than before. Products designed to imitate sausages and burgers, however, often cost more than the meat itself, which is why they suit an occasional treat rather than a daily habit.

Cooking skills make more difference than most people realise. Vegetables served plain and boiled will convince nobody, while the same ingredients roasted until they brown, seasoned with garlic, herbs, lemon or spices and combined with something crunchy become a meal worth repeating. Kitchens in India, the Middle East and the Mediterranean have relied on pulses and grains for centuries and are a useful place to look for ideas.

Anyone curious about the change is usually advised to begin quietly. Choosing one or two days a week, adapting a familiar recipe rather than learning a complicated new one, and keeping a few reliable dishes in mind for busy evenings all reduce the effort involved. Restaurants and staff canteens offer far more options than they did a decade ago, so eating out no longer means abandoning the plan after a fortnight.

extra_data.title: Zoo

headings.text: Away from enclosure towards greater freedom

paragraphs.text: A zoo (short for zoological garden; also called an animal park or menagerie) is a facility in which animals are kept within enclosures for public exhibition and often bred for conservation purposes. The term zoological garden refers to zoology, the study of animals. The abbreviation zoo was first used of the London Zoological Gardens, which was opened for scientific study in 1828, and to the public in 1847. In the early days, the zoo was opened to serve the wealthy and high-status people in society.

Later, it was realized that humans were curious about strange things. Large predators such as lions, bears or rare animals often caused great interest and could attract many people to see them. For that reason, some zoos opened their doors and welcomed all the people. It is noteworthy that in addition to animals, some zoos also displayed humans. Humans were occasionally displayed in cages at zoos along with non-human animals, to illustrate the differences between people of European and non-European origin. This attracted even more attention from the public - people who saw animals or people who were completely unfamiliar to them for the first time.

In the early days, the sole purpose of zoos was entertainment. People simply went to zoos to see things that interested them or that they thought were strange. As time went on, people’s need for information increased. People always asked questions about the things they saw in zoos, such as where they came from, what their previous habitats were, how they reproduced, etc. This led the zookeepers to decide to add that knowledge to the cages in zoos.

In large animals, a limited number of spaces were available in zoos. As a consequence, in the early days, these animals were kept in cramped cages where they could only survive. This greatly reduced the life expectancy of animals in zoos. Later, the government and zoo managers decided to expand the area where the animals were kept. This was also a humane move. In some places, people even arranged the environment to be closer to the wild environment so that the animals could have more space to move. This change in living space improved the quality of life of many animals. Many of them began to reproduce in the zoo's captive environment.

Today, zoos have set themselves apart from other entertainment programs by declaring their role to be education and development of science and awareness among people rather than simply entertainment. In addition, many zoos also carry out conservation or rescue projects for wild animals. There are even some species that only exist in modern zoos and no longer exist in the natural environment.

Over time, the educational mission of zoos has evolved. Today zoos are organized to provide both entertainment and education. This has led to a growing appreciation of wildlife and the urgent need to protect biodiversity. It has been shown that this mission is essential to prevent the loss of valuable animal genetic resources.

It has been shown that zoos are no longer simply places for entertainment but are also considered places for education and conservation. Students will no longer have to learn about animals through books alone and the conservation of endangered species does not need to be organized in projects in the forest anymore.

options: In these performances, he liked to wear bright clothes and paint his face.

explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
Dạng sắp xếp câu: tìm câu mở đầu (không trỏ ngược), rồi bám vào đại từ, từ chỉ định và từ nối để nối dần.

▸ A famous singer — câu cho sẵn: "Jade Nobelton was only 18 when he became a famous singer." Thứ tự 5 câu còn lại:
  1. "Before becoming famous at such a young age, he studied music in high school." → "at such a young age" trỏ về "only 18" ở câu cho sẵn; "Before becoming famous" mở phần quá khứ.
  2. "During his studies, he learnt how to be creative on stage." → "During his studies" bám vào "studied music in high school".
  3. "In his performances, he wore brightly coloured clothes and painted his face." → "his performances" nối "creative on stage".
  4. "This unique way of dressing and performing made people pay attention to him." → "This unique way of dressing" tổng kết câu 3.
  5. "Many people started following him on social media and he became a famous singer." → kết quả cuối, khép lại với "famous singer" ở câu cho sẵn.

▸ The famous singer — thứ tự đúng:
  0. "Jade Nobelton is only 18 years old, and he is a famous singer." → câu cho sẵn, giới thiệu nhân vật.
  1. "Before becoming famous at this young age, he studied art and music at high school." → "this young age" trỏ về "18 years old".
  2. "During this education, he learned to be creative and to practise singing on stage." → "this education" trỏ về việc học ở high school.
  3. "In these performances, he liked to wear bright clothes and paint his face." → "these performances" trỏ về "singing on stage".
  4. "This strange way of dressing and his songs have attracted people's attention." → "This strange way of dressing" trỏ về quần áo sặc sỡ và vẽ mặt.
  5. "They started to follow him on social media, and now he is very popular." → "They" trỏ về "people" ở câu trước, chốt bằng kết quả hiện tại.

▸ A famous singer (Version 2) — thứ tự đúng:
  1. "He is a successful singer with many fans." → câu mở đầu: tiêu đề đã nêu nhân vật nên vào bài dùng luôn "He".
  2. "Before becoming famous, he studied music at school when he was 15." → "Before becoming famous" quay về quá khứ.
  3. "His unique way of dressing and performing made him stand out from others." → "His" cần câu giới thiệu đứng trước.
  4. "This helped him receive many invitations for collaborations and performances." → "This helped him" trỏ ngược về việc nổi bật ở câu 3.
  5. "He eventually became famous among audiences around the world." → "eventually" chốt kết quả cuối cùng.
👉 Mẹo: câu mở đầu là câu duy nhất KHÔNG có đại từ/từ chỉ định trỏ ngược. Sau đó bám mỏ neo: "at his age → 18 years old", "During his studies → studied at school", "these performances → singing on stage".

I suggest making the itinerary flexible, with shorter route options or rest days. The club could also provide clear information about cost, travel insurance, and physical requirements in advance. With good planning, I believe this trip could become a very successful event.
Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]

extra_data.title: Charles Dicken

paragraphs.text: The popularity of Dickens's works in our time remains a global phenomenon. Although he wrote his novels in the 19th century, his works have had a global impact. In addition, these masterpieces helped connect Renaissance drama to the multimedia revolution. Many readers find the characters and themes surprisingly modern.

Shakespeare's plays are difficult to understand and sometimes require the reader to struggle or think twice to figure out the character's thoughts. Sometimes the dialogue tends to be emotional without any connection to the context of the story. There are many passages that are a confusing mess of single words and old classical vocabulary.

Hamlet is a Renaissance tragedy written by Shakespeare. The play is very long and has plot twists that keep the reader guessing. Dickens had a special interest in the work. He told his daughter to keep an eye on Hamlet. For Dickens' novels, he sometimes created serial editions, with new chapters released monthly, keeping readers eagerly awaiting the next issue.

Dickens' legacy is undeniable. His works have been translated and used in over 100 countries and are studied by most schoolchildren in the world. It has even been said that Dickens' legacy belongs not to one era but to all times. It is easy to see that Dickens lives on in society and culture through his language and through his enduring influence on education and the media.

Dickens achieved success at a young age. His first novel, The Pickwick Papers, was published when he was only 24 and became a bestseller. His success increased throughout the 1590s. He was honored as a member of the Lord Chamber Men - those lucky enough to perform for the Queen of England on many occasions. Alongside his novels and plays, he also published many poems in his own style.

As Dickens's reputation grew, the question arose whether to preserve his legacy and make it live on. Dickens himself was always keen to make his mark and to maintain his uniqueness. He even attempted to break the dominance of the popular comedies of the time with a series of dramatic plays.

To mark the 400th anniversary of Dickens’ death, there will be a number of events to help readers, and especially students, better understand his works. There will be videos detailing the content of each of his works to help people excitedly explore the pinnacle of language and the meaning his works bring to our daily lives.

question_text: What is the most important thing to help you sleep well?
options: Blocking noise and light is the key
Beds are best for sleeping
Resting sufficiently is necessary
explanation:
Good afternoon. Today I want to clear up some common ideas about sleep, because there is a lot of confusing advice out there. Ask ten people how to sleep better and you will get ten different answers. Some will tell you that the bed itself matters most — that if you buy the right mattress, good sleep will follow automatically. Others simply say that resting enough is necessary, which is true, but it does not tell you how to actually get that rest. And a few people even believe strange tricks, like sleeping fewer hours to make the deep sleep stronger. As a sleep researcher, I can tell you what the evidence really shows: the key to sleeping well is blocking out noise and light. A quiet, dark room sends a clear signal to the brain that it is time to switch off. Compared with that, the brand of your mattress makes only a small difference.
Now let me say something about insomnia, because it is widely misunderstood. Many people assume it is caused only by physical health problems, but that is not correct — stress, worry and daily habits play just as big a role. Others imagine that people with insomnia secretly sleep too much during the day. Also wrong. The really interesting finding is this: people cannot always recognise the symptoms of their own tiredness. They feel restless, so they keep working or scrolling on their phones late at night, without realising how exhausted they already are. Sadly, that reaction makes the problem worse, night after night.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: Blocking noise and light is the key. Bẫy: "beds are best for sleeping" bị hạ cấp ("makes only a small difference"), "resting sufficiently is necessary" được công nhận là đúng nhưng "does not tell you how" — không phải chìa khóa.
2. Đáp án: People can't always recognize the symptoms of tiredness. Bẫy: "caused only by physical health problems" bị phủ định, "sleep too much" bị phủ định ("Also wrong").

question_text: Four people are talking about shopping online. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: My little village has one bus a day and no real shops, so the delivery van has changed my life. Whatever I order appears at my gate within the week — garden tools, birthday presents, even my dog's special food. The driver knows my house so well he waves at my kitchen window. That magic trick of things simply arriving at my door is the whole reason I shop this way.
Speaker B: I refuse to pay full price for anything, and the internet is where the bargains live. Every evening I check three comparison sites the way other people check the news. The same television my brother bought in town cost me eighty pounds less, delivered. Add the voucher codes and the end-of-season sales, and my yearly savings would pay for a small holiday. My motto is simple: whoever pays the shop price simply has not looked.
Speaker C: I manage a restaurant, which means my days off are rare and short. Shopping in town would eat those precious hours — instead I clear my whole list in the taxi between shifts. Groceries ordered at midnight, shoes chosen while the pasta boils. What used to cost me an afternoon now costs minutes squeezed into the gaps of my day. Those saved hours go to my daughter, and no shop window could compete with that.
Speaker D: I collect vinyl records, and no town on earth stocks what I am hunting for. Online, I wander through shops in Tokyo, Berlin and Chicago without leaving my chair — pressings I had only read about, colours and editions I never knew existed. Last month I finally found a Brazilian record I had chased for nine years. When the hunt matters, the endless online catalogue beats every physical shelf in the country.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---

question_text: Auditions are most important for an actor's career.
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
W: Hi Steve. You've directed so many successful films recently. For me, it's the auditions that make the difference — a good audition is what gives you a great cast, and a great cast is what makes a film stay with the audience. Would you agree?
M: Everyone assumes it's the casting stage, or the special effects, or the beautiful photography, but I don't think so. I've never put much faith in auditions. A lot of actors these days believe that their work on screen is proof enough of what they can do, and I tend to agree with them.
W: So how do you get to know an actor, then?
M: I watch their earlier work, and then I ask them to read a scene from the script. That's how I find out whether someone can really become the character or not.
W: What about improvisation? I'd rather let them improvise — that's when you see what an actor is truly capable of. Performing a scene from a script they've just been handed feels a bit forced to me.
M: I don't agree. When the script is strong enough, a great performance emerges by itself. Actors respond to good writing.
W: Anyway, you've worked with actors from the theatre as well, haven't you? Do you think stage actors really do well on film?
M: They have wonderful expressions and a very strong voice — theatrical, you know. But being a great stage actor doesn't mean you'll be a great screen actor. The two are quite different crafts.
W: True. And another thing — I think actors these days get far too little praise from people. Wouldn't you agree?
M: Yes. I think one way to help actors improve is to give them constructive feedback, and people tend to overlook how much recognition matters to them.
W: So we should praise them as much as possible. It's the best way to recognise their effort.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: W-M-B-B.
1. Auditions most important → The woman: "For me, it's the auditions that make the difference... what gives you a great cast". Người đàn ông phản bác: "I've never put much faith in auditions... their work on screen is proof enough".
2. Respond best to strong scripts → The man: "When the script is strong enough, a great performance emerges by itself". Người phụ nữ ngược lại: "I'd rather let them improvise".
3. Theater vs screen different → Both: anh "The two are quite different crafts", cô đồng ý "True".
4. Praised as much as possible → Both: cô mở "far too little praise", anh "Yes... people tend to overlook how much recognition matters", cô chốt "praise them as much as possible".
👉 Mẹo: câu 1 là bẫy "người hỏi Would you agree? ≠ được đồng ý" — nghe câu trả lời "but I don't think so" để loại Both; câu 2 bắt cặp đối lập script vs improvise.

question_text: The internet makes education more accessible
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
W: You went to that open day at the university last weekend, didn't you? What did you make of it?
M: Impressive, on the whole. Though the place has changed enormously since our day.
W: It has. The thing that strikes me most is that the web has thrown the doors wide open — somebody in a tiny village can now follow lectures from a world-class institution without moving an inch.
M: Exactly, I'm completely with you on that. My cousin is doing a degree from her kitchen table in the middle of nowhere, and paying a fraction of what we did.
W: Quite. It's the best thing that's happened to education in decades.
M: Mind you, there's something you simply can't get down a wire. Mixing with other people — the arguments in the corridor, the societies, the late nights — that's the very heart of university life, and it doesn't survive a screen.
W: Hmm, I'm not convinced by that, I must say. I'll accept that the friendships are pleasant enough, but essential? Plenty of people have got their degrees quietly on their own and done perfectly well out of it.
M: You'd have thought differently if you'd lived in halls.
W: Possibly. What does bother me, though, is the menu of subjects these days. Offering students four hundred different modules isn't the blessing everyone claims — a good many of them walk out with a scattered qualification that means very little to an employer.
M: I don't see it that way at all. Choice is precisely what lets somebody stumble on the thing they turn out to be good at. Narrow it down and you just churn out identical graduates.
W: We'll have to differ on that one, clearly.
M: Fair enough. But here's something I do feel strongly about — universities ought to be pushed to compete with one another. A bit of rivalry drives standards up.
W: I'm not so sure about that, to be honest. All it really does is send them chasing league tables instead of actually teaching anybody anything.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: Internet giúp việc học dễ tiếp cận hơn = Both · Giao tiếp xã hội thiết yếu với đời sống đại học = Man · Chương trình quá đa dạng không hẳn là tốt = Woman · Nên khuyến khích cạnh tranh giữa các trường = Man

1. The internet makes education more accessible → Both: người phụ nữ nêu "the web has thrown the doors wide open", người đàn ông tán thành rõ ràng: "Exactly, I'm completely with you on that."

2. Social interactions are essential to university life → Man: người đàn ông nêu "that's the very heart of university life, and it doesn't survive a screen". Người phụ nữ phản đối: "Hmm, I'm not convinced by that, I must say."

3. A diverse curriculum is not always a good thing → Woman: người phụ nữ nêu "Offering students four hundred different modules isn't the blessing everyone claims". Người đàn ông phản đối: "I don't see it that way at all."

4. Competitions between universities should be encouraged → Man: người đàn ông nêu "universities ought to be pushed to compete with one another". Người phụ nữ phản đối: "I'm not so sure about that, to be honest."

👉 Mẹo: Bẫy nằm ở ý 2 — người phụ nữ nói "I'll accept that the friendships are pleasant enough" nghe như đồng ý, nhưng câu hỏi ngược "but essential?" mới là quan điểm thật của cô ấy, nên đáp án là Man chứ không phải Both.

question_text: Four people are talking about doing exercise. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: I started going to the gym for one reason only: my job. I sit in meetings all day, and by three o'clock my brain used to switch off completely. Since I began training at lunchtime, the afternoons feel like mornings. I close deals better, I write faster, and my manager has actually commented on it. Fitness for its own sake never tempted me — but as a tool for doing my work better, exercise has become the most useful hour of my day.
Speaker B: I keep at it because I know it is good for me, but I will be honest about how it feels: every session empties the tank completely. Twenty minutes in, my legs turn to stone and the clock stops moving. Afterwards I need the whole evening on the sofa just to become a person again. My sporty friends promise it gets easier with time. Three years in, I am still waiting for that famous lightness they talk about.
Speaker C: What keeps me coming back is the crowd. Tuesday badminton with my colleagues, Sunday football with the cousins — half the time we laugh more than we play. Alone on a treadmill I last ten minutes and give up, but put four friends around me and two hours vanish like nothing. The sport is really just the excuse; the jokes, the teasing and the noisy dinner afterwards are the real workout.
Speaker D: Let me say what everyone thinks and nobody admits: I cannot stand any of it. The sweating, the counting, the machines — all of it. My family drags me out for a game occasionally and I spend the whole time planning my escape. People promise I will learn to love it. I am fifty-two; I know what I love, and it is a good book in a comfortable chair.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A = Improve work performance (PARAPHRASE: "I close deals better... the most useful hour" — hiệu quả công việc). B = Find exercise tiring (PARAPHRASE: "empties the tank... legs turn to stone" — không có chữ tiring). C = Have fun exercising with others (keyword "friends... laugh more than we play"). D = Hate exercising (keyword "I cannot stand any of it"). Nhiễu: alone, lose weight.

M: And I'd put a lot of that down to social media. I think it has completely rewritten the way politics actually works these days.

W: That seems a bit harsh on people, doesn't it?
M: Perhaps it is, yes. Anyway, one thing I'm genuinely pleased about is how many more women are standing for office these days.
W: Yes, I agree with you on that one. The last council election here had more women candidates than men, which nobody expected.
M: Long overdue, if you ask me.

question_text: Four people are talking about doing arts. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: Wednesday evening is the highlight of my week: eight of us meet above the bakery with our easels, paint for two hours, then argue about whose sunset is worse over tea and biscuits. Half of us have no talent whatsoever, and it truly does not matter. I joined to meet people after moving to this town, and the painting turned out to be the easiest doorway into friendship I have ever found. We are planning a little group show in the spring.
Speaker B: Every Sunday morning my kitchen table disappears under glue, glitter and coloured card, because that is craft time with my two little ones. We make lopsided animals, potato-print wrapping paper, birthday cards for the grandparents. The floor suffers terribly. But watching a five-year-old concentrate on her wobbly giraffe is worth any mess, and the fridge door has become our family gallery. It is our time together, away from every screen in the house.
Speaker C: People assume drawing is my hobby, but it is actually how I pay my rent. I illustrate children's books for two publishers, so from nine to five I am sketching dragons and checking colour proofs against deadlines. When your passion becomes your profession, it changes — some days the pencil feels heavy, like any tool. Still, I remind myself that plenty of people would trade their desk for mine, deadlines and all.
Speaker D: My painting happens behind a closed door, and that is exactly how I like it. Sunday afternoons, the flat empty, the phone off — just me, the brushes and the radio. Nobody sees the results; most canvases end up stacked in the wardrobe. Friends keep telling me to join a class or share pictures online, and I always refuse. The whole point is that no one is watching. It is the only truly private hour I own.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A = social activity (PARAPHRASE: "easiest doorway into friendship... meet people"). B = with children (keyword "craft time with my two little ones"). C = part of the job (PARAPHRASE: "how I pay my rent... profession... deadlines"). D = alone (keyword "behind a closed door... no one is watching"). Nhiễu: online classes, competitions.

question_text: Exhibitions should be different and diverse
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
M: I called in at the cultural centre on Saturday — it's the third show about the same pottery collection this year.
W: That's precisely my complaint about the place. What it badly needs is far more variety: a different subject every month, different communities, photography one week and textiles the next.
M: Hmm, I don't agree with you there, honestly. A small centre does far better going deep into one thing. Chopping and changing every few weeks would only baffle the regulars.
W: Baffle them? It would bring new faces through the door, which is rather the point.
M: We'll have to differ on that. What did strike me, though, is how little the old customs seem to mean to anyone now. They're quietly draining away — people go through the motions without the faintest idea why.
W: Yes, exactly, I'd say the very same. My grandmother could talk you through every stage of the harvest supper. Ask anybody under thirty and you get a blank look.
M: Which is why I'd go further, actually. Give it twenty years and the local festivals will have vanished completely. Gone, the lot of them.
W: Now hang on, I can't go along with that. Smaller crowds, yes, I'll accept that entirely. But disappearing altogether? No — they change shape and carry on. The village parade has been dying since my mother was a girl.
M: We'll see. My money's on the last one being somewhere around 2045.
W: You're such a pessimist.
M: Realistic. Anyway, the genuine answer to all this is schools. That's where the next generation is really formed, so if children are taught it properly at eleven, the whole thing survives.
W: I'm not convinced, to be honest. Schools are stretched to breaking point as it is, and children pick that sort of thing up at home, from their own families, not from a timetabled lesson.
M: Plenty of families pass nothing on at all these days, though.
W: Then that's where the centre should be putting its effort, not in a classroom.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: Triển lãm nên đa dạng = Woman · Phong tục truyền thống đang mất dần ý nghĩa = Both · Lễ hội địa phương sẽ biến mất = Man · Trường học quan trọng trong việc hình thành thế hệ sau = Man

1. Exhibitions should be different and diverse → Woman: người phụ nữ nêu "What it badly needs is far more variety: a different subject every month, different communities, photography one week and textiles the next." Người đàn ông phản đối: "Hmm, I don't agree with you there, honestly. A small centre does far better going deep into one thing."

2. Traditional customs are gradually losing their significance → Both: người đàn ông nêu "how little the old customs seem to mean to anyone now. They're quietly draining away", người phụ nữ tán thành rõ ràng: "Yes, exactly, I'd say the very same."

3. Local festivals will disappear in the near future → Man: người đàn ông nêu "Give it twenty years and the local festivals will have vanished completely. Gone, the lot of them." Người phụ nữ phản đối: "Now hang on, I can't go along with that... But disappearing altogether? No — they change shape and carry on."

4. Schools are important in shaping future generations → Man: người đàn ông nêu "the genuine answer to all this is schools. That's where the next generation is really formed, so if children are taught it properly at eleven, the whole thing survives." Người phụ nữ phản đối: "I'm not convinced, to be honest... children pick that sort of thing up at home, from their own families, not from a timetabled lesson."

👉 Mẹo: Bẫy chính ở ý 3 — người phụ nữ nhượng bộ "Smaller crowds, yes, I'll accept that entirely" rồi bác bỏ chính điều cần chọn (lễ hội biến mất), nên đáp án là Man chứ không phải Both.

question_text: What does the announcer say about the new novel?
options: It is different from his earlier works
It is romantic and soft
It is less famous than his earlier works
explanation:
Good evening, everyone. Tonight I want to talk about the latest novel by the popular author James Parker. Most of you know him for his soft, romantic stories, and before this book came out, some people even worried that a new direction would make him less famous than before. A few magazines predicted that his loyal readers would simply stop buying. Well, the opposite has happened. The new novel, Shadow in the Night, is completely different from his earlier works, and readers seem to love it for exactly that reason. Instead of gentle love stories, Parker gives us a dark mystery full of secrets and surprising turns. The mood is tense from the first chapter, and several reviewers have said they could not put the book down. Sales in the first month were actually higher than for any of his romantic titles, so the fear that this book would damage his name has disappeared completely.
Of course, the big question now is what Parker should do next. Some fans are begging him to continue with this new style of dark, exciting stories. Others, especially his older readers, hope he will go back to the romantic writing that made him famous in the first place. In my view, neither group should decide for him. What Parker really needs to do is listen carefully to what the critics are saying before he starts his next book. Their reviews point out real weaknesses as well as strengths, and a writer who takes that advice seriously will find the right balance and grow with every book he writes.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It is different from his earlier works — "completely different from his earlier works". Bẫy: "romantic and soft" là phong cách CŨ; "less famous" chỉ là lo ngại ban đầu và đã bị bác bỏ (doanh số cao hơn).
2. Đáp án: He should listen to critics before writing his next work. Bẫy: "continue this genre" là mong muốn của fan mới, "go back to his original genre" là mong muốn của độc giả cũ — người nói gạt cả hai và chốt nên nghe giới phê bình.

question_text: There is too much information on the Internet
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
W: So, how did you get on with that research project you were doing online?
M: Honestly, it nearly finished me off. The real problem is that there's simply far more material out there than any one person could ever get through in a lifetime.
W: I'm not so sure about that, actually. I'd say the sheer volume isn't the issue at all. A big library has more than you could read too, and nobody ever complains about that.
M: Fair enough, but a library has been sorted out for you by somebody. Anyway, what I will say is that digging out anything reliable online is a proper skill in itself.
W: Oh, absolutely, I agree with you there. Knowing which search terms to try, and how to spot a dodgy source, is something you genuinely have to be taught.
M: Exactly. My younger cousin just clicks the very first link and believes every word of it.
W: Well, that brings me to something I've been chewing over. I reckon being online all day is actually changing how our brains work, the way we reason things through.
M: Hmm, I don't see it that way. I'll accept that our habits have shifted, of course. But our actual thinking? No, I'd say that's much the same as it's always been.
W: You say that, but I notice it in myself. I can't sit with a long article any more.
M: Maybe you're just tired. What I would definitely sign up to, though, is that teenagers these days simply can't wait for anything at all.
W: Now that I do agree with, completely. Anything that takes more than three seconds to load and they've given up entirely and moved on.
M: Same with films. My nephew watches everything on double speed, which I find slightly horrifying.
W: Guilty as charged, to be honest. I've started doing exactly that myself.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: Quá nhiều thông tin trên Internet = Man · Tìm thông tin cần kỹ năng = Both · Internet ảnh hưởng cách ta tư duy = Woman · Internet khiến giới trẻ thiếu kiên nhẫn = Both

1. There is too much information on the Internet → Man: người đàn ông nêu rõ "The real problem is that there's simply far more material out there than any one person could ever get through in a lifetime." Người phụ nữ phản đối thẳng: "I'm not so sure about that, actually. I'd say the sheer volume isn't the issue at all."

2. Finding information on the Internet requires skills → Both: người đàn ông nói "digging out anything reliable online is a proper skill in itself", người phụ nữ tán thành rõ ràng: "Oh, absolutely, I agree with you there... is something you genuinely have to be taught."

3. The use of the Internet affects the way we think. → Woman: người phụ nữ nêu "I reckon being online all day is actually changing how our brains work, the way we reason things through." Người đàn ông phản đối: "Hmm, I don't see it that way... our actual thinking? No, I'd say that's much the same as it's always been."

4. The Internet makes young people less patient. → Both: người đàn ông nêu "teenagers these days simply can't wait for anything at all", người phụ nữ đồng ý: "Now that I do agree with, completely."

👉 Mẹo: Bẫy nằm ở ý 3 — người đàn ông nói "I'll accept that our habits have shifted" nghe như đồng ý, nhưng ngay sau đó bác bỏ đúng phần cốt lõi (cách tư duy), nên đáp án là Woman chứ không phải Both.

question_text: A man is talking to a friend about his family. What is his main problem?
options: Persuading his family
Finding a job abroad
Saving money for the move
explanation:
My move abroad is nearly sorted, and honestly, the practical side went smoothly. The job? Signed the contract last month — a good position in Toronto with a company that even pays my flights. Money is fine too; I've been saving for two years and the moving costs are covered. No, my headache is at home: my parents. Every dinner turns into a debate, my mother cries, my father goes silent. Convincing my family this is right — that is the mountain I still have to climb.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – Persuading his family.
• Vì sao đúng: "my headache is at home: my parents... Convincing my family this is right — that is the mountain I still have to climb".
• Finding a job abroad sai: đã ký hợp đồng từ tháng trước ("The job? Signed the contract last month — a good position in Toronto").
• Saving money for the move sai: tiền đã đủ, chi phí chuyển nhà được lo ("I've been saving for two years and the moving costs are covered").
👉 Mẹo: câu hỏi "main problem" — hai phương án nhiễu luôn được nói với nghĩa "đã xong" (signed, covered, sorted). Vấn đề thật đi kèm ẩn dụ khó khăn: my headache, the mountain to climb.

question_text: A woman is talking about her school days. What was the woman good at?
options: Swimming
Football
Running
explanation:
People always assume I was the sporty type at school, and they are half right. Swimming lessons were my weekly nightmare — I sank like a stone and the teacher gave up on me. Running was worse; I was always last in every race, red-faced and furious. But put a ball at my feet and everything changed. I played football for the school team five years straight, captain for the last two. The boys stopped laughing very quickly.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – Plays football.
• Vì sao đúng: "I played football for the school team five years straight, captain for the last two" — thành tích cụ thể, rõ ràng.
• Swimming sai: cô bơi rất tệ, giáo viên bỏ cuộc ("Swimming lessons were my weekly nightmare — I sank like a stone and the teacher gave up on me").
• Running sai: còn tệ hơn, cô luôn về chót ("Running was worse; I was always last in every race").
👉 Mẹo: câu hỏi "good at" — bắt các từ đánh giá: nightmare, worse, always last = kém; team, captain, top scorer = giỏi. Không cần hiểu hết câu vẫn chọn đúng.

question_text: Housing space is more important than farming space.
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
M: Did you see they're turning that empty car park behind the station into allotments?
W: I did, and honestly I think it's the wrong call. In a city as crowded as this one, a plot of land like that ought to go to flats long before it ever goes to vegetables. Housing has to come first.
M: I'm not so sure about that, actually. We've concreted over every green patch for thirty years now and rents are still absurd. Another block on that site wouldn't fix a thing.
W: It would put a roof over forty families, though.
M: Possibly. For me, though, the whole notion of growing food in the middle of a city is tremendously attractive — rooftops full of beans and tomatoes. I find the idea genuinely lovely.
W: Hmm, I don't share your enthusiasm, I'm afraid. It photographs beautifully, but close up it's mud, torn netting and slugs. I simply can't get excited about it.
M: Each to their own, I suppose. There's a practical side too: this city doesn't come close to producing what it eats. We need a great deal more food than we're growing.
W: I'd question that one. I'll accept the import figures, of course, but the shops are stuffed and half of what's on the shelves gets binned at closing time. That isn't a shortage — it's appalling distribution.
M: Well, waste is a separate argument, I'd say.
W: It's the same argument, really.
M: Anyway, the part I don't think anybody could object to is the money side of it. All those small growers, the tool shops, the market stalls — it would put a real lift under the local economy.
W: Yes, I agree with you there completely. Proper work for people who've been out of it for ages, and the money stays in the neighbourhood instead of going off to some warehouse two hundred miles away.
M: Exactly. That's the bit the council ought to be shouting about.
W: They'd rather put up a sign about biodiversity and leave it at that.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: Đất ở quan trọng hơn đất trồng = Woman · Nông nghiệp đô thị hấp dẫn = Man · Thành phố cần thêm lương thực = Man · Nông nghiệp đô thị có lợi cho kinh tế = Both

1. Housing space is more important than farming space. → Woman: người phụ nữ nêu "a plot of land like that ought to go to flats long before it ever goes to vegetables. Housing has to come first." Người đàn ông phản đối: "I'm not so sure about that, actually... Another block on that site wouldn't fix a thing."

2. Urban farming is appealing. → Man: người đàn ông nêu "the whole notion of growing food in the middle of a city is tremendously attractive... I find the idea genuinely lovely." Người phụ nữ phản đối: "Hmm, I don't share your enthusiasm, I'm afraid... I simply can't get excited about it."

3. Cities need more food. → Man: người đàn ông nêu "this city doesn't come close to producing what it eats. We need a great deal more food than we're growing." Người phụ nữ phản đối: "I'd question that one. I'll accept the import figures, of course, but... That isn't a shortage — it's appalling distribution."

4. Urban farming will benefit the urban economy. → Both: người đàn ông nêu "it would put a real lift under the local economy", người phụ nữ tán thành: "Yes, I agree with you there completely."

👉 Mẹo: Bẫy chính ở ý 3 — người phụ nữ nói "I'll accept the import figures, of course" nghe như đồng tình, nhưng cô phủ nhận đúng kết luận (thiếu lương thực), nên đáp án là Man chứ không phải Both.

question_text: A student is talking about housing. Where does he live now?
options: In a small village
In an apartment
In a town hall
explanation:
People ask how I'm settling in since starting university, and my answer always gets a laugh. I grew up in a small village — two shops and a church — but that's long behind me now. When I arrived, I hunted for an apartment near campus, and the waiting lists were two years deep, completely hopeless. Then came the surprise: the council had converted the old town hall into student rooms! So now I live in a town hall — chandelier on the ceiling, balcony over the square. Best address I'll ever have!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – In a town hall.
• Vì sao đúng: "the council had converted the old town hall into student rooms! So now I live in a town hall — chandelier on the ceiling, balcony over the square".
• In a small village sai: đó là nơi cậu LỚN LÊN, đã là quá khứ ("I grew up in a small village — two shops and a church — but that's long behind me now").
• In an apartment sai: cậu có tìm nhưng danh sách chờ dài hai năm, hoàn toàn vô vọng ("the waiting lists were two years deep, completely hopeless").
👉 Mẹo: câu hỏi "where does he live NOW" — loại nơi đi kèm "I grew up / that's behind me" và nơi chỉ là ý định thất bại ("I hunted for... hopeless").

question_text: What is the importance of advertising?
options: It increases the product price
It can help reach new customers
It can build brand recognition
explanation:
Let me say a few words about advertising, because many business owners still see it as an expense rather than an opportunity. First, let me deal with a common worry. Some companies fear that spending on advertising will force them to increase the product price, and in a badly-run campaign that can happen. But a well-planned campaign usually pays for itself many times over. People also like to say that advertising is mainly about building brand recognition — making sure customers remember your name and your logo. Recognition is pleasant, certainly, but a name that people remember and never buy from is worth very little. In my view, the real importance of advertising is simpler and more practical: it helps a business reach new customers. A good campaign travels far beyond your existing audience and puts your product in front of people who had never heard of you last month. That is where real growth comes from, and that is why even successful companies keep advertising.
Now, a word of warning about sports sponsorship, because it is not as safe as it looks. Companies usually hope their sponsorship will attract more fans to the sport, and they dream of boosting ticket sales and sales of shirts and equipment. Sometimes that happens. But think about what happens when things go wrong. If a tournament is hit by cheating or bad behaviour, the heavy advertising around it means the story spreads everywhere, and the sponsorship can generate negative publicity for the sport itself. Both the company and the sport can walk away damaged. So sponsor carefully, and always have a plan for bad news.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It can help reach new customers. Bẫy: "increases the product price" chỉ là lo ngại ("in a badly-run campaign"), "build brand recognition" bị hạ cấp ("worth very little" nếu không ai mua).
2. Đáp án: They can generate negative publicity for the sport. Bẫy: "attract more fans" và "boost ticket sales" đều là kỳ vọng ("hope", "dream"), còn cảnh báo thật nằm sau "But think about what happens when things go wrong".

question_text: Four people are talking about online shopping. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: Between two jobs and three children, my week has no spare hours in it. A trip to the shopping centre used to swallow an entire Saturday morning — the drive, the parking, the queues at every till. Now I do the same list from my phone during my lunch break, in eleven minutes flat. Those rescued Saturday mornings belong to the playground now. For a person whose diary is full, that change is worth more than any discount.
Speaker B: I am the one in my family who compares everything, and the numbers always tell the same story. The jacket in the high-street window costs a third more than the identical one on my screen, and with the discount codes my daughter finds me, the gap grows even wider. Last month I furnished half the kitchen for what one shop wanted for the oven alone. My friends laugh at my spreadsheet — until they see my receipts.
Speaker C: My building has no lift and my knees are past their best, so what won me over is simple: everything arrives at my door. The rice, the washing powder, even the new armchair — a nice young man carries it up the stairs, and I sign with a smile. My daughter set the whole thing up for me two years ago. I have not dragged a heavy bag up those four floors since, and I do not miss it at all.
Speaker D: I live in a small town with exactly two clothes shops, and both stock the same five brands. Online, the shelf is endless — colours, sizes, styles, brands from countries I could not place on a map. Last week I found the exact model of running shoe my podiatrist recommended, in my width. The lady in our local shop just laughed and said she had never heard of it. That endless variety is what keeps me clicking.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A = It saves time (PARAPHRASE: "eleven minutes flat... rescued Saturday mornings"). B = It is cheaper (PARAPHRASE: "costs a third more in the window... see my receipts"). C = Products are delivered (keyword "everything arrives at my door"). D = There are more choices (keyword "the shelf is endless... endless variety"). Nhiễu: easy to return, safer to pay online.

question_text: A person calls a friend about his new car. How much does the small car cost him?
options: 3250 pounds
3550 pounds
4250 pounds
explanation:
Hi Mark, it's me. I finally went to the car dealer this morning, and yes, I had to choose between the two models again. The bigger one is beautiful, but they want four thousand two hundred and fifty for it — more than I can manage. The salesman started the small one at three thousand five hundred and fifty, we talked for a while, and in the end it costs me three thousand two hundred and fifty. I pick it up on Friday!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – 3250 pounds.
• Vì sao đúng: "in the end it costs me three thousand two hundred and fifty" — cụm "in the end" báo hiệu đây là giá CHỐT sau khi mặc cả.
• 3550 pounds sai: đó là giá người bán CHÀO ban đầu cho xe nhỏ ("The salesman started the small one at three thousand five hundred and fifty").
• 4250 pounds sai: đó là giá của xe TO, đã bị loại vì quá khả năng ("they want four thousand two hundred and fifty for it — more than I can manage").
👉 Mẹo: câu hỏi giá tiền luôn thả đủ 3 con số. Khoanh số đi sau "in the end / finally / we agreed on", gạch số đi sau "started at / they want / originally".

question_text: Four people are talking about protecting the environment. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: In our house the war is against the meter on the wall. Lights off the second a room empties, the washing machine only runs full, and we swapped every bulb for the efficient kind. My son even unplugs the chargers at night because, he says, they drink secretly in the dark. Our bills have almost halved, and I like to think the power station burns a little less because of our small savings.
Speaker B: I made one big decision last spring: the car stays in the garage on weekdays. I take the number forty-two to the office instead, rain or shine. It adds fifteen minutes each way, and I read on the top deck, so honestly I have gained time rather than lost it. One less engine crawling through the morning jam — that is my contribution, and my head arrives at work calmer too.
Speaker C: Mine will sound lazy, but hear me out: I do almost all my buying from the sofa. One delivery van serving my whole street replaces forty separate trips to the shopping centre — forty engines, forty parking circles. I group my orders so everything comes in one box, once a week. My neighbour teases me about it, but I think my armchair habit is greener than her Saturday drive to the mall.
Speaker D: My obsession is the tap. Short showers with a timer, a bowl in the sink for washing vegetables, and that bowl then feeds the garden. I fixed the dripping bathroom tap the day I read how many litres it wastes in a year — the number shocked me. My children think I am strict about it, and I am. Clean water is the thing we will miss first, so every drop I keep matters.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A = using less electricity (PARAPHRASE: "war against the meter... lights off... bills halved"). B = not driving to work (PARAPHRASE: "the car stays in the garage on weekdays... number forty-two to the office"). C = shopping online (keyword "buying from the sofa... orders... one box"). D = using less water (keyword "tap... short showers... every drop"). Nhiễu: cycling, recycling bottles.

question_text: What does the writer believe helps her the most in her writing process?
options: Writing every day for 15-20 minutes
Create dedicated periods for writing
Finding a quiet space to work
explanation:
Hi everyone. People often ask me how I finished my new book, so today I want to share what I learned about the writing process — and about writer's block. When you read advice for writers, two suggestions come up again and again. The first is to write every single day, even if only for fifteen or twenty minutes. The second is to find a completely quiet space where nobody can disturb you. I tried both, honestly, and neither worked well for me. Writing for twenty minutes a day left me stopping just when the ideas started to flow, and the silent room made me sleepy rather than creative. What truly helps me the most is creating dedicated periods for writing — long, planned blocks of time that fit my own rhythm. I write best in the late morning, so I protect those three hours and let nothing interrupt them. Once I organised my week this way, my writing moved forward steadily.
But I also want to be honest about my biggest mistake. In the middle of the book, I got completely stuck for almost two months. I had a clear plan for the story, and I never ignored the feedback my editor sent me — those were not the problem. The problem was pride. I refused to ask other people for advice. I thought a real writer should solve everything alone, and that is the thing I regret most. When I finally called two writer friends, their questions unlocked the story in a single afternoon. So please, if you get stuck, do not wait as long as I did.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: Create dedicated periods for writing. Bẫy: "viết 15-20 phút mỗi ngày" và "tìm chỗ yên tĩnh" đều được nhắc rồi bị loại ("neither worked well for me").
2. Đáp án: Refuse to seek advice of others — điều cô ấy hối tiếc. Bẫy: "ignoring feedback from editors" bị phủ định ("never ignored"), "writing without a plan" bị phủ định ("had a clear plan").
