question_text: Adjusting the pace of lessons may help children learn more efficiently
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
W: My cousin has taken both her children out of school and is teaching them at home now.
M: Has she really? And what do you make of that?
W: Well, I've come round to it, actually. The big thing for me is speed. If a child races through maths and crawls through reading, you can simply adjust. Slow down here, speed up there. They cover far more ground that way.
M: I'm not so sure it works like that in practice. One parent, two children, no training. I think you end up moving at the pace of whoever complains loudest. It looks neat on paper and falls apart by Wednesday.
W: Hmm. Maybe with two.
M: What bothers me most, though, is the other children. They join a club on a Thursday and everyone decides that's enough. It isn't remotely the same as seeing the same faces every single morning.
W: No, I agree with you entirely there. A once-a-week meet-up doesn't replace a room full of people you can't escape from. That's where you learn to rub along with someone you don't much like.
M: Exactly. You can't timetable that.
W: You can't.
M: Mind you, for some families it genuinely is the better option. If a child is a competitive swimmer, or the family moves every eight months, or the child is simply miserable by nine in the morning, then a fixed timetable just doesn't fit their life.
W: I'd push back on that, actually. That's precisely when a child needs the routine most. Pulling them out only makes their world smaller.
M: Fair enough, though I'd still say it.
W: For me it comes down to one thing. Can the parents actually do the job? Have they got the subject knowledge, the patience, the hours? If they have, marvellous. If not, it's a slow disaster.
M: I'll accept that some parents manage it brilliantly, but I don't think that's the deciding factor at all.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: Điều chỉnh tốc độ bài học giúp học hiệu quả hơn = Woman · Hoạt động nhóm thỉnh thoảng không thay thế được tiếp xúc thường xuyên với bạn học = Both · Học tại nhà có lợi cho trẻ khó theo thời khoá biểu cố định = Man · Thành công của homeschooling phụ thuộc vào khả năng dạy và hỗ trợ của gia đình = Woman
1. Adjusting the pace of lessons may help children learn more efficiently → Woman: Nữ nêu "If a child races through maths and crawls through reading, you can simply adjust." Nam phản đối: "I'm not so sure it works like that in practice."
2. Occasional group activities may not completely replace regular contact with classmates → Both: Nam nêu "They join a club on a Thursday and everyone decides that's enough. It isn't remotely the same as seeing the same faces every single morning." Nữ tán thành: "No, I agree with you entirely there."
3. Home education can benefit children whose circumstances make a fixed school timetable difficult → Man: Nam nêu "for some families it genuinely is the better option". Nữ phản đối: "I'd push back on that, actually. That's precisely when a child needs the routine most."
4. The success of homeschooling depends on whether a family can provide suitable teaching and support → Woman: Nữ nêu "Can the parents actually do the job? Have they got the subject knowledge, the patience, the hours?" Nam phản đối: "I'll accept that some parents manage it brilliantly, but I don't think that's the deciding factor at all."
👉 Mẹo: Câu cuối của nam bắt đầu bằng lời khen ("I'll accept that some parents manage it brilliantly") nhưng vế "but" mới là quan điểm thật — đáp án là Woman, không phải Both.

question_text: What should students do when choosing a career?
options: Choose the same career as their friends
Be flexible and open minded
Focus only on the salary offered
explanation:
As a careers adviser, I meet hundreds of final-year students every spring, and the same two traps catch them every time. The first trap is friendship. Whole groups walk into my office planning to apply for identical jobs at identical companies, because choosing the same career as your friends feels less frightening than deciding alone. The second trap is the salary line in the job advert — students ranking their futures purely by starting pay, as if nothing else about a job existed. Both paths lead to the same place: sitting at a desk, three years later, wondering whose life you are living. What I ask of every student instead is to be flexible and open-minded. Interview widely, say yes to industries you never considered, treat the first job as one step in a forty-year journey. Careers reward curiosity far more often than they reward certainty.
About the application process itself, let me clear away some nonsense circulating online. One post claims companies now prefer handwritten applications for the personal touch — complete fiction; everything is digital and has been for years. Another insists most jobs no longer require qualifications — also wrong; your degree remains the ticket to the interview room. What genuinely deserves your attention is this: the market grows more competitive every single year. Where ten graduates once applied for a role, a hundred apply today. So collect skills, gather real experience, polish the story only you can tell — because the candidates beside you are doing exactly that, right now.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant thứ 3 của Life after university — khác lời Đề 07 và Đề 24.)
1. Đáp án: Be flexible and open minded. Bẫy: "same career as friends" và "focus only on salary" là hai "trap".
2. Đáp án: They are becoming more competitive. Bẫy: "handwritten applications" ("complete fiction") và "no longer require qualifications" ("also wrong").

question_text: What does the speaker say mostly affects concentration?
options: Concentration is primarily influenced by individual effort.
Concentration depends mostly on environment.
Concentration depends mainly on external distractions.
explanation:
As a study skills coach, the complaint I hear most from students is: I cannot concentrate. And almost every student arrives with the same two theories about why. The first theory blames themselves — concentration is a matter of individual effort, and they are simply not trying hard enough. The second theory blames the world — external distractions like phones and noisy flatmates make focus impossible. Both theories feel true, and both point in the wrong direction. What the psychology research keeps showing is that concentration depends mostly on your environment. Change the room and you change the mind. A clear desk, steady lighting, a consistent place used only for study — these quiet factors extend your attention far more reliably than gritting your teeth ever will. My first assignment for every student is never about willpower. It is about redesigning the corner of the room where they work.
The second thing I teach is harder to accept: attention runs out. Some students proudly tell me they excel at managing the limits of their concentration, and others insist they can always recognise the moment their focus fades. Testing shows almost nobody actually can. The truth is that people often fail to consider the limits of concentration at all. Focus is a resource that drains silently, like a phone battery with no percentage on the screen. You keep pushing, quality quietly collapses, and you blame the difficulty of the material. Learn to take real breaks before you think you need them — that is where good grades hide.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 13 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: Concentration depends mostly on environment. Bẫy: "individual effort" và "external distractions" là hai "theory" đều "point in the wrong direction".
2. Đáp án: People often fail to consider the limits of concentration. Bẫy: "excel at managing" và "always recognise" bị bác ("Testing shows almost nobody actually can").

question_text: What is the most important thing to help you sleep well?
options: Blocking noise and light is the key
Beds are best for sleeping
Resting sufficiently is necessary
explanation:
Let me begin this health talk with the question I am asked most: what is the single most important thing for a good night's sleep? People arrive with strong opinions. The furniture believers insist the bed is everything — invest in the perfect mattress and sleep will follow by itself. The common-sense camp simply says that resting enough is necessary, which is true but circular: telling a poor sleeper to rest more is like telling a poor swimmer to drown less. What the research actually crowns as most important is neither of these. It is blocking out noise and light. The sleeping brain monitors its surroundings all night, and every beam of light or burst of sound pulls it briefly toward waking. Seal the curtains, silence the notifications, and even an average mattress will serve you well. Comfort helps — darkness and quiet decide.
On insomnia, allow me to correct the record as well. It is not a condition caused only by physical health problems; anxiety, habits and irregular schedules cause at least as many sleepless nights as any illness. And the strange belief that insomniacs secretly sleep too much during the day is simply false — most get less rest in total, not more. What deserves everyone's attention is a quieter discovery: people cannot always recognise the symptoms of their own tiredness. The exhausted brain misreads its fatigue as restlessness, reaches for one more episode, one more scroll — and buries itself deeper in the very problem it cannot feel.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant thứ 4 của Sleep — options bộ Đề 03: Beds / Resting sufficiently.)
1. Đáp án: Blocking noise and light is the key. Bẫy: "beds are best" và "resting sufficiently is necessary" đều được nhắc rồi hạ ("neither of these").
2. Đáp án: People can't always recognize the symptoms of tiredness. Bẫy: "only physical health problems" và "sleep too much" đều bị bác.

question_text: What is one of the strong qualities of these modern works?
options: Focus exclusively on historical events and figures
Strictly adhere to classical artistic conventions
Have something to say about modern society
explanation:
Welcome to our contemporary art review. The new wave of artists on display this season has divided opinion sharply, so let me offer some perspective. Traditionalists complain loudly. They want art that focuses exclusively on historical events and figures, preserving our shared heritage on every canvas. They also wish younger painters would strictly follow the classical conventions — correct proportions, familiar techniques, respectful subjects. These new works do neither, and that is precisely their strength: they have something to say about modern society. Walk through the gallery and you will see paintings about loneliness in crowded cities, screens that glow brighter than faces, jobs that disappear overnight. Whether you love or hate these pieces, they are talking about the world you actually live in — and art that speaks to its own time has always been the art that survives it.
A word of preparation before you visit: do not expect these works to explain themselves. Some visitors assume the core message will be stated clearly in the opening room, like a headline. Others hope for direct, simplified moral lessons — pollution bad, kindness good. You will find neither. The meanings in these works are not easily identified, and the artists intend it that way. A canvas may look like an ordinary kitchen until you notice the missing chair; a sculpture may seem playful until the shadow it casts changes your mind. Bring patience, look twice, argue with your companions afterwards. The confusion is not a failure of the art. It is the invitation.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: Have something to say about modern society. Bẫy: "historical events" và "classical conventions" là mong muốn của traditionalists — "These new works do neither".
2. Đáp án: The meanings are not easily identified. Bẫy: "stated in the opening" và "direct moral lessons" — "You will find neither".

question_text: Four people are talking about visiting a new museum. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: I will be honest: museums are my wife's love, not mine, and Saturday was her birthday choice. I walked the halls at a polite pace, admired what required admiring, and was back at the entrance café within fifty minutes while she was still in the second room. The building is impressive, I suppose. But my legs were done, my interest was done, and the cake selection downstairs deserved serious attention.
Speaker B: My visit turned into an accidental adventure — the place is a labyrinth. I followed the arrows to the Egyptian rooms and somehow surfaced among medieval armour, twice. The floor plan they hand out disagrees with the actual corridors, I swear. A kind guard finally walked me to the exhibition I had actually come for, one hour late. Beautiful collections, genuinely — but next time I am bringing breadcrumbs to drop behind me.
Speaker C: What won me over completely were the screens. Point your phone at any exhibit and the app resurrects it — the broken temple rebuilds itself in front of you, the faded painting recovers its colours, and a soft voice tells the story at your own pace. My favourite was the interactive table where you could virtually unwrap a mummy, layer by layer. The objects are ancient; the experience is anything but. This is how history should be shown.
Speaker D: One afternoon was criminal shortness for that collection — I saw perhaps a third before the closing bell chased us out. I have already booked the first Saturday of next month, and this time I am starting on the top floor where I never arrived. The membership card is under consideration too, since three visits pay for it. Places like that are not visits; they are relationships, and mine has only just begun.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A = Finished the visit quickly (PARAPHRASE: "back at the entrance café within fifty minutes"). B = Got lost during the visit (PARAPHRASE: "labyrinth... surfaced among medieval armour... walked me to the exhibition"). C = Enjoyed the use of technology (keyword-lite "screens... app... interactive table"). D = Wants to visit again (PARAPHRASE: "already booked the first Saturday of next month"). Nhiễu: souvenirs, ticket price.

question_text: What is the strength of the book?
options: It is a very short story.
It has a good description of a specific period of time.
It focuses only on famous people.
explanation:
On this week's book club podcast: the biography that everyone seems to be reading on the train. Let me begin by correcting two things people say about it without having opened it. It is not a very short story — my edition is well over five hundred pages, and none of them feel wasted. And it certainly does not focus only on famous people; some of the most moving chapters follow the subject's childhood neighbours and a schoolteacher history had completely forgotten. The book's real strength is its description of a specific period of time. The author reconstructs the whole era in loving detail: what a loaf of bread cost, what songs played from the radios, what fears kept ordinary families awake at night. You come away knowing not just one life, but the entire world that life was lived in — and that is a rarer achievement than it sounds.
The critics have been busy with this book too, and their verdict is worth hearing. Early reviews worried it might be too difficult to understand, with its jumps in time and shifting narrators. One sceptic even suggested the vivid scenes must contain fictional details. Read the endnotes and both worries dissolve — the prose is clear, and every scene is anchored to letters, diaries or interviews. What the critics have settled on instead is a single word: unconventional. This is an unconventional biography, one that breaks the genre's polite rules on nearly every page. And in a year of safe, forgettable biographies, that is precisely why it stands out.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 19 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: It has a good description of a specific period of time. Bẫy: "very short story" và "focuses only on famous people" đều bị bác ngay đầu.
2. Đáp án: It is an unconventional biography. Bẫy: "too difficult to understand" và "fictional details" là lo ngại "dissolve" khi đọc kỹ.

question_text: What makes the video stand out from others?
options: The high marketing budget involved.
The participation of famous celebrities.
Its production techniques.
explanation:
Twenty million views in ten days — that is what this short film achieved, and half the marketing industry is trying to work out why. Let me walk you through it. The first assumption everyone makes is celebrities: surely some famous face carried it to success. Watch the film — there is not a single well-known person in it; the cast are complete unknowns. The second assumption is money: a huge marketing budget quietly pushing it into every feed. The creators have opened their accounts, and the promotion spending was close to zero. What actually makes the video stand out is its production techniques. The camera moves in ways amateur videos never attempt, the cuts land precisely on the music, and the sound design wraps around you like a film in a cinema. Ordinary viewers cannot name these techniques, but they feel them within seconds — and quality that can be felt gets shared.
Beyond this one video, when do videos in general become more successful? Creators chase two popular answers. Some translate everything into multiple languages, hoping to multiply their audience by geography. Others study long-term trends and follow them faithfully. Neither approach is wrong, exactly — but the data points to something simpler: release timing. A video published at the right moment, when its audience is online and its topic is in the air, can outperform an identical video published a week earlier or later. In this business, when you speak matters almost as much as what you say.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 15 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Its production techniques. Bẫy: "celebrities" và "marketing budget" đều bị bác bằng chứng cứ.
2. Đáp án: They should be released at the right time. Bẫy: "translated into multiple languages" và "follow long-term trends" — "Neither approach is wrong, exactly — but...".

question_text: What should you do to better control your short-term spending?
options: Monitor your spending for a weekly plan
Rely on credit cards to control spending
Put aside a large sum every single day only
explanation:
On today's money programme: how to actually control your spending, starting with the short term. Beginners usually try one of two things. Some rely on credit cards, believing the monthly statement will somehow keep their daily costs under control — until the statement arrives and the shock does the controlling instead. Others go to the opposite extreme and try to put aside a large sum every single day, which lasts about a week before life gets in the way. Neither works. What does work is boring and reliable: monitor your spending and build a weekly plan. Write down what you spend for seven days, look at where the money actually goes, and set a simple limit for each category the following week. Coffee, transport, evenings out — when you can see the numbers, you control them. When you cannot, they control you.
For the long term, the game changes, and so should your method. I meet people who proudly keep all their savings in one single account, where one emergency can empty everything. I meet others who refuse to make any long-term financial plans because the future feels too uncertain to think about. Both are mistakes, but the bigger mistake is trying to figure everything out alone. My strongest advice: seek guidance from someone with real experience. A relative who has paid off a house, a colleague who invested through a crisis, a qualified adviser — people like this have already paid for the lessons you are about to learn. Borrow their experience; it is the cheapest thing in finance.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 08 bài 1 — nhiễu khác.)
1. Đáp án: Monitor your spending for a weekly plan. Bẫy: "credit cards" và "large sum every day" đều bị bác ("Neither works").
2. Đáp án: Seek advice from someone who have experience. Bẫy: "single account" và "avoid long-term plans" đều được nhắc là sai lầm.

explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---

extra_data.title: Mountain (Version 2)

paragraphs.text: The term "mountain" has evolved over time, reflecting not only physical characteristics but also cultural significance. Before the 19th century, people were quite shy when it came to conquering mountains. Today, with the development of technology, reaching the highest peaks has become easier. In contemporary discussions, mountains may symbolize challenges to overcome or destinations for adventure, transcending their geographical attributes.

Climbing a mountain often leads to a profound sense of accomplishment. It represents not just reaching a physical summit but also conquering personal fears and pushing one's limits, creating memories that last a lifetime. Besides, mountain climbing also creates Adrenaline - a hormone that creates a feeling of excitement like when playing other adventure sports.

In today's digital age, sharing achievements has become prevalent. Climbing a mountain is frequently documented on social media, turning personal milestones into public spectacles that inspire others while also raising questions about authenticity.

In recent years, some climbers have become more focused on taking photos for social media than respecting the mountains they visit. Long lines form near popular summits as people wait for the perfect picture, often ignoring weather warnings or safety advice. In some cases, this obsession with online fame has led to serious accidents. It shows how personal image is sometimes valued more than safety or responsibility.

Mount Everest, once a symbol of human courage, has now become a worrying example of how adventure can harm nature. Every climbing season, long lines of climbers crowd the narrow paths to the summit, leaving behind waste and pollution on the fragile slopes. What used to be a personal challenge has turned into a commercial race, where success is measured by photos and fame rather than respect for the mountain. This situation is disturbing because it shows how our desire to conquer the world's highest peak has created serious environmental and moral concerns.

As the number of climbers on Mount Everest continues to rise, the need to focus on sustainability has become urgent. Local authorities and environmental groups are now introducing stricter waste management rules, encouraging climbers to bring back what they carry, and limiting the number of expeditions each season. Some teams have even started "clean-up climbs" to remove rubbish left behind on the slopes. These efforts remind us that protecting the mountain is just as important as reaching its peak. True success on Everest should mean leaving the mountain cleaner and safer for future generations.

Shared experiences in challenging environments, like mountains, can deepen intimacy in relationships. Couples or friends who navigate the challenges of climbing together often find their bonds strengthened through mutual support and understanding.

question_text: Mountain (Version 3)
options: Our changing definition of mountains
A sense of achievement
Publicising one's achievements
A disturbing revelation
The wrong priority
A focus on substantiality
A more intimate relationship
explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn so sánh cách hiểu về núi xưa và nay: người xưa leo núi vì vẻ đẹp và sự thích thú, còn ngày nay đỉnh núi trở thành đích đến mang tính biểu tượng cho thành công và sức bền.
2. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói việc chinh phục đỉnh núi mang ý nghĩa cá nhân sâu sắc — là ẩn dụ cho thành công, vượt rào cản, khiến cảm giác đạt được rất đáng giá.
3. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói về hiện tượng "summit selfie": ảnh ở đỉnh từ chỗ để lưu niệm đã thành cách công bố thành tích với người khác, càng mạnh hơn nhờ mạng xã hội.
4. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn kể bức ảnh của Thomas năm 1993 phơi bày "the unsettling reality" — hàng trăm người xếp hàng một chờ lên đỉnh, gương mặt kiệt sức và bức xúc. Cụm "unsettling reality" chính là "a disturbing revelation".
5. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói giới phê bình kết luận đỉnh núi đã thành mục đích tự thân, người leo coi nhẹ quá trình và khâu chuẩn bị, chạy theo danh tiếng — tức đặt sai thứ tự ưu tiên.
6. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói trực tiếp về trách nhiệm và tính bền vững: rác thải, suy thoái môi trường, thiếu tôn trọng hệ sinh thái địa phương.
7. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn kêu gọi quay về gốc rễ đích thực: tận hưởng việc đi bộ, quan sát, chậm lại; tự truyện của Cherke cho thấy leo núi đem lại mối liên hệ gần gũi hơn với thiên nhiên.

extra_data.title: Mountain (Version 3)

paragraphs.text: Even before the nineteenth century, mountains had always exerted a powerful attraction on travellers. They captivated visitors largely because of their natural beauty and the sense of awe inspired by dramatic landscapes. For early explorers, climbing to the summit was primarily about enjoyment and wonder, rather than proving personal strength. In contrast, today the peak is no longer seen merely as a scenic viewpoint but as a highly symbolic destination. Reaching the top has increasingly come to represent success, endurance, and a once-in-a-lifetime accomplishment that many people aspire to achieve.

For a large number of climbers, conquering a mountain summit embodies profound personal significance. The "summit" is often interpreted as a metaphor for success in life, a clear representation of overcoming barriers and pushing human limits. The physical obstacles encountered on the climb mirror psychological struggles, which makes the achievement deeply rewarding. Over time, mountaineering has evolved into a cultural practice where people challenge themselves for adventure, resilience, and self-affirmation. Consequently, the scenery or encounters along the trail have become secondary to the psychological triumph of standing at the very top.

Mountaineering as a celebrated "achievement" has been amplified by the phenomenon of the "summit selfie." Even in the pre-digital era, photographs at the summit were considered valuable mementoes, proof of the effort invested. What began as a way to preserve memories gradually turned into an opportunity to broadcast one's success to others. The rise of social media has intensified this trend, as climbers are often more concerned with curating a perfect image than immersing themselves in the experience. In many cases, the journey itself becomes overshadowed by the simple desire to showcase the fact of having reached the summit.

The photograph captured by Thomas in 1993 exposed the unsettling reality of contemporary mountaineering. It depicted hundreds of people queuing in a single file line to reach the summit - an image that contrasts starkly with the solitude once associated with genuine exploration. The climbers' expressions reflected exhaustion and frustration rather than determination or joy, suggesting that the climb had lost its authenticity. Once published online, the image provoked widespread debate about whether the meaning of summiting had been reduced to mere spectacle. For many critics, it illustrated how the essence of mountaineering has been compromised by mass participation and social validation.

From this picture, critics conclude that the summit has become an end in itself, often detached from the original spirit of exploration. Many people now seem to disregard the multifaceted nature of mountaineering, treating it simply as a fashionable objective. For some, neither the genuine process of climbing nor the authentic arrival at the peak matters, as their motivation is largely external. Furthermore, the preparation that should accompany such an endeavour - rigorous physical training, budgeting, and logistical planning - is frequently underestimated. As a result, the experience risks being superficial, emphasising prestige rather than true engagement with the mountain.

One of the most urgent debates surrounding contemporary mountaineering concerns sustainability. Popular climbing destinations often suffer from waste accumulation, environmental degradation, and disrespect for local ecosystems. Many activists argue that this trend-driven approach to climbing must be reconsidered in order to preserve fragile landscapes. Responsibility, they emphasise, should be integral to every stage of the climbing journey, from preparation to leaving the site clean. Ultimately, they believe that the summit can only be considered "worthwhile" if the path toward it contributes positively to both the environment and the climber's personal growth.

Perhaps the time has come to reassess our perspective on climbing and return to its more authentic roots. Instead of pursuing mountains solely for recognition, individuals could rediscover the joy of walking, observing, and slowing down. In her autobiography, Cherke described how hiking offered her moments of reflection and a deeper connection with the natural world. Such experiences remind us that mountains provide not only physical challenges but also opportunities for serenity and contemplation. By cultivating a more intimate relationship with nature, climbing may once again regain its balance between personal fulfilment and environmental respect.

question_text: What do people think about this promotion campaign?
options: It makes exaggerated claims about the product.
It provides too little information about the product.
It focuses too much on the product's low price.
explanation:
Our consumer affairs segment tonight looks at the advertising campaign everyone is arguing about. What do people actually think of it? I have read hundreds of comments this week, and the pattern is clear. It is not that the campaign gives too little information — if anything, the advertisements are crowded with facts and figures. Nor do people complain about an obsession with low prices; the price is barely mentioned at all. The complaint that appears again and again is that the campaign makes exaggerated claims about the product. Viewers see promises of instant, almost magical results, and instead of being convinced, they become suspicious. Several commenters used the same phrase: too good to be true. When your audience starts quoting that proverb back at you, your advertising has achieved the opposite of its purpose.
As for my own professional view, the company is worried about the wrong things. Executives fear the campaign targets the wrong group of customers — my analysis says the targeting is actually precise. They also fret that it has not attracted enough public attention, yet everyone I meet has seen these advertisements. The genuine problem is financial: the campaign costs far too much compared with the return it can possibly bring. Prime-time slots, expensive studios, three separate filming locations — the bill is enormous, and even the most optimistic sales projections cannot repay it. In advertising, fame is easy to buy. Profit is the part that requires arithmetic.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 26 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: It makes exaggerated claims about the product. Bẫy: "too little information" và "low price" đều bị phủ định.
2. Đáp án: It costs too much to make compared with the possible return. Bẫy: "wrong group" và "not enough attention" là lo ngại sai của công ty.

question_text: What is the key to a long career in music?
options: Having a large number of fans.
Believing in her musical instincts.
Winning many awards early.
explanation:
Tonight on our music industry programme, we ask the oldest question in the business: what keeps an artist's career alive for decades? The easy answers come first. A large number of fans, people say — surely millions of followers guarantee a long career. History disagrees; the industry is a graveyard of artists who had enormous fan bases and vanished within a few years. Then there are the early awards — win the big prizes young and your future is secure. Also false, and sometimes worse than false, because early trophies can lock an artist inside the style that won them. What the long careers share, according to every manager I have interviewed, is something internal: the artist believes in her own musical instincts. She chooses the songs that feel true to her, resists advice that bends her away from her sound, and accepts that some albums will confuse people. Audiences stay loyal to artists who stay loyal to themselves.
As for the state of the industry today, let me push back on two common claims. Commentators say modern performers have a lot of control now, thanks to streaming and social platforms. And cynics complain that new performers only care about money. Neither matches reality. The truth is harsher: performers find it extremely hard to get started. More talent is competing for attention than at any point in history, and without backing, brilliant musicians remain invisible. Every debut you hear on the radio is a survivor of a contest most people lose.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 17 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Believing in her musical instincts. Bẫy: "large number of fans" ("History disagrees") và "winning awards early" ("Also false") đều bị bác.
2. Đáp án: Performers find it hard to get started. Bẫy: "have a lot of control" và "only care about money" — "Neither matches reality".

question_text: What do these two famous writers have in common?
options: They both wrote in the same genre
They both were born in the same country
They both make references to each other in their work
explanation:
In this week's literature lecture, we look at two writers who changed modern fiction — and at what actually connects them, because students always guess wrong. The first guess is that they wrote in the same genre. In fact, one spent his life on realistic novels while the other moved between fantasy, essays and poetry. The second guess is that they were born in the same country. Also wrong — an ocean separated their birthplaces, and they met in person only twice. What they truly share is more unusual: they make references to each other in their work. Open one writer's short stories and you will find the other's characters walking through them; read the second writer's essays and whole passages answer arguments the first had made years before. Across different languages and continents, their books carried on a lifelong conversation of mutual respect.
Now, what should you expect when you read them? Do not expect simple language and structure — anyone who tells you these are easy books has not read them. And do not assume their works are based on real events; both invented freely, even when history appears in the background. What is genuinely special is that the meaning of their work is not always easily identified. Both writers hid ideas beneath the surface — symbols, private jokes, arguments in disguise. You may finish a chapter unsure of what it truly said, return a year later, and find a different book waiting for you. That richness is exactly why we still study them.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 05 bài 2 — nhiễu khác: same genre / same country.)
1. Đáp án: They both make references to each other in their work. Bẫy: "same genre" và "same country" đều bị phủ định ngay đầu.
2. Đáp án: The meaning of their work is not always easily identified. Bẫy: "simple language" và "based on real events" đều bị phủ định.

question_text: What does the speaker say is a key benefit of making plans?
options: They make life more predictable.
They help you make decisions.
They reduce the need for communication.
explanation:
As a life coach, I spend half my time defending the humble plan, so let me do that again tonight. When I ask workshop groups what plans are for, the answers rarely change. Plans make life predictable, says the front row — you always know what tomorrow holds. Plans reduce the need for communication, jokes the back row — write it down once and stop discussing it. Small truths, both of them, but they miss the centre of the target. The key benefit of making plans is that they help you make decisions. A plan is a record of your priorities, written while your head was calm. So when a tempting offer or a sudden problem arrives on a chaotic afternoon, you do not have to think from zero — you hold the choice against the plan, and the answer usually reveals itself. People with plans decide faster, regret less, and can always explain their reasons.
Naturally, planning has its difficulties, and I will name the real one — because the usual complaints are wrong. Planning does not discourage risk-taking; my most adventurous clients are my most organised ones, since a plan makes risks survivable. Nor does planning work only in professional settings — ask anyone who has organised a family wedding. The genuine difficulty is that planning requires you to set yourself limits. A plan that includes everything is a wish list. To plan is to choose, and to choose is to give things up: projects, distractions, open doors. That small pain of limiting yourself is the price of clarity — and it is the best bargain I know.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 22 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: They help you make decisions. Bẫy: "predictable" và "reduce communication" — "Small truths... but they miss the centre".
2. Đáp án: It requires you to set yourself certain limits. Bẫy: "discourages risks" và "only professional situations" đều bị bác.

question_text: What does this guidebook offer to its audience?
options: It focuses solely on historical landmarks.
It creates an adventure.
It is difficult to navigate.
explanation:
Before my last big trip, I decided to write the travel guidebook I had always wished existed, and it has finally been published. Let me tell you what it offers. Readers expecting a book that focuses solely on historical landmarks will be surprised — the famous monuments are in there, but only as a starting point. And a few early reviewers worried it might be difficult to navigate, with all its side stories and detours. In practice, the opposite happens: those detours are the whole idea. The book offers its audience an adventure. It encourages you to leave the main square, follow a local story down a side street, try an activity no tour bus ever stops for, and come home with memories that belong only to you. Every chapter is built around one simple question: what would make this journey unforgettable?
Who is the book for? I will be honest about that too. Some booksellers assumed it caters only to seasoned travellers, the people with a hundred stamps in their passports. Others, seeing all the unusual suggestions, wondered whether the style was outdated compared with travel apps. Neither is quite right. What I have found is that the book is suitable for particular generations — it clicks most strongly with younger readers, people in their twenties and thirties who want experiences rather than checklists. Older readers often prefer a classical guide, and that is perfectly fine. A book, like a journey, does not have to be for everyone.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It creates an adventure. Bẫy: "focuses solely on historical landmarks" bị phủ định ("only as a starting point"), "difficult to navigate" bị bác ("the opposite happens").
2. Đáp án: It is suitable for particular generations. Bẫy: "caters only to seasoned travelers" và "outdated" đều là giả định bị bác ("Neither is quite right").

question_text: Why hasn't he gone to college?
options: He couldn't afford the tuition fees.
He wasn't ready to start higher education.
He didn't get good enough grades.
explanation:
Today I want to tell you about one of my former students, because his story answers a question parents ask me constantly: is it a disaster if a young person delays university? Let me start with why he did not go straight to college. It was not money — his family had planned for the fees, and a scholarship covered part of them anyway. It was not his grades either; his results would have opened most doors he cared about. The honest reason is that he was not ready for higher education. Thirteen years of classrooms had drained him, and he knew that arriving at university exhausted would waste the whole opportunity. So, against plenty of advice, he stopped for a year — worked in a warehouse, travelled cheaply, lived away from home for the first time.
Now the interesting part: what did that break actually teach him? He worked part-time for months, but ask him and he will tell you the job itself taught him little beyond patience. He certainly came back appreciating education more — yet that gratitude was a side effect, not the lesson. What he really learned from the year, in his own words, was how to be more independent. He managed his own money, cooked his own disasters, fixed his own problems with nobody checking his work. When he finally entered university, professors kept mistaking him for an older student. Independence, it turns out, is not taught in any lecture hall — but it improves every lecture that follows.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của gap year — góc người kể là giáo viên cũ.)
1. Đáp án: He wasn't ready to start higher education. Bẫy: "tuition fees" và "grades" đều bị phủ định.
2. Đáp án: How to be more independent. Bẫy: "working part-time" ("taught him little") và "importance of education" ("a side effect, not the lesson").

question_text: When did she become a Nutritionist?
options: When she did a biology degree.
When she worked at a healthcare center.
After working in a hospital.
explanation:
Welcome to our careers podcast. My guest today is one of the country's best-known nutritionists, and I asked her how it all began. She told me her route was unusual. In her field, the typical story is a nurse who discovers nutrition after years of working in a hospital, or a dietitian who finds the specialty while employed at a healthcare centre. Not her. She qualified as a nutritionist while she was still doing her biology degree. A university research project on diet caught her imagination in her second year, she took the professional exams alongside her coursework, and she walked out of graduation with both a degree and a licence. The career, she says, chose her before she had even finished studying.
Her fame has an equally surprising origin. When people meet her, they assume she must have become famous after appearing on some TV show, and one persistent internet rumour claims she invented a new type of health food. She laughs at both stories — no television, no miracle product. What actually happened is that she spent years answering a national nutrition helpline, quietly solving people's problems three evenings a week. Worried parents, confused patients, exhausted athletes — thousands of callers over the years, each with a small question that mattered enormously to them. Their gratitude spread her name from kitchen to kitchen long before any journalist knew it. Fame built that way, she told me, is slow — but it never disappears overnight, because it is made of trust.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 15 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: When she did a biology degree. Bẫy: "hospital" và "healthcare center" là con đường "typical" của người khác.
2. Đáp án: After solving people's problems in a helpline. Bẫy: "TV show" và "inventing food" là tin đồn bị cười bác ("no television, no miracle product").

question_text: How did many art critics describe Jame Panos' paintings?
options: They were full of bright colours and happiness.
They would be characterized by sadness.
They mainly focused on modern city life.
explanation:
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the National Gallery. Our new exhibition presents more than thirty paintings by the Greek artist Jame Panos, most completed in the final decade of his career. Before we enter, let me prepare you for what the critics have long said about his work. Visitors sometimes arrive expecting canvases full of bright colours and happiness — Mediterranean light, blue seas, festival scenes. Others assume a Greek artist of his generation must have painted modern city life. Both expectations dissolve in the first room. What the critics have always described in Panos' paintings is sadness — a quiet, dignified melancholy that fills every frame. Empty chairs at family tables, harbours after the boats have gone, old women watching roads that no one walks down anymore. His genius was to make sorrow beautiful without ever making it comfortable.
And how do visitors experience the exhibition as a whole? The comment book downstairs answers better than I can. Nobody describes it as a lesson about modern architecture, though buildings appear in many works. Nobody calls it a celebration of future ideas, for Panos had little interest in tomorrow. Visitor after visitor writes the same discovery: the exhibition feels like a window into the past. Through his eyes we see the villages before the tourists, the crafts before the factories, the silences before the traffic. Stand before the final painting — his grandmother's kitchen, unfinished at his death — and half a century simply falls away. Few artists open that window. Fewer still leave it open so wide.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: They would be characterized by sadness. Bẫy: "bright colours and happiness" và "modern city life" là kỳ vọng "dissolve in the first room".
2. Đáp án: A window into the past. Bẫy: "modern architecture" và "future ideas" — "Nobody describes... Nobody calls...".

question_text: Describe the two pictures.
explanation: The first picture shows a young woman looking at photographs while holding a camera. She is sitting at a table with many printed photos, a notebook and a laptop, so she may be choosing photos for an album, a diary or a travel story. The second picture shows a dairy farm. There are several cows standing in a barn, and a woman is feeding one of them with hay. She is wearing a blue uniform, gloves and boots, so she looks like a farm worker. In the background, a man is cleaning or working near the milking equipment. There are also some milk cans on the right side of the picture. Overall, the first picture is about keeping memories with photos, while the second picture shows people taking care of cows on a dairy farm.

question_text: What is the speaker's main criticism of the promotion campaign?
options: It makes exaggerated claims about the product.
It provides too little information about the product.
It focuses too much on the product's low price.
explanation:
As a marketing consultant, I was asked to evaluate this promotion campaign, and I will share my conclusions openly. Some colleagues suggested the campaign provides too little information about the product — actually, the opposite is true; the advertisements are packed with details and specifications. Others thought it focuses too much on the low price, but price barely appears in any of the materials. My main criticism is more serious: the campaign makes exaggerated claims about the product. The advertisements promise results that are simply too good to be true — perfect skin in three days, twice the energy in a week. When promises reach that level, customers do not get excited; they get suspicious. Instead of building trust, the campaign plants doubt, and doubt is the most expensive thing a new product can create. Honest, realistic messages would convince far more people than these fireworks ever will.
There is also the question of money, and here my worry is different from what the company expects. They fear the campaign targets the wrong group of customers — it does not; the audience selection is actually quite clever. They also worry it has not attracted enough public attention, yet the view numbers are perfectly healthy. The real problem is the mathematics: the campaign costs too much compared with the return it can realistically bring. Celebrity fees, prime-time slots, three production studios — the spending is enormous, and even optimistic sales forecasts cannot cover it. A campaign can win every award in the industry and still sink the product it was meant to sell.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: It makes exaggerated claims about the product. Bẫy: "too little information" và "focuses on low price" đều bị phủ định.
2. Đáp án: It costs too much to make compared with the possible return. Bẫy: "wrong group of customers" và "not enough attention" đều bị bác ("it does not", "perfectly healthy").

question_text: What is the importance of advertising?
options: It increases the product price
It can help reach new customers
It can build brand recognition
explanation:
Our small business workshop continues, and tonight's topic is advertising — the expense every owner complains about and no successful company lives without. Let me deal with the complaints first. Owners tell me advertising will force up their product prices, since the cost must land somewhere. Managed badly, it can; managed well, the extra sales carry the cost easily. Marketing people love to answer that advertising builds brand recognition, making your logo familiar to everyone. Nice, but familiarity alone pays no invoices — plenty of recognised brands have gone bankrupt while everyone knew their name. The true importance of advertising is plainer: it helps you reach new customers. Every business eventually exhausts its circle of regulars. Advertising is how your product walks into streets, screens and conversations where nobody has heard of you — and new customers are the only fuel a growing business runs on.
Now, about sponsoring sports tournaments, hear my warning before you sign anything. The hesitations owners usually mention are the wrong ones. Too expensive? Sponsorship packages now start at very modest prices. Unfair competition from the big brands? The audience remembers good sponsors of any size. The danger nobody budgets for is reputational: sponsorship can generate negative publicity for the sport itself, and your name sinks with it. One cheating scandal, one crowd riot, one doping headline — and every photograph of the shame includes your logo in the corner. Sponsor if you wish, but read the risk before you admire the reach.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant thứ 3 của Advertising — khác lời Đề 04 và Đề 21.)
1. Đáp án: It can help reach new customers. Bẫy: "increases the product price" ("Managed badly, it can") và "brand recognition" ("familiarity alone pays no invoices") đều bị hạ.
2. Đáp án: They can generate negative publicity for the sport. Bẫy: "too expensive" và "unfair competition" là "the wrong ones".

question_text: What should you do to better control your short-term spending?
options: Monitor your spending for a weekly plan
Rely on credit cards to control spending
Put aside a large sum every single day only
explanation:
My bank asked me to give this talk to young account holders, so let me speak plainly about controlling your money. For short-term spending — the daily coffees, the weekend shopping — I have watched two popular methods fail again and again. The first is trusting your credit card to do the controlling, on the theory that the monthly statement keeps you honest. It does not; it only delivers the bad news after the spending is done. The second is the heroic approach: putting aside a large sum every single day. It feels powerful for a week and collapses by the second Friday. What actually works is quieter: monitor your spending and turn it into a weekly plan. Track every payment for seven days, see where the money truly goes, then give each category a sensible limit for the next week. Control begins the moment you can see clearly.
For the long term, the biggest dangers are different. Some people keep every saved penny in a single account, which one emergency can wipe out. Others refuse to make any long-term financial plans at all, because thinking about the distant future feels uncomfortable. My advice stands above both: seek guidance from someone with genuine experience. Find the aunt who quietly paid off her house, the colleague who saved through a recession, or a licensed adviser. Their scars are your shortcuts. Every financial mistake you are about to make, somebody has already made — and will happily help you avoid, if you simply ask.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant thứ 3 của chủ đề financial — khác lời Đề 08 và Đề 23.)
1. Đáp án: Monitor your spending for a weekly plan. Bẫy: "credit cards" và "large sum every day" — hai phương pháp "fail again and again".
2. Đáp án: Seek advice from someone who have experience. Bẫy: "single account" và "avoid long-term plans" là hai "danger" bị cảnh báo.

question_text: According to the speaker, how should we learn to work?
options: Independently without any guidance
By following strictly fixed instructions
Effectively
explanation:
Welcome to our learning and development workshop. Question one on your handout asks: how should we learn to work? Over the years I have collected the answers people give. The ambitious ones say we should learn to work independently, with no guidance from anyone — proving ourselves by never asking for help. The cautious ones prefer the opposite: follow strictly fixed instructions, step by step, exactly as the manual says. I want to challenge both camps today. Independence without guidance usually means repeating avoidable mistakes, and rigid instructions stop making sense the moment the situation changes. What we should actually learn is how to work effectively. Effective work means understanding which tasks genuinely move the needle, organising your energy around them, and letting go of activity that merely looks busy. Learn that skill, and every job you ever hold becomes easier.
Question two is about progress — real career progress, not just yearly pay rises. Some of you wrote that the safest path is to maintain a predictable daily routine, and others said the wise employee avoids any risks in the workplace. I understand the comfort in those answers, but comfort is exactly the problem. The people who genuinely move forward are the ones willing to experiment. They volunteer for the unfamiliar project, test the new tool before anyone asks them to, try a method that might fail. Most experiments teach you something; a few change your career entirely. Routines protect what you have. Experiments create what you will have next.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 10 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Effectively. Bẫy: "independently without guidance" và "strictly fixed instructions" đều bị thách thức ("I want to challenge both camps").
2. Đáp án: Experiment. Bẫy: "predictable daily routine" và "avoid any risks" đều bị bác ("comfort is exactly the problem").

question_text: What is the way to have a good sleep according to the speaker?
options: Sleeping fewer hours increases deep sleep quality
Blocking out noise and light is key
Drinking coffee before bed helps relax the mind
explanation:
Welcome to our health programme. Tonight: sleep, and the strange advice people give about it. Over the years I have heard everything. One listener wrote in convinced that sleeping fewer hours actually improves the quality of deep sleep — the idea being that a tired brain sleeps harder. Another swears by a cup of coffee before bed, claiming it relaxes her mind. I have to be direct with you: neither idea survives contact with the research. Cutting your hours simply builds up exhaustion, and caffeine at night keeps the brain alert exactly when it should be winding down. What the sleep laboratories keep confirming, study after study, is far less exotic: blocking out noise and light is the key. Darkness tells the brain to produce the hormones of rest, and silence lets it stay there. Thick curtains and a closed door will do more for your sleep than any clever trick.
Now, a few words about insomnia, because the myths here are just as stubborn. It is often assumed that insomnia is caused only by physical health problems, but stress, habits and worry are equally powerful causes. And no — people with insomnia do not secretly sleep too much in the daytime; most barely rest at all. The finding that deserves your attention is this one: people cannot always recognise the symptoms of their own tiredness. They mistake exhaustion for restlessness, reach for the phone or the laptop, and push the body further from sleep — night after night, without ever understanding why.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 03 bài 1 — cùng đáp án, lời khác.)
1. Đáp án: Blocking out noise and light is key. Bẫy: "sleeping fewer hours" và "coffee before bed" đều bị bác ("neither idea survives contact with the research").
2. Đáp án: People can't always recognize the symptoms of tiredness. Bẫy: "caused only by physical health problems" và "sleep too much" đều bị phủ định.

6. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói người leo cần suy nghĩ lại mục tiêu và thói quen, bảo đảm du lịch toàn cầu trong tương lai không gây hại môi trường — tức chú trọng hơn vào tính bền vững.

extra_data.title: Mountain (Version 4)

paragraphs.text: In the early 1800s, people were believed not to enjoy climbing mountains. Later, as mountain climbing became a popular trend, interest grew rapidly. However, there is evidence that humans have always been fascinated by mountains. The difference now is that people focus mainly on reaching the summit to admire the majestic views rather than simply exploring the mountain itself.

Climbing to the top of a mountain creates the same adrenaline rush as other extreme sports. But it goes far beyond that. Because of the sheer size and grandeur of the mountains, the experience becomes a powerful metaphor, making climbers feel deeply inspired. This intense feeling can even become addictive, as people unconsciously develop a strong desire to keep reaching the peak.

People have always enjoyed capturing and sharing the moment of standing on a mountaintop. This practice existed even before social media, as climbers admired the view or described their experiences to others. With the rise of social media, this trend has become even more common. Now, almost everyone takes selfies and posts them online for friends and family to see after reaching the summit.

Recently, some climbers have begun questioning whether this focus on the summit is truly meaningful. The most beautiful views might not be from the peak itself, and the path to the summit is often exhausting, requiring great physical strength. This approach excludes many people and overlooks the beauty found all along the mountain, not just at the top.

A photo taken on Mount Everest in 2020, showing a "traffic jam" of climbers, shocked the world. It revealed how many climbers were rushing to reach the summit during the short window of good weather. This image raised concerns about overcrowding and highlighted how Everest, once seen as a remote and unreachable peak, has now become a site of intense competition and environmental strain.

The viral photo made some people feel that climbing Everest had lost its charm. However, mountain climbing itself is not the problem. Instead, climbers must carefully reflect on their goals and habits, ensuring that future global tourism does not negatively impact the environment. A more mindful approach can protect mountains for generations to come.

Perhaps we should approach mountains with a gentle mindset, seeing them as companions rather than challenges to conquer. In the 1940 book The Living Mountain by Shepherd, the author describes climbing near her family farm. She wandered the mountains without specific goals, treating each climb as a visit to old friends instead of a mission to claim victory over nature.

question_text: What do these two famous writers have in common?
options: They both wrote in the same genre
They both were born in the same country
They both make references to each other in their work
explanation:
Good evening, book lovers, and welcome to our authors series. Tonight: two giants of modern literature, and the connection between them that most readers get wrong. When I ask audiences what these two writers share, somebody always says they wrote in the same genre. They did not — one built quiet family novels, the other wild experimental fiction, and critics of their time saw them as opposites. The next guess is that they were born in the same country. Wrong again; they grew up on different continents and wrote in different languages. Their real bond is hidden inside the books themselves: they make references to each other in their work. Characters from one writer's novels appear, lightly disguised, in the other's stories. Essays answer essays across the decades. Scholars have counted more than forty of these hidden greetings — a lifelong correspondence conducted entirely through published pages.
What should you know before reading them? Two warnings, or rather, one false warning and one true one. Forget the claim that they use simple language and structure — these are demanding books that ask for your full attention. And ignore anyone who says their works are all based on real events; both writers invented worlds freely. The true warning is this: the meaning of their work is not always easily identified. They buried their ideas under symbols and quiet jokes, trusting readers to dig. Some chapters only open on the second reading, and some only years later. But what you dig up, you keep forever.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant thứ 3 của Famous writers — khác lời Đề 05 và Đề 24.)

question_text: Why do some readers struggle to connect with the characters in the novel?
options: There are too many main characters to follow.
They are difficult to relate to.
Their motivations are explained too clearly.
explanation:
The new novel has generated real interest — and real complaints, so today let us examine what readers are actually saying. Start with the characters, the most discussed issue. The problem is not that there are too many main characters to follow; the cast is actually small, just four central figures. And nobody claims their motivations are explained too clearly — if anything, the author explains generously. Yet readers report, again and again, that the characters are difficult to relate to. Despite all the background details on the page, the figures feel distant, like people described in a report rather than people you know. Their sorrows are stated but never felt, their joys announced but never shared. Emotional connection is the one thing description alone cannot buy, and its absence runs through every chapter.
The storyline attracts the second wave of criticism, and here the verdict is even plainer. The book is not too complex for a general audience — the structure is simple and linear. Nor do experts complain that the plot twists are too predictable for specialists; the twists are serviceable enough. The accusation that sticks is that the storyline lacks originality. Readers list the familiar ingredients on every forum: the stormy opening, the inherited house, the letter hidden in the attic. We have read this novel before, one reviewer wrote, under a dozen different titles. Competence, sadly, is not the same as freshness — and freshness is what this novel never finds.

1. Đáp án: They are difficult to relate to. Bẫy: "too many main characters" ("cast is actually small") và "motivations explained too clearly" đều bị phủ định.

On today's programme we discuss marketing with the notes from my interview with a leading industry expert. I asked her the blunt question first: does advertising still matter? Her answer cut through the noise. Advertising, she said, is not primarily about reducing production costs — that is a factory problem, not a marketing one. And the fashionable claim that advertising has become less effective because of digital media made her laugh; the channels changed, she said, but the effect did not. The core purpose remains what it always was: advertising helps a business reach new customers. Every company begins with a circle of people who know it. Advertising is the machine that carries the product beyond that circle, into homes and screens where the brand has never been heard of. Growth lives outside the circle — and advertising is the bridge.
Then we turned to sport, and her tone changed. Sponsors love to believe their money guarantees a win for the sponsored teams — pure superstition, she said; trophies cannot be bought so directly. Nor is modern sponsorship focused exclusively on amateur local events; the money flows mostly to the giant tournaments. Her genuine concern was for the audience: sponsorship, she warned, is not always good for sports fans. Ticket prices climb to satisfy corporate partners, kick-off times move to suit television schedules rather than supporters, and stadiums fill with billboards where banners used to hang. The money enriches the game, she said — but somebody should ask the fans what it costs them.

question_text: What should people do to maintain a healthy environment?
options: Limit industrial production to strictly rural areas
Replace all personal vehicles with electric bicycles
Make a daily effort to recycle, reduce waste, and use energy carefully.
explanation:
Thank you all for coming to our community environment evening. The question I am asked most often is: what should an ordinary person actually do? And I notice the suggestions people bring are usually enormous. One gentleman last month wanted the town to replace every personal vehicle with electric bicycles by next year. A student group proposed limiting all industrial production strictly to rural areas, far away from where people live. I admire the passion, but plans like these are neither practical nor what the science asks of us. The experts' advice is far more modest: make a daily effort to recycle, reduce your waste, and use energy carefully at home. Sort your rubbish properly, refuse the packaging you do not need, switch things off when you leave the room. Multiply those small habits by a whole town, then a whole country, and the effect becomes enormous — without a single dramatic law.
At the same time, we must talk honestly about deforestation, because misinformation is spreading. You may have heard the argument that clearing forests primarily benefits the local economy, at least in the short term. Some even claim that cutting old trees creates more resilient ecosystems for the future. Every serious study says otherwise. Deforestation harms nature directly, and the damage travels straight back to us: the climate warms faster, floods strike harder, and communities near cleared land report growing health problems from polluted air and water. When we lose a forest, we are not trading nature for money. We are borrowing from our own children.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 11 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Make a daily effort to recycle, reduce waste, and use energy carefully. Bẫy: "electric bicycles" và "limit industry to rural areas" là đề xuất bị chê "neither practical".
2. Đáp án: They harm nature and cause problems like climate change and health issues. Bẫy: "benefit the local economy" và "resilient ecosystems" bị bác ("Every serious study says otherwise").

question_text: How to maximise productivity?
options: Effective time management
Effective allocation of resources
Effective utilization of personnel
explanation:
Let me share what I have learned about productivity after coaching office teams for fifteen years. Whenever a company calls me in, the managers already have their theories. Half of them believe the answer is a better allocation of resources — newer laptops, bigger budgets, smarter software. The other half talk about utilisation of personnel, moving people between roles like chess pieces until the puzzle fits. Those levers matter in a big organisation, but when I sit with an individual employee, neither explains why one person finishes at five o'clock what another cannot finish by midnight. The difference, almost every time, is effective time management. The productive person decides each morning what truly matters, gives those tasks the best hours of the day, and defends that time politely but firmly. Nothing I teach produces results faster than that one habit.
I must also be honest about the limits. When people abandon productivity systems, they give predictable reasons. Beginners protest that the methods are too complicated — though after one honest week, most systems turn out to be embarrassingly simple. Specialists insist no method fits their particular kind of job — occasionally true, mostly an excuse. The genuine obstacle, the one that defeats almost everyone, is that using these strategies takes real, continuous effort. The calendar does not fill itself in; the priorities do not choose themselves. A productivity system is like a gym membership: owning one changes nothing. Showing up every day is the entire secret.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---

question_text: What is the way to have a good sleep according to the speaker?

In tonight's wellbeing segment, we tackle sleep — and the peculiar folklore that surrounds it. My inbox this week contained two classics. A listener wrote that sleeping fewer hours makes the remaining sleep deeper, so we should all cut back to five hours. Another swears her evening espresso relaxes her mind for bed. As a doctor, I must gently demolish both. Short sleep does not deepen sleep; it simply builds a debt your body collects later with interest. And caffeine before bed relaxes nobody — it blocks the very chemical that makes you drowsy. What five decades of sleep science actually tells us is wonderfully unglamorous: block out noise and light, and sleep improves. Darkness starts the brain's night-time chemistry; quiet keeps it running. Before you buy supplements or gadgets, buy thicker curtains.
On insomnia, the misunderstandings run even deeper. Patients arrive convinced their sleeplessness must come from a physical illness alone — yet in most cases, stress and habits are doing the damage alongside anything physical. Relatives sometimes whisper that the insomniac secretly naps all day; almost never true. The finding I most wish everyone knew is this: people cannot always recognise the symptoms of their own tiredness. Exhaustion disguises itself as restlessness, as irritation, as one more hour of scrolling. The tired brain is precisely the brain least able to notice it is tired — which is why the phone stays lit at two in the morning, and the problem quietly feeds itself.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---

question_text: What does the speaker say is one major strength of successful television series?
options: They focus mainly on famous actors.
They maintain consistent quality throughout.
They are usually shorter than films.
explanation:
Television series have taken over our evenings, and as a media researcher I am often asked why some series succeed while hundreds disappear. People love simple answers. Many point to famous actors — put a film star on the poster and success follows. Others argue that series win because the episodes are shorter than films, easier to fit into a busy evening. Both factors help a launch, but they do not explain survival. Watch the series that run for five or ten years and you will find one shared strength: they maintain consistent quality throughout. The writing in season six is as sharp as in season one, the acting never relaxes, and the production standard holds from the first episode to the last. Audiences forgive a weak episode; they abandon a series that becomes reliably weaker. Consistency, not star power, is what keeps millions returning every week.
The way series are made is also changing, and it is worth understanding why. Some commentators claim streaming platforms have reduced production costs — in reality, budgets for major series have never been higher. Others complain television is becoming less creative, though this decade has produced some of the boldest storytelling ever filmed. The real change is quieter: viewer habits now influence the way series are made. Because platforms can see exactly when audiences pause, rewatch or give up, writers shape episode length, cliffhangers and season structure around real viewing data. For the first time in history, the audience is silently sitting in the writers' room.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: They maintain consistent quality throughout. Bẫy: "famous actors" và "shorter than films" được nhắc rồi hạ ("they do not explain survival").
2. Đáp án: Viewer habits influence the way that series are made. Bẫy: "reduced production costs" và "less creative" đều bị phủ định.

question_text: What was one major problem the railways faced?
options: The lack of qualified engineers and staff
Extreme weather damaging the tracks
Not making enough money
explanation:
Our history podcast continues with the darkest chapter in the story of the railways: the crisis of the mid-twentieth century. First, let us clear up what did not cause it. Listeners often write in blaming extreme weather for damaging the tracks — but the maintenance records show the network handled storms and floods as well as it ever had. Others point to a lack of qualified engineers and staff, yet the training academies were full and thousands of skilled workers stayed loyal to the railways their whole lives. The real problem was brutally simple: the railways were not making enough money. Families were buying cars, companies were switching their goods to trucks, and every year the ticket offices counted fewer passengers while the repair bills for ageing bridges and engines grew larger. An industry built for a previous century was bleeding, slowly and openly.
And how did the leadership respond? Here the story becomes a lesson for every manager. Advisers presented bold options: one group proposed selling major assets to international investors, another suggested suspending all operations entirely for a total restructure. The leader in charge said no to both. His decision was to continue the policies that had already been implemented in earlier years — same routes, same prices, same organisation — trusting that the good times would somehow return on their own. They never did. Historians now describe those wasted years as the clearest example in transport history of how waiting, when the world is changing, is itself the riskiest decision of all.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 11 bài 1.)
1. Đáp án: Not making enough money. Bẫy: "extreme weather" và "lack of engineers" đều bị bác bằng chứng cứ.
2. Đáp án: Continuing policies that had already been implemented. Bẫy: "selling assets" và "suspending operations" là đề xuất bị từ chối ("said no to both").

Why do some television series run for a decade while others vanish after one season? As a screenwriter, I get asked this at every dinner party, so here is my honest answer. Others point out that episodes are shorter than films, easier to squeeze into a weekday evening. True, but brevity gets you sampled, not loved. The strength that actually separates the survivors is consistency: successful series maintain their quality from the first episode to the last. The jokes stay sharp in season five, the plots stay tight, the acting never coasts. Audiences will forgive one bad night; what they never forgive is the feeling that a show has stopped trying.
And the way we make series is changing under our feet. Commentators claim streaming platforms have reduced production costs — as someone who reads the budgets, I promise you they have never been higher. Critics complain that television is becoming less creative, while the boldest storytelling of my lifetime is happening right now. The real shift is this: viewer habits now influence how series are made. The platforms know the exact minute you paused, the episode where you gave up, the scene you replayed. That data flows back to writers like me, shaping episode length, story pacing, even which characters survive. Whether we admit it or not, the audience has joined the writing team.

Let me tell you about the book everyone in my reading club is talking about — a new biography of a famous physicist. Why has it become so popular? People guess the usual reasons. Some assume a famous celebrity endorsed it on television; nobody did. Others think it must be full of colourful illustrations; in fact it contains hardly any pictures at all. The real reason is the writing itself: the author uses simple language to describe complex ideas. Quantum physics, relativity, the strange behaviour of light — everything is explained through everyday comparisons that a reader with no scientific background can follow. My neighbour, who left school at sixteen, finished it in a weekend and then explained an experiment to me over the fence. That is what good science writing does, and the bestseller lists show how rare it is.
Of course, no successful book escapes criticism, and this one has its share. Interestingly, the critics do not complain that it focuses too much on entertainment instead of facts — the science has been checked and praised. Nor does anyone call it too short to be meaningful; at four hundred pages, it is substantial. What people actually criticize is that it is very similar to the author's previous book about the same scientist. The structure, the tone, even some of the stories repeat. Readers who loved the first book call this familiarity comfortable; reviewers call it lazy. Either way, if you have not read the earlier biography, this problem will not bother you at all.
