question_text: Put the sentences in the correct order.
options: Families had a great time sampling healthy snacks and learning useful tips about overall wellness.
The wellness fair took place on Saturday afternoon, promoting healthy habits and lifestyles.
After the workshops, prizes were given to those with the most creative health posters.
The fair also featured activities such as cooking demonstrations, mindfulness sessions and a fun run.
Over sixty participants joined the event, with Dr Patel leading an exciting fitness workshop.
Then, we presented our topic for 10 minutes.
Finally, each group member took turns answering the questions.
First, we prepared the materials for our group presentation.
Throughout the presentation, we used images to explain our ideas.
After the presentation, other students asked questions.
explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
Dạng sắp xếp câu: tìm câu mở đầu (không trỏ ngược), rồi bám vào đại từ, từ chỉ định và từ nối để nối dần.

▸ Wellness fair — thứ tự đúng:
  0. "Last weekend, the community organised a special event to inspire people to live healthier lives." → câu cho sẵn, giới thiệu sự kiện.
  1. "The wellness fair took place on Saturday afternoon, promoting healthy habits and lifestyles." → gọi tên sự kiện đã nhắc ở câu cho sẵn và cho mốc thời gian.
  2. "Over sixty participants joined the event, with Dr Patel leading an exciting fitness workshop." → "the event" trỏ về hội chợ, thêm số người và hoạt động đầu tiên.
  3. "The fair also featured activities such as cooking demonstrations, mindfulness sessions and a fun run." → "also" nối thêm hoạt động sau workshop.
  4. "After the workshops, prizes were given to those with the most creative health posters." → "After the workshops" nối tiếp ngay sau các workshop/hoạt động vừa nêu, kể phần trao giải.
  5. "Families had a great time sampling healthy snacks and learning useful tips about overall wellness." → câu kết: tổng kết cảm nhận chung của người tham dự về cả sự kiện.

▸ A group presentation — thứ tự đúng:
  1. “First, we prepared the materials for our group presentation.” → câu mở đầu: nêu chủ thể và bối cảnh, không trỏ ngược về câu nào.
  2. “Then, we presented our topic for 10 minutes.” → mốc thời gian “Then” — kể tiếp sự việc vừa xảy ra.
  3. “Throughout the presentation, we used images to explain our ideas.” → nối tiếp mạch nội dung của câu ngay trước.
  4. “After the presentation, other students asked questions.” → mốc thời gian “After” — kể tiếp sự việc vừa xảy ra.
  5. “Finally, each group member took turns answering the questions.” → mốc thời gian “Finally” — kể tiếp sự việc vừa xảy ra.

sentences.text: Families had a great time sampling healthy snacks and learning useful tips about overall wellness.

extra_data.instruction: The sentences below make a complete text. Put them in the correct order.
givenSentences: Last weekend, the community organised a special event to inspire people to live healthier lives.

question_text: Media exaggerates the benefits of the programme
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
M: There have been so many volunteer events recently that it's almost impossible not to talk about them on my podcast.
W: Fair enough.
M: First of all, these volunteer groups have become incredibly popular — the media everywhere is covering them. But honestly, I think what these events actually achieve is being blown out of proportion.
W: I agree with you there. The press keeps saying these groups are going to change the whole world and fix the environment, when in fact they only deal with a tiny part of the problem. There are plenty of other issues going on.
M: Like littering — for me that's one of the biggest problems in society today. People assume dropping one wrapper has a tiny effect, but it all adds up until it becomes a huge issue.
W: Hmm, I'm not sure it's as serious as you make out — there are far bigger things to worry about. But let's leave that to one side. What I want to say is that these volunteers are getting a lot of publicity — interviews, posts, articles — and I think that's a good thing. Whether they do it for fame, for personal reasons or for the community, it makes no difference to the result: it still draws more people into volunteering.
M: I don't see it that way. If people who volunteer for their own benefit get all that publicity, it doesn't just attract more volunteers — it can backfire. You end up with people volunteering to boost their ego rather than to help the community, and that does change what the programme achieves.
W: OK, let's go back to the litter problem, since you feel so strongly about it. What do you think should be done?
M: The best approach is to introduce penalties. Other countries have very tough punishments — heavy fines, even prison — and the figures show those countries have far lower rates of littering.
W: I'll accept the figures, but I don't think punishment is the most appropriate answer here. A fine changes behaviour for a week and then people forget. What actually works is education and making it easy to do the right thing — more bins, clearer signs, campaigns in schools. Change the habit, not just the price of breaking it.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key theo đề thật 16/9: Media exaggerates = Both · Littering main problem = Man · Volunteers' motivations don't affect the outcome = Woman · Punishment most effective = Man.
1. Media exaggerates the benefits → Both: anh nói "blown out of proportion", cô "I agree with you there".
2. Littering is a major problem → The man: "one of the biggest problems in society today". Cô không đồng ý: "I'm not sure it's as serious as you make out".
3. Motivations do not affect the outcome → The woman: "Whether they do it for fame, for personal reasons or for the community, it makes no difference to the result". Anh phản bác: "it can backfire... that does change what the programme achieves".
4. Punishment is the most effective way → The man: "The best approach is to introduce penalties". Cô: "I don't think punishment is the most appropriate answer".
👉 Mẹo: câu 2 và 3 là bẫy — người nói đồng ý với SỐ LIỆU nhưng không đồng ý với KẾT LUẬN thì vẫn không phải Both.

question_text: Children are interested in tech-based learning
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
Man: I've been considering the way children and teenagers use technology these days. Many of them seem eager to learn through devices such as computers, tablets, and various educational applications.
Woman: I think so too. Digital learning activities often make lessons more engaging, and students are generally enthusiastic about using technological tools in the classroom.
Man: On the other hand, technology may have a negative impact on communication skills. Because some children spend a great deal of time online, they can struggle to interact with others in person.
Woman: That's a good point. Although they may be comfortable communicating through texts or online messages, they sometimes lack confidence when having face-to-face conversations.
Man: Another concern is that a lot of parents are unsure how to control or monitor their children's use of technology. Families may need more guidance to establish suitable boundaries and rules at home.
Woman: I understand that concern, but I also think children are capable of managing their own online behaviour. If they receive the right education and support, they can learn when to limit their screen time and how to communicate appropriately and responsibly on the internet.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Người nam nói trẻ em "seem eager to learn through devices such as computers, tablets, and various educational applications." Người phụ nữ đồng tình: "I think so too. Digital learning activities often make lessons more engaging."
2. Người nam nêu: "they can struggle to interact with others in person." Người phụ nữ đồng ý: "That's a good point... they sometimes lack confidence when having face-to-face conversations."
3. Người nam lo ngại: "a lot of parents are unsure how to control or monitor their children's use of technology. Families may need more guidance..."
4. Người phụ nữ phản biện: "I also think children are capable of managing their own online behaviour. If they receive the right education and support, they can learn when to limit their screen time."

question_text: Why did the new podcast fail?
options: The content was too long
The creators did not promote their show effectively
It faced too much competition
explanation:
Let us talk about the podcast that everyone predicted would succeed — and did not. The interviews were thoughtful, the sound was clean, and the episodes were a reasonable length; anyone claiming the content ran too long has not checked, because most episodes finished under forty minutes and listeners who started them stayed to the end. Nor was the market to blame. Yes, podcasting is crowded, but during those same months several smaller shows in noisier categories found their audiences and grew. The failure had one address: promotion. The creators uploaded each episode and simply waited, assuming discovery would happen by itself. No clips shared online, no visits to neighbouring shows, no message to the communities who would have loved the topic. In podcasting, the microphone is only half the work; the megaphone is the other half, and they never picked it up.
Does one quiet failure say anything bad about podcasting itself? I think not, and I will go further. Dismissing the medium as a waste of time — as some critics still do — misses what actually happens between a host and a loyal audience. Calling it mere entertainment for the commute sells it equally short. A good podcast is one of the great community builders of our age. Strangers gather around a shared curiosity, week after week, write in with their stories, and meet in comment threads and live events. Radio spoke to millions; podcasts gather thousands into rooms — and the rooms are what matter.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant podcast #3. Phương án "too many listeners" đã thay bằng "It faced too much competition".)
1. Đáp án: The creators did not promote their show effectively. Bẫy: "content too long" ("has not checked") và "competition" ("several smaller shows... grew").
2. Đáp án: It is a great way to build a community. Bẫy: "waste of time" và "only entertainment" — "misses what actually happens... sells it equally short".

question_text: Four people are talking about doing exercise. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: Exercise has become essential in my life, especially with my demanding and stressful job. The workload can be overwhelming at times, leaving me feeling exhausted and overwhelmed. That's why I turn to exercise as a way to unwind and rejuvenate. Whether it's going for a run, practicing yoga, or even just taking a brisk walk, exercise helps me release stress and clear my mind. I've noticed that after exercising, I feel more focused, energized, and ready to tackle my work with renewed vigor. It's incredible how something as simple as exercise can greatly improve my work performance and overall well-being. Speaker B: Honestly? Exercise wears me out. The idea of getting all sweaty and sore doesn't excite me at all. Every time I try to work out, it feels like I'm running on empty within minutes. And people say it gives them energy? Are we talking about the same thing? I feel more tired just thinking about the treadmill. I know it's supposed to be good for me, and I try to do it for my health, but I don't get that rush people talk about. Exercise for me is just exhausting. Why do something that makes me want to lie down for three days afterward? Speaker C: Exercising is a blast when you're with the right people. I've joined a few group classes, and they're like a party every time. The music is pumping, everyone's in sync, and it feels like we're all in this together. Working out alone can get boring, but with friends, you laugh, you encourage each other, and suddenly, an hour has flown by. We push each other, you know? It's kind of amazing half the time, I forget I'm even working out. I actually look forward to it. The camaraderie makes it worth every minute. Speaker D: Exercise? Ugh, I can't stand it. I know it's supposed to be good for you and all that, but I find it completely miserable. The sweat, the strain, the way my muscles burn afterward, it's like a punishment. People say it'll get better or that I'll start to like it eventually, but I've tried, and I still hate it. Honestly, life's too short to spend it doing something you can't stand. There are other ways to be healthy that don't involve torturing myself. I'd rather read a book than jog any day.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
• Improve work performance → Speaker A: tập xong "I feel more focused, energized, and ready to tackle my work" — tập để làm việc tốt hơn.
• Hate exercising → Speaker D: "I can't stand it... it's like a punishment", đã thử nhưng vẫn ghét.
• Find exercise tiring → Speaker B: "Exercise wears me out... it feels like I'm running on empty within minutes" — thấy mệt chứ không thấy khỏe ra.
• Have fun exercising with others → Speaker C: "Exercising is a blast when you're with the right people", tập nhóm vui như đi tiệc.
• Enjoy exercising alone và Exercise to lose weight là 2 phương án nhiễu — C còn nói ngược lại ("Working out alone can get boring"), và không ai nhắc tới giảm cân.

⚠️ Phân biệt B và D: cả hai đều KHÔNG thích tập, nhưng B nhấn vào cảm giác KIỆT SỨC (tiring), còn D nói thẳng là GHÉT (hate).

extra_data.title: Consumer age

headings.text: Important lessons for all of us

paragraphs.text: In today's modern consumer age, people tend to own more than they used to. A worker only has 5-6 pairs of shoes in his entire life. And he will repair them when they break or wear out, not throw them away. Nowadays, if we have a phone, it is expected that you will use such electronic devices throughout your life.

Mrs. Judith Levine - a journalist and her husband decided to change their lifestyle to be as minimalist as possible. They only buy what is absolutely necessary, such as food for work. They do not go to the cinema, cafes, restaurants. As a writer, I can say that she is saving for a purpose of publishing her findings as a book.

To make this experiment as realistic as possible, Ms. Levine and her husband decided not to tell anyone, because they knew that once their friends knew about this plan, they would mention the issue of paying for the couple's share when they went out together. Therefore, the couple was determined to keep it a secret from friends, family and strangers.

Published in 2006, the book Not Buying It when reread 10 years later still holds its value. They believe that journalist Ms. Levine has the ability to predict future consumer trends. The minimalist lifestyle she mentioned has become a trend today.

The couple wanted to buy a gift as a gift. However, that went against their point of not buying unnecessary things. And they decided to make it themselves to have a lower spending level. However, none of them have any aesthetic talent, so they finally decided to give a meaningful and practical gift to the recipient, which is a piece of their jewelry.
Ms. Levine does not have an office, which is quite inconvenient when she has to meet partners in a coffee shop. When working alone, she often goes to the public library and finds it very convenient.
Lessons about minimalism in today's consumer trends: buy things that are really necessary, switch from driving cars and motorbikes to cycling and walking.

question_text: The internet makes education more accessible
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
Woman: That looks interesting. What are you up to?
Man: Oh, I just came across this interesting report about universities and how they're evolving in the digital age. It talked about the impact of the internet, student experiences, and even competition between institutions. It got me thinking, there's so much to unpack when it comes to how education is changing, don't you think?
Woman: Yeah, I've been reading about similar things lately. It's amazing how different opinions can be on what makes a good university experience. I think we can both agree that the internet has made education more accessible. It's great how people from different backgrounds can now access high-quality education without being physically on campus.
Man: Absolutely, I agree with that. It's a game-changer for those who can't afford to relocate or attend in person. But I still believe that social interactions are a crucial part of university life. Online education can never truly replace the friendships, group work, and networking that happen in a physical setting.
Woman: Hmm, I'm not so sure. While social interactions can be important, I think online learning allows students to focus more on their studies without all the distractions of campus life. Not everyone benefits from that kind of environment.
Man: I see your point, but I think universities provide a unique space for students to develop their social skills alongside their academic ones. Another thing I'm really in favor of is encouraging competition between universities. When universities compete, it drives innovation and pushes them to offer better resources.
Woman: I disagree there. Competition can sometimes lead to universities focusing too much on rankings and flashy features instead of the quality of education. It can become more about marketing than genuine improvement.
Man: That's a fair concern. But competition also forces universities to constantly improve, which can benefit students in the long run. What about the diversity in curricula? I'm curious where you stand on that.
Woman: To be honest, I'm not a fan of having too many options in the curriculum. A diverse curriculum sounds good in theory, but it can overwhelm students and take away from the depth of learning in core subjects.
Man: I can see that perspective, but I think having variety gives students the flexibility to explore different fields. It can be especially beneficial for those who are unsure of their career paths.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Người phụ nữ nói: "I think we can both agree that the internet has made education more accessible." Người nam trả lời: "Absolutely, I agree with that."
2. Người nam nhấn mạnh: "But I still believe that social interactions are a crucial part of university life." (Tương tác xã hội là thành phần quan trọng đối với đời sống đại học).
3. Người phụ nữ bày tỏ quan điểm: "To be honest, I'm not a fan of having too many options in the curriculum. A diverse curriculum sounds good in theory, but it can overwhelm students..."
4. Người nam ủng hộ ý tưởng này: "Another thing I'm really in favor of is encouraging competition between universities."

extra_data.title: Early Australia

headings.text: Technology helps uncover the ocean’s secret
A new evidence that leads to speculation
Determination of the explorers through the ages

paragraphs.text: Some researchers are rethinking the traditional narrative of how Australia was settled. While it is widely believed that the first people arrived via land bridges from Southeast Asia during the Ice Age, new theories suggest otherwise. Alternative histories propose that early humans may have used rudimentary boats to cross from distant shores far earlier than previously estimated. These claims are controversial but are supported by some archaeological findings and oral traditions of Indigenous communities. Such ideas challenge the Eurocentric view of exploration and emphasize the ingenuity of early seafarers long before written records existed.

The vast Australian outback and its harsh deserts have long posed a formidable challenge to resettlement and development. For thousands of years, the central areas of the continent were difficult to inhabit due to extreme heat, scarce water sources, and isolation. Even after European arrival, these natural barriers prevented deeper exploration and settlement for decades. Today, the environment still remains an obstacle, limiting infrastructure, agriculture, and population growth in these regions. The Australian landscape, while beautiful and iconic, continues to shape the way communities are formed and connected.

Advancements in marine technology have revolutionized our understanding of ancient migration routes to Australia. Underwater sonar mapping and satellite imaging have revealed submerged land masses and potential seafaring paths once used by early humans. Archaeologists are now uncovering tools and fossils deep beneath coastal waters, which provide new insights into how long ago people arrived on the continent. These discoveries would not be possible without modern equipment that allows exploration of areas previously inaccessible. As research continues, scientists hope to fill in many historical gaps that have puzzled historians for centuries.

It is now widely believed that the journey to Australia wasn't completed in one go. Instead, early humans likely reached the continent in stages, moving through island chains and coastal areas over generations. This theory is supported by the distribution of artifacts and remains across Southeast Asia and Northern Australia. The idea of gradual migration, rather than a single wave, helps explain the diversity of early populations found on the continent. This step-by-step approach also reflects how ancient peoples adapted to different environments as they moved closer to the Australian mainland.

In recent years, new evidence has emerged from both land and sea, prompting scientists to re-evaluate earlier assumptions. A set of ancient tools discovered in a Northern Territory cave doesn't match previously known Aboriginal designs, leading some to speculate about earlier migrations or even contact with other civilizations. Additionally, genetic studies hint at complex interactions with now-extinct human species. These findings, while not yet definitive, open the door to exciting discussions and possibilities about Australia's earliest human history.

Many of the first explorers to attempt crossing Australia's interior were ill-prepared for the harsh conditions they encountered. Without sufficient knowledge of the land or survival skills in such a hostile environment, numerous expeditions ended in tragedy. The lack of understanding of the Aboriginal methods of finding water, navigating terrain, and managing heat led to avoidable suffering. It wasn't until later that European settlers began to adapt, learning from Indigenous Australians how to travel and survive in such an unfamiliar landscape.

Despite the many difficulties, both ancient and modern explorers showed incredible perseverance in reaching and understanding Australia. Whether navigating unknown seas in simple rafts or trekking across searing deserts with limited supplies, their determination pushed the boundaries of what was thought possible. Stories of survival and discovery continue to inspire awe, reminding us of the strength and courage required to explore the unknown. Through the centuries, this spirit of exploration has become a core part of Australian history and identity.

question_text: What does she say about working at home?
options: There are no distractions
Not good as expected
Video calls are superior to face-to-face conversation
explanation:
Before I began working from home, I imagined paradise: no commute, no meetings that could have been emails, and above all, silence. I truly believed there would be no distractions once the chatting colleagues were gone. Reality re-educated me within a week. The distractions did not disappear; they changed uniform. The washing machine calls, the doorbell rings, the fridge whispers, and family members assume that being home means being available. As for video calls — useful, yes, but let nobody tell you they beat face-to-face conversation. Explaining a complicated problem through a frozen screen and a delayed microphone cured me of that idea permanently. So when friends ask for my honest verdict after a full year, I give them three words: not as expected. There are real advantages, but the dream and the reality live at different addresses.
Let me pass on what I have actually learned. First, forget the magazine photos — you do not need a big home office. My best work happens at a small desk in the corner of the bedroom. Second, do not believe anyone who says this lifestyle requires no self-motivation; with nobody watching, discipline is the entire game. And the biggest lesson: there is no universal answer. How well working from home goes depends on your situation and your personality. My neighbour thrives alone; I miss the noise of other humans. Learn which kind of worker you are — preferably before you sign anything.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 02 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Not good as expected. Bẫy: "no distractions" ("changed uniform") và "video calls superior" ("cured me of that idea").
2. Đáp án: It depends on your situation and personality. Bẫy: "big home office" và "no self-motivation" đều bị phủ định.

extra_data.title: Coffee

headings.text: A remedy of unjust revenue distribution
Coffee encourages the art of conversation
A habit that has become a big economy
Health risks versus health benefits debate
The custom of coffee drinking begins to spread

paragraphs.text: The custom of drinking coffee has been around for a long time, perhaps as long as 1500 years ago. There were times when drinking coffee was banned in many places. At that time, coffee houses were opened in some places in Egypt and Ethiopia. Later, the custom of drinking coffee spread to Italy and all over Europe. Not long after that, the Dutch introduced coffee to Asia. Later, the habit of drinking coffee became popular all over the world.

Coffee was first used in Africa but Europe is known as the largest coffee consuming region in the world. In the 18th century, many people from different professions such as writers, philosophers and politicians used coffee to stay awake during discussions and meetings. Coffee houses became meeting places for people to share ideas and debate hot topics in society. These places made it easy for people to share their intellectual thoughts and played an important role in business and society at that time.

Nowadays, many people have the habit of drinking coffee in the morning to wake up, or going to coffee shops in the evening to meet and socialize with each other. Coffee shops are popping up everywhere, providing places for people to relax and talk to each other. Coffee has become a global business, with personal coffee makers even appearing in households. Famous global coffee brands have become giant companies, using their brands and communication strategies to attract millions of coffee lovers around the world.

Coffee consumption in Europe accounts for about 90% of global coffee production, making it the largest market in the world. Meanwhile, some other countries in Africa such as Egypt and Ethiopia rely heavily on coffee exports to sustain their economies. However, there is a problem of injustice: workers in these African countries face terrible living and working conditions, with incomes as low as $1 a day. While wealthy European countries make huge profits from coffee, people in coffee-growing countries do not receive a fair share of their efforts and hard work.

To address this injustice, certification schemes for agricultural production have been introduced. If coffee meets certain certification standards, it can be sold at fair prices, preventing growers from having to sell at rock-bottom prices. However, there are problems with this solution. In reality, only about 5% of coffee meets the standards. Many small coffee producers in developing countries are too poor to pay the certification fees, leaving them even further behind in the global coffee market.

There is much debate about the effects of coffee on human health. It is true that coffee can help many people stay awake and concentrate. It contains antioxidants, which can help prevent diseases. But while drinking coffee, people often add sugar and milk and these can be harmful to your health. This can easily cause diseases such as diabetes or obesity for those who use it.

There is a legend about coffee. In the past, a monk observed that birds became more active and lively when they ate a small fruit. The monk then drank the juice from the fruit and stayed awake praying and talking until late at night. So it can be said that thanks to these birds, people knew about the coffee plant.

question_text: Exhibitions should be different and diverse
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
M: So the new cultural centre opens next month. Has anyone told you what's actually going in it?
W: Only scraps. But if I had any say, I'd want the exhibitions changing all the time. Folk art one month, photography the next, then something borrowed from abroad. A proper mixture.
M: I'm not so sure about that, honestly. A place like that needs one clear identity. If you chop and change every few weeks, nobody ever works out what the building is for.
W: Oh, I'd find that deadly dull. Same cases, same labels, year after year.
M: Well, we see it differently. What does genuinely worry me is that the old customs are quietly fading away. Hardly anyone under thirty knows the words to anything any more.
W: I agree with you there, completely. My grandmother could name every single step of the harvest dance. My sister's children have never even heard of it.
M: Exactly. It slips away in one generation and then it's gone.
W: It really does.
M: Which is why I'd say the village festivals themselves will have vanished within ten or fifteen years. Finished.
W: Hang on, that's far too gloomy. I'll grant you the crowds are smaller than they were, but disappear? No. They shrink, they change shape, and then somebody's daughter revives them. I don't see it that way at all. Ours died out in the eighties and it's back now, bigger than ever.
M: And the other thing is the classroom. It's the schools that will decide what the next lot grow up caring about. Put it on the timetable and you've saved it.
W: I really don't think so. Children take their values from home, not from a lesson on a wet Tuesday afternoon. A school can tick a box; it can't make anybody care.
M: I'd still back the teachers over the parents, every time. Give me one hour a week on that timetable and I'd change a whole generation.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: Triển lãm nên đa dạng, luôn đổi mới = Woman · Phong tục truyền thống đang mất dần ý nghĩa = Both · Lễ hội địa phương sẽ biến mất = Man · Trường học quan trọng với thế hệ sau = Man
1. Exhibitions should be different and diverse → Woman: Nữ nêu "I'd want the exhibitions changing all the time. Folk art one month, photography the next". Nam phản đối: "I'm not so sure about that, honestly. A place like that needs one clear identity."
2. Traditional customs are gradually losing their significance → Both: Nam nêu "the old customs are quietly fading away". Nữ tán thành: "I agree with you there, completely."
3. Local festivals will disappear in the near future → Man: Nam nêu "the village festivals themselves will have vanished within ten or fifteen years". Nữ phản đối: "I'll grant you the crowds are smaller than they were, but disappear? No."
4. Schools are important in shaping future generations → Man: Nam nêu "It's the schools that will decide what the next lot grow up caring about." Nữ phản đối: "I really don't think so. Children take their values from home, not from a lesson on a wet Tuesday afternoon."
👉 Mẹo: Ở ý 3 nữ nhượng bộ một nửa ("I'll grant you the crowds are smaller") rồi mới bác bỏ — nghe thấy "I'll grant you" đừng vội chọn Both, hãy nghe hết câu sau chữ "but".

question_text: Singers can be good role models for young people.
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
W: You took your daughter to that concert on Saturday, didn't you? How did it go?
M: Brilliant, thanks. And I came away thinking the singer was actually rather a good influence on her. People up on that stage can set a genuinely positive example for teenagers.
W: I'm not so sure about that, to be honest. They're performers, not teachers. Handing them that kind of responsibility seems risky to me.
M: Some of them handle it rather well, though, in fairness.
W: One or two, maybe. Anyway, she and I could never agree on what to put on in the car. I've always thought what you like in music is completely your own business. Nobody can argue you out of it.
M: Oh, I agree with you entirely there. I gave up trying to convert anybody to my records years ago.
W: Quite right too. Although I do think there's something that goes beyond all that. Put a piece of music on anywhere in the world and people respond the same way. It speaks across everything.
M: Hmm, I don't see it that way. I'll accept that a good tune travels, certainly, but the meaning doesn't travel with it. What sounds joyful to me might well be a funeral song somewhere else.
W: That's rather a bleak way of looking at it, if you ask me.
M: Realistic, I'd say. Sensible, even.
W: Well, here's one you might come round to. I'm convinced music gets used quite deliberately to push us about emotionally. Think of adverts, or the soundtrack in any film.
M: No, you're absolutely right there. Supermarkets do it, adverts do it, everybody does it. Slow the tempo right down and people apparently wander round the aisles and spend more.
W: Frightening, really, when you stop and think about it.
M: It works, though. That's precisely why they keep on doing it.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
Key: Ca sĩ có thể là hình mẫu tốt cho giới trẻ = Man · Gu âm nhạc là chuyện rất cá nhân = Both · Âm nhạc là ngôn ngữ toàn cầu = Woman · Âm nhạc có thể thao túng cảm xúc = Both

1. Singers can be good role models for young people. → Man: người đàn ông nêu "People up on that stage can set a genuinely positive example for teenagers." Người phụ nữ phản đối: "I'm not so sure about that, to be honest. They're performers, not teachers."

2. Taste in music is a highly personal thing. → Both: người phụ nữ nêu "what you like in music is completely your own business. Nobody can argue you out of it." Người đàn ông tán thành: "Oh, I agree with you entirely there."

3. Music is a universal language → Woman: người phụ nữ nêu "Put a piece of music on anywhere in the world and people respond the same way. It speaks across everything." Người đàn ông phản đối: "Hmm, I don't see it that way... the meaning doesn't travel with it."

4. Music can be used to manipulate people's feelings → Both: người phụ nữ nêu "music gets used quite deliberately to push us about emotionally", người đàn ông đồng ý rõ: "No, you're absolutely right there. Supermarkets do it, adverts do it, everybody does it."

👉 Mẹo: Bẫy ở ý 3 — người đàn ông nói "I'll accept that a good tune travels" nghe rất giống đồng ý, nhưng ngay sau đó bác bỏ phần cốt lõi (ý nghĩa không đi theo), nên đáp án là Woman chứ không phải Both.

question_text: What does the speaker say is one major strength of successful television series?
options: They focus mainly on famous actors
They maintain consistent quality throughout
They are usually shorter than films
explanation:
Every year my students ask me to name the secret of a successful television series, hoping for a shortcut. Here is the honest lecture. The shortcuts people believe in are famous actors — and yet the graveyard of cancelled shows is full of A-list faces — and shorter running times, the idea that episodes beat films simply by asking less of your evening. Neither survives contact with the ratings data. The quality that actually predicts long life is consistency. The series that run for years maintain their standard from first episode to last: the writing stays sharp in season six, the acting stays committed, the production never visibly saves money. Audiences are generous with a single weak hour, but they are merciless with decline. The moment a show feels like it has stopped trying, the loyalty it spent years building evaporates in weeks.
As for how series are made today, ignore two fashionable complaints. Streaming did not make production cheap — budgets have climbed to historic highs. And television is not growing less creative; by any honest measure this is a bold era. The real transformation is quieter and more interesting: viewer habits now shape production itself. Platforms watch us watching — where we pause, what we skip, when we abandon — and that data flows back into the writers' rooms, adjusting episode lengths, pacing, even storylines. For the first time since the medium was born, the audience is not just receiving television. It is quietly co-writing it.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant TV series #3.)
1. Đáp án: They maintain consistent quality throughout. Bẫy: "famous actors" và "shorter than films" — "Neither survives contact with the ratings data".
2. Đáp án: Viewer habits influence the way that series are made. Bẫy: "reduced production costs" và "less creative" đều bị bác.

extra_data.title: Charles Dicken

paragraphs.text: The popularity of Dickens's works in our time remains a global phenomenon. Although he wrote his novels in the 19th century, his works have had a global impact. In addition, these masterpieces helped connect Renaissance drama to the multimedia revolution. Many readers find the characters and themes surprisingly modern.

Shakespeare's plays are difficult to understand and sometimes require the reader to struggle or think twice to figure out the character's thoughts. Sometimes the dialogue tends to be emotional without any connection to the context of the story. There are many passages that are a confusing mess of single words and old classical vocabulary.

Hamlet is a Renaissance tragedy written by Shakespeare. The play is very long and has plot twists that keep the reader guessing. Dickens had a special interest in the work. He told his daughter to keep an eye on Hamlet. For Dickens' novels, he sometimes created serial editions, with new chapters released monthly, keeping readers eagerly awaiting the next issue.

Dickens' legacy is undeniable. His works have been translated and used in over 100 countries and are studied by most schoolchildren in the world. It has even been said that Dickens' legacy belongs not to one era but to all times. It is easy to see that Dickens lives on in society and culture through his language and through his enduring influence on education and the media.

Dickens achieved success at a young age. His first novel, The Pickwick Papers, was published when he was only 24 and became a bestseller. His success increased throughout the 1590s. He was honored as a member of the Lord Chamber Men - those lucky enough to perform for the Queen of England on many occasions. Alongside his novels and plays, he also published many poems in his own style.

As Dickens's reputation grew, the question arose whether to preserve his legacy and make it live on. Dickens himself was always keen to make his mark and to maintain his uniqueness. He even attempted to break the dominance of the popular comedies of the time with a series of dramatic plays.

To mark the 400th anniversary of Dickens’ death, there will be a number of events to help readers, and especially students, better understand his works. There will be videos detailing the content of each of his works to help people excitedly explore the pinnacle of language and the meaning his works bring to our daily lives.

question_text: Why hasn't he gone to college?
options: He couldn't afford the tuition fees.
He wasn't ready to start higher education.
He didn't get good enough grades.
explanation:
On today's education programme, a story I often share with worried parents: the young man who did not go to college with his classmates. Why not? The neighbourhood had theories. Money troubles, whispered some — wrong; the family had saved carefully and could afford the fees. Poor grades, assumed others — wrong again; his results were comfortably good enough. The real reason was the one nobody guessed because it sounds so simple: he was not ready for higher education. He told his parents that his mind felt like a full cup — pour in more, and everything would spill. Rather than waste the most expensive years of his education arriving empty, he asked for time. To their credit, they gave it.
What did the break actually give him back? He spent months working part-time in a bakery, but he laughs when people assume the job was the lesson — it mostly taught him to wake at four. He returned valuing education more than ever, yet even that, he insists, was not the point. The real lesson of his break was independence. He learned to run his own timetable, answer for his own mistakes, and make decisions without a teacher's rubric or a parent's reminder. When he finally began university a year later, tutors described him as the most self-directed student in the room. The year everyone called lost, he now calls the most efficient year of his education.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant gap year #3 — góc người dẫn chương trình.)
1. Đáp án: He wasn't ready to start higher education. Bẫy: "tuition fees" và "grades" là "theories" bị bác.
2. Đáp án: How to be more independent. Bẫy: "working part-time" ("mostly taught him to wake at four") và "importance of education" ("not the point").

question_text: What is the speaker's opinion about security cameras at work?
options: People are unnecessarily worried about them
Most people don't even realize cameras are present
Cameras should be placed to ensure complete coverage
explanation:
When the security cameras appeared in our office last spring, the reaction was immediate. Colleagues whispered about being watched, and a few genuinely believed management had stopped trusting us. Months later, I can offer a calmer view: people are unnecessarily worried about these cameras. And let me correct two claims I keep hearing. First, the idea that most staff do not even notice the cameras — untrue in our building, where everyone noticed within an hour and discussed nothing else for a week. Second, one colleague's campaign for cameras covering every single corner of every room — an overreaction in the opposite direction that would help nobody. The cameras sit in shared spaces: entrances, corridors, the storage area. They are there for safety, not surveillance, and no one reviews footage without a reason.
Think practically about what the cameras actually do for us. If equipment disappears or an accident happens near the loading door, there is finally a record instead of a guessing game. Their quiet presence also discourages trouble before it starts. I know some people still find them intimidating, and others repeat that cameras only matter after something bad has already happened. I would ask both groups to reconsider. We should feel reassured by their presence, not threatened. A company that installs safety equipment is not accusing its staff — it is protecting them. Once that idea settles in, the little lens above the doorway stops feeling like an eye and starts feeling like a seatbelt.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 08 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: People are unnecessarily worried about them. Bẫy: "don't realize cameras are present" ("untrue in our building") và "complete coverage" ("overreaction").
2. Đáp án: People should feel reassured about their presence. Bẫy: "intimidating" và "only useful after incidents" — "I would ask both groups to reconsider".

question_text: Why do people like to change the look of their homes?
explanation: I think people like to change the look of their homes for several reasons. The most common one is that living in the same space for a long time can feel boring, so even a small change such as new paint or new furniture makes the house feel fresh again. Another reason is that our needs change over time. For example, when someone starts working from home, they may need to turn a spare room into an office. Finally, a home shows who we are, so people decorate it to express their personality and to feel proud when friends or relatives come to visit.

question_text: What does the expert say being professional is all about?
options: To maintain a positive attitude
To create a good working environment
To make a good impression
explanation:
Good morning, and thank you for inviting me to speak about professionalism. When I ask audiences what the word means, I hear the same two answers everywhere. Creating a good working environment, say the managers. Making a good impression, say the juniors. Fine answers — but notice that both describe outcomes, not causes. In my view, professionalism is, at its centre, about maintaining a positive attitude. The colleague who stays constructive on a bad day, who greets the difficult client with patience, who offers help before being asked — that attitude is the seed. The pleasant environment and the strong impression are simply what grows from it. Get the attitude right and the rest arrives on its own; fake the rest without the attitude and everyone notices within a month.
The second thing I want to say is about time. Some people in this room may believe professionalism means today what it meant forty years ago — the suit, the firm handshake, the strict hierarchy. It does not. Others may hope that once they learn today's rules, the definition will finally hold still. It will not. Our definition of professionalism is changing, and it keeps changing. Flexibility now sits where formality sat; cultural understanding matters as much as punctuality; using new tools well counts as basic manners. The professionals who flourish are not the ones who memorised one era's rulebook — they are the ones who notice when the rulebook is being rewritten. Thank you.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 01 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: To maintain a positive attitude. Bẫy: "good working environment" và "good impression" — "both describe outcomes, not causes".
2. Đáp án: Our definition of it is changing. Bẫy: "same as 40 years ago" ("It does not") và "will not change anymore" ("It will not").

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I had a fairly unpleasant experience in a phone shop in Ba Dinh about eighteen months ago. I went in to complain about a handset that kept restarting itself. The young man behind the counter barely looked up. He told me it was obviously my fault for installing too many applications. Then, while I was still speaking, he turned round to chat to his colleague about lunch. What annoyed me most was not what he said. It was that he treated me as though I were invisible. At that moment I felt a hot mixture of anger and embarrassment. I went completely quiet, which is what I always do. I could feel my face burning while I gripped the receipt hard enough to crease it. Underneath the anger there was something smaller and more uncomfortable. I had been made to feel unimportant in a room full of other customers. I asked calmly to speak to the manager. She turned out to be perfectly reasonable and replaced the phone within ten minutes. I learned two things from that afternoon. The first is that staying calm is not weakness. Shouting would have felt good for about four seconds and would have got me nothing. One quiet sentence to the right person solved it. The second lesson is closer to home. extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about a time when I was surrounded by nature. It was during a trip with my school friends last February. We took a bus to a village about forty kilometres from the city and walked on a small path between the rice fields to a quiet forest. The walk took about three hours. The weather was cool and dry, and we saw buffalo, birds and a small river. We ate bread and boiled eggs under a big tree. How did I feel? At the beginning I felt hot and tired, because my shoes were not good for that path. But after one hour I felt very relaxed and light. There were no horns and no traffic, only the birds and the wind, and we did not use our phones for the whole morning. I slept very well that night. Do I think people should spend more time in nature nowadays? Yes, I do. First, it helps people reduce stress and feel calmer, because life in the city is busy and noisy. Second, walking and hiking are good for our health. Finally, it gives us a break from phones and screens. A park is free and it is near us, so even a short walk every week really helps. Now I go to the park near my house every Sunday.

groups.question: Do you think building tall towers is a good solution for growing cities? Why?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: My cousin moved into a flat on the thirty-fourth floor of a tower in Ho Chi Minh City last year. I stayed with her for a long weekend in December. Coming from a narrow three-storey house, the whole experience felt slightly unreal to me. The lift alone took nearly a minute, and I could feel my ears popping like on an aeroplane. Her living room had a glass wall facing the river. At night the traffic below looked like a slow stream of orange light with no sound at all. Given the choice, though, I would still take a house at street level, although I can see the attraction. What I loved was the silence, since there were no motorbike horns and no neighbours' karaoke. In Vietnam that is close to a miracle. Even so, I would miss the small things a ground-floor life gives you. Stepping outside for noodles in slippers, chatting to the woman who sells fruit on the corner, coming home without waiting eight minutes for a lift. On whether towers are a sensible answer for growing cities, I would say yes, with conditions. Land is limited and terribly expensive, so when millions of people want to live near their offices, the only direction left is upwards. Dense cities also mean shorter journeys. The danger is that developers build the flats and forget the park and the school. Height is fine, but height without planning is not.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: One weekend in June I visited my uncle's flat in Ho Chi Minh City. His flat is on the twentieth floor of a new building. I went up in the lift with my sister, and it was very fast. From his window I could see the whole city. The cars on the street looked very small. We stayed there for two nights and slept very well. There was no noise from the traffic at all. For me, a house at street level is still better. In a tall building the air is fresh and it is quiet. But I like to walk out of my door easily. I also like to buy breakfast near my house. In my uncle's building I had to wait for the lift every time. One morning the lift was broken, and we used the stairs. I'd say tall towers are good for growing cities. Cities have many people and not much land, so we must build up. Tall buildings give homes to many families near their work. That saves a lot of time every day. But the city must also build parks and schools near them. Without that, life in a tower is not comfortable for children.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Finishing my master's dissertation nearly broke me, and I am not usually dramatic about work. I had eleven weeks to write about eighteen thousand words. At the same time I was teaching four evenings a week. For the last month I got up at five to write before the day started. The worst point came in November, when my laptop died. I lost about two days of work because I had been careless with backups. I remember sitting on the floor of my room, not even angry, just empty. A colleague lent me an old computer and I carried on. If all that effort had not been enough, I would have felt worse than I like to admit. It is not really about the qualification. I had told everybody I was doing it. Those eleven weeks were my proof that I could still finish something hard. I would like to say I would send it again calmly. The truth is I would spend a month feeling that all that work had proved nothing. Is it better to work hard steadily or hard for a short period? My experience says steadily, although I have never quite managed it. Eleven weeks of intensity gave me a dissertation and a chest infection. groups.question: Why do you think many people struggle to learn a foreign language?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Before I applied for my current job, I signed up for a three-month evening English course at a small centre near Cau Giay. I did it purely because I panicked about the interview. Classes ran twice a week from half past six until half past eight. There were about fourteen of us, mostly office workers who arrived straight from work looking half asleep. Our teacher was a woman called Ms Hoa, who had studied in Manchester and refused to let anyone hide at the back. Her method was quite demanding. There were almost no grammar lectures, constant pair work, and a two-minute presentation every single lesson. At first I hated it. I had always learned English by writing things in a notebook, so I felt exposed speaking in front of strangers. By the sixth or seventh week, though, I realised I was thinking in English rather than translating. I have been grateful ever since. On the wider question, I think people struggle with foreign languages because they treat them as subjects to memorise rather than habits to build. You cannot really learn a language the way you learn history. There is also the fear of sounding stupid, which stops adults in particular from opening their mouths. Without speaking there is very little progress. Finally, most learners have no real reason to use the language day to day. So whatever they learn on Tuesday has quietly disappeared by the weekend.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: When I was in grade ten, I was really afraid of English. Three years ago I finally took an English course near my house. I needed better English for a new job. The class was in the evening, twice a week. There were fifteen students and most of them were office workers. Our teacher was a young woman called Ms Linh. She did not teach much grammar. Instead we practised speaking in pairs every lesson. She also gave us a short topic every week. At first I did not like her method at all. I felt shy and my face went red every time. I preferred writing new words in my notebook. But after two months I could speak more naturally. I even answered the phone in English at work. Now I am really thankful for her lessons. Her class changed my opinion about learning English. I think many people find languages difficult for three reasons. First, they study a language like a school subject. They learn rules but they never practise. So they cannot speak in a real situation. Also, they are afraid of making mistakes. So they stay quiet and they do not improve. Finally, most people do not use English in daily life. They forget the new words after one week.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Two years ago I signed up for a twenty-one kilometre run, which was ambitious for someone whose main exercise was walking to the fridge. A close friend of mine had been training for months and dared me to join her. I agreed largely because I did not want to look weak in front of her. From that evening I had four months to turn myself into somebody who could actually run. What I enjoyed most was not crossing the finishing line, surprisingly, but the ordinary training mornings in the middle. There was a week in January when I ran fourteen kilometres without stopping for the first time. I remember standing beside the lake at six in the morning, grinning at nobody in particular. I also loved having a reason to be outside before the city woke up. The quiet competition with my friend kept us both honest. Looking ahead, I have already registered for something else. In November I am attempting a full marathon in Ho Chi Minh City. That is twice the distance and, according to everyone who has done it, rather more than twice the difficulty. My training plan starts in three weeks and involves four runs a week. The long one is every Sunday morning and will eventually reach thirty kilometres. My friend is doing it again as well, so we have agreed to book the same hotel and to complain only to each other.

At first I could only run two kilometres. I bought good shoes after the first month, and my knees felt better. In November I finished the race in two hours and forty minutes. I enjoyed the training mornings more than the race day. One morning in January I ran fourteen kilometres without stopping. I stood beside the lake and I felt so happy. I also liked the quiet city before everyone woke up. The air was cool and the streets were almost empty. I am planning another challenge for next year. I will try a full marathon in Ho Chi Minh City. My training plan will start in October with four runs a week. The long run will be every Sunday morning. My friend will run with me again. We will book the same hotel near the start line.

I also loved having a reason to be outside before the city woke up. The quiet competition with my friend kept us both honest. Looking ahead, I have already registered for something else. In November I am attempting a full marathon in Ho Chi Minh City. That is twice the distance and, according to everyone who has done it, rather more than twice the difficulty. My training plan starts in three weeks and involves four runs a week. The long one is every Sunday morning and will eventually reach thirty kilometres. My friend is doing it again as well, so we have agreed to book the same hotel and to complain only to each other.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Planning my mother's sixtieth birthday party took me roughly four months, which sounds ridiculous for a single evening. She has a very large family and extremely strong opinions. I started in January with a spreadsheet and contacted about thirty relatives scattered across three provinces. Then I booked a restaurant in Hai Phong that could take fifty people. The hardest part was keeping it secret, especially since my younger brother is incapable of lying to her. What I enjoyed most, oddly, was the conspiracy. I ended up on the phone to aunts and cousins I normally speak to once a year. All of us were hiding the same thing from the same person, and that created a strange sort of closeness. I also enjoyed tracking down her two surviving school friends, which took six weeks and three wrong numbers. Right now I am in the middle of planning something else. My parents' fortieth wedding anniversary falls in December. This time I want to take them somewhere rather than throw a party, because my mother has never been on an aeroplane. I am pricing four days in Da Lat, and my brother is handling the paperwork for their identity documents. We are also trying to book the hotel my father talks about from a work trip in 1998. The difficult part will be persuading them to accept it. They will insist that the money is wasted on them.

The hardest part was keeping the secret. My little brother almost told her twice. On the day she cried when she saw everyone. What I enjoyed most was talking to my big family. I spoke to aunts and cousins that I rarely meet. We all shared the same secret, so we felt close. I also found two old school friends of my mother. That took me three weeks and many phone calls. Now I am planning something new. My parents will have their fortieth anniversary in December. This time I want to give them a holiday. My brother and I are looking at hotels in Da Lat. extra_data.sampleAnswer: About two years ago, in the spring of 2024, my cousin Linh dragged me along to the Imperial Citadel in Hue. She mainly needed somebody to carry her camera bag. I was not expecting much, since I had already seen photographs of it a hundred times. We arrived early in the morning, before the tour groups turned up. The whole place was silent apart from a gardener sweeping leaves near the main gate. The part I remember most clearly is Thai Hoa Palace, with its enormous red lacquered columns covered in gold dragons. Between old buildings and modern ones, I would choose the old ones almost every time. A new tower can be impressive for about ten minutes. An old building makes you curious. You start wondering who chose that doorway, why the roof is that shape, and what the room smelled like when it was full of people. I like the imperfection as well, the worn steps and the creaking floors. Modern buildings are more comfortable, and I would rather work in one. For the near future, I am planning a trip to Hoi An and My Son with my sister at the end of October, once the rain has eased. She has booked the tickets already. I want to see the Cham towers in particular. This time I have promised myself I will hire a proper guide, instead of wandering about reading the small signs and understanding nothing.

He said students walked for weeks to take the exams there. I took many photos of the red gates and the old trees. We stayed for about two hours and then had noodles nearby. I prefer old buildings to modern ones. A modern building looks nice, but it looks the same everywhere. An old building has a story, so I feel curious. I ask myself who lived there and how they worked. Old buildings are not comfortable, but they are interesting. Next month I will visit another old place. groups.question: Is there a habit of your own that you are planning to change soon? Tell me about it.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: About four years ago a colleague asked me to stop interrupting people in meetings. It was one of the more uncomfortable conversations of my working life. We were walking to the car park after a long planning session in the spring. He said it very calmly, without any fuss. Apparently I finished other people's sentences all the time, especially when I liked an idea. My first reaction was defensive. I remember explaining that I was only being enthusiastic and did not mean anything by it. He just nodded and let me talk myself out. By the evening I felt embarrassed. I could suddenly remember at least four times when I had done exactly that. The strange thing is that I had never noticed the habit myself. Within a week the embarrassment turned into something closer to thanks. Nobody else had bothered to tell me for years. There is another habit I am planning to deal with soon. I check my phone constantly while people are talking to me. My girlfriend pointed it out last month. She used more or less the same tone my colleague had used. From the first of next month I will leave the phone in my bag during meals and meetings. I have asked her to say something whenever she catches me. I am also going to switch off every notification except calls. I would rather be embarrassed now than told off again in four years.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: My old flatmate always said I was too slow in the morning. He was right, and two years ago my manager told me the same thing. I often arrived at the office ten minutes after nine. I thought it was a small thing. One morning she called me into her room. She spoke quietly and asked me to change. At first I felt angry and a bit embarrassed. My face was hot and I wanted to explain. I said the traffic was always bad in the morning. But that evening at home I thought about it again. I understood that she was right. My team had to wait for me every day. Since that day I have never been late again. I now leave my house ten minutes earlier. I also felt thankful, because nobody else told me. Now I have another habit that I want to change. I look at my phone too much before bed. So I sleep badly and I feel tired at work. From next Monday I will leave my phone in the kitchen at night. I will also buy a small clock for my bedroom. My sister will check me every week. I hope this new habit will last.

groups.question: What did you learn from that experience?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: There was a moment in my second year at university that I still think about. I was sitting in a statistics lecture, completely lost, and about forty other students were nodding as if everything made perfect sense. My hand went up almost before I had decided, and I asked the lecturer what the symbol on the slide actually meant. It felt like the most stupid question in the room. He paused, smiled, and said it was the question everyone should have asked. Then he spent ten minutes going back over the idea properly. These days I much prefer asking in front of everyone, although it took that lecture to convince me. Speaking to a teacher privately afterwards is far more comfortable, and it is the right choice if the question is about your own work. But asking in the room is simply quicker. The answer reaches everybody, the teacher finds out which part of the explanation failed, and the whole group moves on together. What I learned that day was that confusion is almost never mine alone. Three classmates thanked me in the corridor afterwards, because they had been just as lost. The silence had only been thirty people protecting their pride. I also learned that a few seconds of embarrassment costs far less than two weeks of pretending to understand. I use that in meetings at work now, and one awkward question early has saved my team from a very expensive misunderstanding.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: While I was still a student, I was often too shy to ask questions. One day in a statistics class I did not understand the lesson at all. There was a strange symbol on the slide, and I had no idea about it. Everyone around me looked calm, so I felt stupid. My hands were cold and my heart was fast. But I raised my hand and asked the teacher to explain it. He smiled and explained the whole idea again for ten minutes. He also drew a simple picture on the board for us. Personally, I prefer asking in front of the whole class. It saves time, because everyone hears the same answer. The teacher also learns which part was not clear for us. But for a personal problem, I speak to the teacher after the lesson. For example, I ask about my own marks in private. Three classmates thanked me in the corridor after that class. So I learned that other people are often confused too. A few seconds of shyness is better than two weeks of confusion. Now I always ask questions in meetings at work. Last month one small question saved my team a lot of money.

groups.question: Do you think a day at an amusement park is better for a family than a day in the countryside? Why?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Last April my cousin turned thirty. Instead of a quiet dinner, she took six of us to an amusement park in Ho Chi Minh City. I had not been there since I was about ten. We arrived at nine in the morning because she said the queues would double by lunchtime. She was completely right. The heat was awful and my shirt was soaked within an hour. I also lost a pair of sunglasses on the second ride. Even so, I had not laughed like that in years. If a friend asked me to go on a really frightening ride tomorrow, I would complain loudly and then get on it. That is more or less what happened with the roller coaster that day. I would spend the whole queue regretting it and arguing with myself. Then come those thirty seconds before the drop, when everybody goes quiet, and that makes it worth it. What I could not stand is being the only one at the bottom holding everybody's bags. Is a day at a park better for a family than a day in the countryside? For a mixed group I would say the park wins. It solves the problem of keeping a five-year-old and a grandmother happy in the same place. There are gentle rides, scary rides, food and shade, so nobody is left out. The countryside is cheaper and much better for you. But it asks everyone to want the same thing at the same pace.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I was about twenty when my class went to an amusement park in Da Nang. It was a very hot day in June. There were about twenty of us in the group. We ate ice cream in the shade and took a lot of photos. In the afternoon we tried a small roller coaster together. It was a simple day, but we still talk about it now. If a friend asked me to go on a very frightening ride, I would feel nervous. Personally, I would still say yes to that friend. I do not want to stand alone and hold everybody's bags. I would be afraid in the queue and very quiet before the start. After one minute I would enjoy it and want another ride. For a family with children, a day at the park is better. There are gentle rides for small children and fast rides for teenagers. So every person in the family finds something to do. The countryside is cheaper and much quieter than a park. But children get bored there after two or three hours.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: My friend Tuan and I once spent a whole afternoon in a coffee shop laughing about one photograph. It was a rainy Saturday in October, near my old office. He had found an old picture of the two of us at a school talent show in 2011. We were wearing matching shirts our mothers had chosen. We were also holding guitars that neither of us could actually play. We started retelling the story and kept correcting each other's version. Every correction was funnier than the last one. At one point the waitress came over, not to take an order, but to ask us to be a bit quieter. Afterwards I felt light, and that is hard to describe. My body was tired, as if I had been running, and my mind was completely calm. My face genuinely ached. I walked home in the rain and did not mind it at all. That night I slept properly for the first time in a very busy week. There was a little sadness under it too, because I realised how long it had been. If somebody told me they no longer laugh much with their friends, I would say the problem is usually time. Stop waiting for a free evening, because it will never appear. Put one in your diary and treat it like a work meeting. Meet the friends who know your history, and leave your phones in your bags.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: One night last August I laughed a lot with my old school friend Lan. We met in a small restaurant near my office. We had not seen each other for two years. She showed me a video from our school trip in 2014. In the video I was dancing very badly on a bus. My hair was long and my shirt was terrible. We watched it five times and we could not stop laughing. Other people in the restaurant turned and looked at us. We stayed there until the staff cleaned the tables. Afterwards I felt light and very relaxed. My face hurt a little from laughing so much. On the way home I was still smiling on my motorbike. All my problems at work felt smaller that evening. I also felt a bit sad about it. We live in the same city, but we meet only once a year. For a person who does not laugh with friends now, I have simple advice. The problem is usually time, not friendship. So put a date in your diary and keep it. Meet the old friends who know your story well. And leave your phone in your bag during dinner. Now we plan our dinners in advance.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I am not somebody who visits galleries regularly, so the exhibition I saw in Hanoi two winters ago stands out clearly. A university friend was studying fine art and more or less marched me into a small museum near the Old Quarter on a cold Sunday. Most of it passed me by, to be honest. Then I turned a corner and found a huge lacquer painting of a village at dusk, maybe three metres wide. It was made in the traditional Vietnamese way, with layers of resin and eggshell. I stood in front of it for perhaps fifteen minutes. What I felt there surprised me completely. I had expected mild interest, and instead I suddenly missed home very badly. It reminded me of my grandmother's village, the flat light before the rain and the smoke from cooking fires. I also felt a bit silly, standing there with wet eyes over a painting of a place I could visit any weekend. Underneath all that was admiration, since a lacquer work of that size apparently takes months of patient polishing. On whether art matters in people's lives, I think it does, although I would not have said so ten years ago. Art puts a shape on feelings that are hard to explain in words. When a painting affects you, you realise other people have felt the same thing. It also forces you to slow down, and almost nothing else does that.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: When I moved to Hanoi, a friend took me to a small art shop. It was in the old town, near a busy market. The shop was small and full of pictures. Most of the paintings showed flowers, but one was different. It was a picture of a fisherman on a river in the early morning. The colours were grey and orange. I stood in front of it for ten minutes. The shop owner told me the artist was from Hue. I felt calm and a little sad when I saw it. The picture reminded me of my grandfather. He was a fisherman too, and he died when I was twelve. I did not expect to feel that in a small shop. I was also surprised, because I never liked art before. I took a photo of the painting and sent it to my mother. For me, art is important in people's lives. Art helps us feel things that we cannot say in words. It also makes us stop and look slowly. Our life is very busy and very noisy. A few quiet minutes like that are good for everybody. I bought a small print for my room that day. Now I visit a small gallery about once a month.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: I am not somebody who visits galleries regularly, so the exhibition I saw in Hanoi two winters ago stands out clearly. A university friend was studying fine art and more or less marched me into a small museum near the Old Quarter on a cold Sunday. Most of it passed me by, to be honest. Then I turned a corner and found a huge lacquer painting of a village at dusk, maybe three metres wide. It was made in the traditional Vietnamese way, with layers of resin and eggshell. I stood in front of it for perhaps fifteen minutes. What I felt there surprised me completely. I had expected mild interest, and instead I suddenly missed home very badly. It reminded me of my grandmother's village, the flat light before the rain and the smoke from cooking fires. I also felt a bit silly, standing there with wet eyes over a painting of a place I could visit any weekend. Underneath all that was admiration, since a lacquer work of that size apparently takes months of patient polishing. On whether art matters in people's lives, I think it does, although I would not have said so ten years ago. Art puts a shape on feelings that are hard to explain in words. When a painting affects you, you realise other people have felt the same thing. It also forces you to slow down, and almost nothing else does that.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The longest journey I have made was the train from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City. It takes about thirty-two hours if nothing goes wrong. I did it in 2022 with my flatmate Tuan, mainly because flights were expensive that week. We had also convinced ourselves that it would be romantic. We shared a six-berth compartment with a retired couple and a woman travelling with a very talkative eight-year-old. For the first twelve hours it was wonderful. There were rice fields, small stations, and the sea appearing suddenly near Lang Co. After that, frankly, it became a test of patience. I read an entire novel and ate three identical rice boxes. I also learned more about the retired gentleman's opinions on football than I strictly needed to. By the end I was stiff, unwashed and slightly confused from lack of sleep. I was also oddly pleased with myself. I remember stepping onto the platform feeling as though I had genuinely earned the arrival. Why some people love long journeys and others cannot bear them probably depends on how you see empty time. If hours with nothing to do feel like a rare gift, a long train ride is almost a holiday. If they feel wasted, every minute becomes annoying. Physical comfort obviously matters too, since a bad back changes everything. And some people travel to arrive while others travel to travel. Those two types will never really understand each other.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: It happened on a train from Hanoi to Da Nang last year. The journey took about seventeen hours. I went with my friend Tuan because the plane tickets were expensive. We shared a small room with four other people. The room was hot and quite noisy at night. A baby cried near my seat for one hour. In the morning I really enjoyed the view. I saw rice fields, small stations and then the sea. I took photos through the window for a long time. After ten hours the journey became boring. I read a book and ate the same rice box twice. Tuan slept most of the afternoon. By the end I felt tired and dirty. My back hurt and I wanted a shower. But I also felt proud of myself. I remember stepping off the train and smiling. Some people love long journeys and some people hate them. I think it depends on your idea of free time. If you like quiet hours, a long train is a gift. If you are always in a hurry, every minute feels wasted. Comfort is important too, because a bad seat changes everything. Personally, I would do that journey again one day.

It cost me more than I could really afford that month, so I lived on instant noodles for a fortnight. If I had to wear a uniform every day, I think I would feel two things at once. Part of me would be relieved, because deciding what to wear before seven in the morning takes real patience. A uniform removes that problem completely. The other part of me would find it a bit dull. You lose the one chance in the day to say something about yourself without speaking. That experience taught me a few things about clothes that I did not expect. The first is that fit matters far more than price or label. The suit worked because the sleeves were right, not because it was expensive. The second one is more useful.
