extra_data.sampleAnswer: I would never describe myself as an adrenaline junkie, so the fact that I have been paragliding once still amazes my family. It happened three summers ago in Da Lat. A cousin of mine had booked it as part of his birthday weekend, and there was one place left. I agreed at midnight after a couple of beers, which is generally when I make my worst decisions. We drove up to a hillside and an instructor strapped me into a harness. He explained that my only job was to keep running towards the edge and never stop. What I enjoyed most was not the view, although the pine forest below us was beautiful. It was the silence about thirty seconds after take-off, once the ground had fallen away. I had braced myself for a falling feeling that never arrived. Instead there was just wind and a strange calm, and I remember laughing out loud at how quiet it was. The second thing I enjoyed, honestly, was landing and being able to tell everybody about it. I do think people should take risks sometimes, but in a controlled way. When you choose to be scared, with an instructor and proper equipment, you find out things about yourself. Most of us live inside very narrow routines, and one frightening afternoon opens up what you think you can do. Being reckless is different, though. Risking your life with no training is not brave, it is just silly.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: My cousin invited me to try rock climbing two summers ago. We went to a climbing centre in the city. It was a Sunday afternoon in July. The wall was about ten metres high. The place was full of young people. A teacher put a rope on me. He showed me how to hold the small stones. My arms were shaking after five minutes. I fell down twice, but the rope was safe. I climbed the wall three times that day. I enjoyed the moment when I reached the top the most. I looked down and I could not believe it. The people below me clapped, and I felt like a happy child. My cousin took a photo of me up there. I still keep that photo on my phone. I also enjoyed the feeling in my body afterwards. I was tired but very awake. I drank a lot of water after that. Personally, I think people should take safe risks sometimes. When we try something new, we learn that we are stronger. Before that day I always said I was afraid of heights. Now I know that is not completely true. But we must use good equipment and listen to a teacher. I will never climb a real mountain alone.

groups.question: What are the benefits of taking a holiday away from work?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The holiday I still think about was four days in Ninh Binh in the summer of 2023. I went with three university friends. We rented bicycles that were far too small for us, and my knees hit the handlebars. We stayed in a homestay run by a woman who fed us enormous breakfasts. Most of our time went on the river, between the limestone mountains. The best evening was the second one. The electricity failed across the whole village, so we sat outside on plastic chairs with the family. We drank tea with them until midnight. Between the countryside and a city, I choose the countryside without much hesitation. A city holiday leaves me with a list of museums I should see and restaurants I should try. Then I feel vaguely guilty about the ones I missed. In the countryside there is nothing to finish, so I actually rest. Cities are good for a short break of two or three days, when you want something new rather than a proper rest. The benefits of a real holiday go well beyond sleep, which you can get at home. A break stops the routine for a while, the same road, the same screen, the same small worries. Somewhere unfamiliar, you start noticing things again. Problems that felt enormous go back to a sensible size. You also find out that the office survived without you, which does a person good.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Around Tet 2024 my family went to Phu Quoc island for five days. We stayed in a small hotel near the beach. Every morning my sister and I swam before breakfast. The water was warm and the beach was almost empty. My father loved the fresh fish in the little restaurants. My small nephew played in the sand all day long. One evening we watched the sunset together on the sand. It was quiet, and nobody looked at a phone. My mother took a photo of all of us that evening. That was my favourite holiday in the last few years. For me, holidays near the sea or in the countryside are better. In a city I feel that I must visit many places. So I come home more tired than before. In the countryside I can sleep late and walk slowly. But a city is fine for a short trip of two days. A holiday away from work has clear benefits. First, we rest our body and our mind. Then, we spend real time with our family. At home we are always busy with work and housework. Also, after a holiday I work better and I get new ideas. So everybody needs a real break once a year.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: During my first month in Da Nang I got food poisoning very badly. I could not even stand up. I did not know a single person in the building. My neighbour was a woman in her fifties who ran a small shop downstairs. I did not even know her name at that point. She noticed that my door had stayed shut all day. She knocked, found me in a bad state, and simply took over. She rang a taxi and came with me to the clinic. She waited there for two hours. Then she made me rice porridge for the next three days. I felt grateful, obviously, but also rather uncomfortable. That is the honest part. Taking that much kindness from a stranger left me feeling that I owed her something huge. It took me a while to see that she did not think of it as a debt at all. I am planning something similar myself next month. My cousin Trang is moving to Hanoi in September to start university. She has never lived away from home before. I have already booked three days off work to go up with her and find a room. I know which districts are cheap and which landlords to avoid. I will also cook for her that first week and show her how the buses work. Nobody ever explains those things. If she feels less lost than I did, that is enough.

Everything was still inside it. I felt very lucky and very thankful. I did not know Lan well at that time. So I was a bit shy about taking her money. But she smiled and said it was normal between colleagues. Her kindness made me feel safe in a strange city. Now she is one of my best friends. Next month I will help someone in the same way. My younger brother will start university in Hanoi. He has never lived away from home before. I will go with him and find a room near his school. I will also show him the buses and the cheap markets. I want him to feel less lost than me. I think a small help means a lot at that moment. That week taught me a lot about kindness.

groups.question: What did you learn from spending that time together?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: For most of last year I lived with my grandmother, who is eighty-six. My parents were working in another province, so somebody had to be in the house. I was thirty at the time, so the age gap was huge. At the beginning I assumed the days would be slow and a bit boring. In fact she kept a stricter timetable than I did. She was up at half past five and at the market by six. After lunch she had a nap that nobody was allowed to interrupt. If a much younger person gave me advice, I think I would take it well now. Ten years ago I would have been quietly offended, and I am not proud of that. It depends on how it is said, though. I would not enjoy a lecture from anybody. I work with people in their early twenties who understand things I do not. The first time one of them corrected me in a meeting, my face went hot. Then I realised she was simply right. What I learned that year came through cooking. Once I started helping her in the kitchen, we had something to do with our hands. The conversation came on its own, while my polite questions about her health had produced nothing. She talked about the years after the war very calmly. I listened instead of waiting for my turn to speak. She showed me that my own way of living is only one choice.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Some years ago I looked after my nephew for two weeks in the summer. He is six years old, and my sister was away for work. I am thirty, so we are very different people. He woke me up at six o'clock every morning. We went to the park before the sun got hot. We drew pictures of animals and made a paper boat together. In the evening I read him the same story again and again. He never got bored of it. If a much younger person gave me advice, I would listen carefully. A few years ago I would feel uncomfortable about it. Now I know that young people understand many things that I do not. They are much faster with technology than me. Last month a new colleague showed me a quicker way to make a report. She is only twenty-three, and she was completely right. I learned two things in those two weeks. First, I learned to be more patient with people. A child does everything slowly, and I could not hurry him. Then, I learned to enjoy small things again. My nephew was happy for a whole afternoon with one paper boat. Now I try to slow down at the weekend.

groups.question: How do you think adults should encourage children to take part in activities outside school?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Last spring my neighbourhood ran a Saturday reading club for the children on our lane. A friend who organised it asked whether I would take one of the sessions. I said yes without thinking it through. That is how I found myself in front of fourteen children between six and ten years old, holding a picture book about a lost dog. My plan lasted about four minutes. They wanted to interrupt, argue with the dog's decisions and tell me about their own pets. So in the end I let them retell the story themselves. I wrote their versions on a large sheet of paper while they shouted ideas at me. Being involved was more tiring than a full day at work, and far more enjoyable than I expected. What surprised me was how quickly the quieter ones spoke up once it stopped being a lecture. I went back for another four Saturdays after that. On how adults should encourage children into activities outside school, my main advice would be to stop turning everything into a competition. Let the child choose from three or four options. Do not sign them up for the one that looks good on a form. Keep it close to home and cheap, because a two-hour journey kills any enthusiasm. And parents should join in sometimes instead of waiting outside on their phones. Children copy what adults actually do far more than what they are told.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: My mother asked me to help at a summer camp for children last year. Our neighbour organised it in the local culture house. There were about twenty children between seven and ten. I looked after the drawing class for three Saturdays. On the first day I was really nervous. The children asked many questions and did not listen to me. I did not know how to start the lesson. But after twenty minutes they started to draw happily. I gave them paper, colours and one simple topic. I felt tired but also very happy at the end. One shy boy showed me his picture of a dog. He did not speak much, but he smiled at me. That small moment made my whole week better. I went back for two more Saturdays after that. The children still say hello to me in the street. For me, adults should encourage children in a gentle way. First, let the child choose the activity. A child will not enjoy a class that the parents chose. Also, keep the activity near home and cheap. A long journey kills the fun very quickly. Finally, parents should join the activity sometimes. Children copy adults, so a parent should not wait outside.

It was held in a hotel outside the city, and I wanted nothing to do with it. It fell on the same weekend as a friend's wedding, and the hotel was ninety minutes away. I was also fairly sure I would never use half the functions being taught. I complained to my manager, lost the argument politely, and went. Generally speaking, I prefer choosing my own tasks, though I would not want complete freedom either. When I decide the order of my own work, I take responsibility for it. I also notice that I make excuses far less often. Being told exactly what to do is comfortable for about a fortnight and then becomes suffocating. That said, when I am new to something I would much rather be given clear instructions than left to guess. Inventing your own method badly can waste weeks. On whether to deal with unpleasant jobs immediately or later, I am firmly on the side of doing them first. A task you are avoiding does not sit quietly. It follows you around all day and spoils everything else. The real cost is not the hour it takes but the six hours of dread beforehand. I now start every morning with whichever job I like least. By half past nine the rest of the day feels almost easy.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: My team at work had to attend a three-day training course last year. It was about new accounting software. The hotel was far from my house, about two hours away. The course was on a weekend, so I lost my free days. I told my manager that I did not want to go. She said everybody must attend, so I went. The first morning was slow and I felt bored. But the second day was more useful than I expected. I even learned two useful things for my job. I still use one of them every week. In general, I prefer choosing my own tasks. When I choose, I feel responsible and I work harder. When somebody tells me every step, I feel bored and slow. But new workers need clear instructions at the beginning. I'd say it is better to do an unpleasant task immediately. A job that you avoid stays in your head all day. You cannot enjoy anything else, so you feel tired. The task usually takes only one hour. Now I start every morning with the job I like least. For example, I answer difficult emails before nine. Then the rest of the day feels much easier.

groups.question: Do you think it is better to spend free time alone or with other people? Why?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: My last completely free day was a Sunday about three weeks ago, and I am rather proud of how little I did. I woke up without an alarm at around half past eight and made a proper breakfast instead of eating standing up. Then I took a book to a small coffee shop near my flat, where the owner knows my order. I sat there for two hours. In the afternoon I met my sister for a walk around the lake, and we ate far too much street food. In the evening I watched an old film with my phone face down in another room. If I suddenly had a whole week with nothing planned, my honest guess is that I would enjoy the first three days enormously. After that I would start to panic slightly. The beginning would be wonderful, with no alarm and long breakfasts. By about Thursday, though, I would feel guilty and would probably invent a project, repainting a wall or learning something, simply to justify the time. Between spending free time alone or with other people, I would choose alone for most of it. Being with friends is enjoyable, but it is still a kind of performance, and afterwards I usually need an hour of silence. On my own my thoughts slow down and I have my best ideas. Even so, a whole weekend without speaking to anybody leaves me flat. The ideal is a quiet day with one good conversation in the middle.

groups.question: How do you think people should respond when they see a stranger in difficulty?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: One evening in July I was walking home from the market. I noticed an elderly man standing beside a broken-down motorbike near the roundabout, looking completely defeated. It had started raining, the sort of heavy rain that arrives without warning, and nobody was stopping. I am not a mechanic at all, so all I could really offer was my phone. I called a repair service and waited with him under a shop awning for about twenty-five minutes. We ended up talking about his grandchildren the whole time. When the mechanic arrived he tried to give me money, which I refused. Between people I know and strangers, both matter, but I find helping a stranger easier. With family and friends there is history involved, and help can quietly turn into an obligation on both sides. With somebody you will never see again it is simple. You give what you can, they say thank you, and that is the end of it. On how people should respond when they see a stranger in trouble, my advice is to be specific rather than heroic. Do not stand there wondering whether somebody else will act, because everybody is thinking exactly the same thing. Ask one direct question, such as whether they need a phone call or a lift. If the situation looks unsafe, ring the police or an ambulance instead of getting involved yourself. Even five minutes of real help beats watching from across the road.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: One morning in May I helped a stranger near my house in Hanoi. A young woman was standing beside her bicycle on the pavement. The chain was broken and her hands were dirty. She looked worried, and nobody stopped for her. She was on her way to work that morning. I asked her if she needed some help. Then I helped her push the bicycle to a small repair shop. The shop was about two hundred metres away. The man there fixed it in ten minutes. It only cost twenty thousand dong. She thanked me many times and bought me a cold drink. I prefer helping strangers. When I help a friend, sometimes they feel they must pay me back. With a stranger it is very simple. I help, they say thank you, and we both go home happy. To me, people should stop and ask one clear question. They can simply ask the person if they need help. Many people only look and then walk away. That is not enough for me. If the problem is serious, they should call the police or an ambulance. They should not just take a video with their phone. A small action can change someone's whole day.

groups.question: Do you think it is better to repair things yourself or to pay a professional? Why?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Last autumn the drawer in my kitchen cabinet collapsed, and rather than replace the whole unit I decided to repair it myself. I watched a couple of videos, borrowed a drill from my neighbour, and spent most of a Saturday measuring and sanding. My first attempt was a disaster because I fitted the runners upside down. The drawer opened at an angle, like something in a haunted house. I took it apart and started again, this time writing the measurements on the wood instead of trusting my memory. When it finally slid open smoothly and closed with a click, I felt far more proud than the job deserved. It was only a drawer, and yet I stood in the kitchen opening and shutting it about ten times. There was relief mixed in as well, partly because I had saved a fair amount of money. I had also privately expected to fail and to admit it when I returned the drill. Is it better to repair things yourself or to pay a professional? For small household jobs I would always try myself first. The tools pay for themselves quickly and you keep the skill for life. Anything involving electricity, gas or a ladder I hand over without thinking twice. The sensible rule is to weigh up the cost of failure. If getting it wrong is only annoying, do it yourself. If it is dangerous, pay somebody who knows.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Two months ago the fan in my bedroom stopped working. The weather was very hot, so I decided to repair it myself. The room was really uncomfortable without it. First I watched a short video on the internet. Then I opened the fan with a screwdriver. Inside there was a lot of dust and one loose wire. I cleaned every part with an old cloth. After that I fixed the wire and closed the cover. My little brother helped me hold the screws. It took me about two hours in total. When the fan started again, I laughed out loud. I felt very proud of myself that afternoon. My mother did not believe me at first. She came into the room and checked it twice. I was also happy because I saved a lot of money. Before that day I always thought I was bad with my hands. For small things, I prefer to repair them myself. It is cheaper and I learn a new skill. But for big things I pay a professional. For example, I never touch the electricity in the walls. That work is really dangerous for a normal person. So my rule is simple. Small job, do it yourself. Big job, call a real worker.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The busiest time of my life was the six months before my centre opened. That was roughly from March to August 2022. I was doing three jobs at once. I taught in the mornings, met builders in the afternoons and wrote course material at night. For about three weeks I ate almost nothing but rice and instant noodles. A proper meal felt like a luxury back then. If I had to work at that pace again now, I would find it much harder. At twenty-six I could survive on five hours of sleep. I even treated being exhausted as something to be proud of. Now my body sends me the bill the next morning. I would probably still say yes, because I am stubborn. But I would insist on one full day off every week. I would also pay somebody to do the paperwork instead of pretending I could manage it all. What that period taught me was quite simple. Being busy and being productive are two different things. Half of the things I rushed to finish did not need doing at all. I also learned to write everything down instead of keeping the list in my head. That sounds small, but it changed the way I slept. Most of all, I learned to ask for help earlier. My sister quietly took over the accounts in July. I should have asked her back in April.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: When I finished university, I looked back at my final year. That year was the busiest time of my life. I studied in the morning and worked in a shop in the evening. I also had a small job at the weekend. I often came home at ten at night. Then I had to write my reports for the next day. I slept about five hours every night for months. My days were long and always the same. My friends said I looked tired all the time. My mother was worried about me too. If I had to work at that pace again, I would not be happy. I am older now, so I get tired more quickly. I think I would feel stressed and worried every day. Maybe I would say yes, but I would ask for help. That period taught me two important lessons. First, I learned that rest is not lazy. A tired person works slowly and makes many mistakes. Then, I learned to write a simple list every morning. The list helped me see the important jobs first. Now I plan my week on Sunday evening. I also keep one free evening for my family. I never want to be that busy again.

groups.question: What advice would you give someone who finds it hard to concentrate when reading on a screen?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: These days most of my reading happens on a screen. The clearest example was a novel I read on my phone during a long train journey to Da Nang in April. The trip took around seventeen hours and I had forgotten to pack a paperback. So I downloaded a thriller before we left and read almost the whole thing in the dark, with the brightness turned right down. Nobody around me was disturbed, which would not have been true with the overhead light on. I felt oddly divided about reading that way. There was real satisfaction in carrying a whole library in my pocket, looking up new words instantly and making the text larger as my eyes grew tired. At the same time I felt slightly cheated by the end. Messages kept appearing at the top of the screen, and twice I caught myself checking social media in the middle of a chapter. My eyes were sore, and I could not really feel how far through the book I was. For anyone who struggles to concentrate on a screen, my advice is practical rather than moral. Switch on aeroplane mode before you start, because willpower loses that fight every time. Read in one block of forty minutes instead of picking the book up for two minutes at a time. Use a proper reading app rather than a browser. If that still fails, buy the paper version of the books that really matter to you.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Just before Tet my teacher sent me a long article on the internet. It was about how to learn English faster. I read it on my laptop in my room. I started after dinner on a quiet evening. It took me about one hour in total. The article had many pictures and short paragraphs. I could click on new words and see the meaning at once. I also saved some sentences in my notebook. At first I felt happy about reading that way. It was free, fast and easy to find. But after thirty minutes my eyes were tired. I rubbed my eyes many times. Messages came on the screen and I stopped reading many times. So I felt a little annoyed with myself. To me, a few small changes can help with this problem. First, turn off the internet or use aeroplane mode. Then your phone cannot disturb you for a while. Second, read for twenty minutes and then rest your eyes. Look out of the window at something far away. Third, make the letters bigger and the light softer. Also, sit at a table, not on your bed. These small changes work well for me. If the text is very important, I print it on paper.

groups.question: Do you think it is better to go to bed early and get up early, or to work late at night? Why?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The worst night I can remember was the one before I gave a presentation to our company's board, back in March last year. I went to bed at about half past ten, feeling reasonably confident. Then I lay there rehearsing the opening slide in my head until roughly three in the morning. Every time I nearly drifted off, I thought of another question they might ask. Around one o'clock I made the classic mistake of picking up my phone. That finished off any remaining chance of sleeping. In the end I got perhaps two hours. The next day was fairly grim. I was irritable, my eyes ached, and I could not concentrate on anything longer than a paragraph. Strangely, the presentation itself went reasonably well, probably because I was too tired to be nervous. Then I fell asleep on the bus home and missed my stop by two stations. On the wider question, I am firmly on the side of early nights and early mornings. I spent most of my twenties arguing the opposite. Work done at six in the morning is simply better work. The phone is silent, nobody expects a reply, and my head is clear. Late-night work feels productive because it is dramatic. I have gone back to those files the next day and found half of it unusable. I would admit, though, that some people genuinely think best at midnight. Forcing them to start at six would be a waste.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: In the middle of last year I could not sleep before an important interview. I went to bed at ten o'clock as usual. But my brain did not stop working. I thought about every possible question. I also worried about the traffic in the morning. At one in the morning I picked up my phone. That was a big mistake, because I felt awake again. In the end I slept only two hours. The next day I felt terrible. My eyes hurt and I had a headache all morning. I could not concentrate on simple things. I could not remember simple English words either. I drank three cups of coffee, but it did not help. Luckily the interview went quite well. The manager was friendly and asked easy questions. After that I went home and slept for eleven hours. Personally, I think going to bed early is much better. In the morning my head is clear and the house is quiet. Nobody sends me messages before seven o'clock. Work at night feels productive, but it is not. I often check my night work the next day and find mistakes. So I try to finish my work before eleven. Now I keep my phone in the kitchen at night.

groups.question: How do you think more people could be encouraged to get involved in their local area?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Every year my neighbourhood organises a clean-up along the canal before the Lunar New Year. Last January I joined it for the first time, mostly because the woman who runs our residents' group is impossible to say no to. We started at seven on a Saturday morning, about forty of us in borrowed gloves. We spent four hours pulling plastic bags and polystyrene out of the water. There was a retired teacher next to me who has lived on that street for fifty years. He told me stories about swimming in the canal as a boy. Taking part felt surprisingly good. I had expected to be bored and slightly annoyed about losing my lie-in. Instead I finished the morning knowing perhaps fifteen neighbours by name, people I had passed silently for years. It felt good to do something physical as well, since most of my work happens on a laptop. Underneath that sat a small, uncomfortable guilt, because the canal had been in that state for years. I had never once thought it was my problem. If we want more people involved locally, organisers have to make it easy and short. Nobody with a full-time job will commit to a monthly committee. But almost anyone will give two hours on a Saturday if they know exactly when it starts and finishes. Advertise it in the group chats people actually read, ask individuals directly rather than posting a notice, and finish with food.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: My neighbour told me about a tree planting day in our local area. It was last April, and about thirty people came. We started at seven in the morning. We planted small trees along the road near the market. Each of us planted about five trees. The sun was already strong at eight o'clock. I worked with an old man who lives next to me. He showed me how to make the hole deeper. We finished at eleven and then we ate lunch together. We drank tea under a big tree after that. I felt tired but very happy while I was taking part. My hands were dirty and my back hurt a lot. But I liked working with my neighbours. Before that day I did not know their names. Now we say hello every morning. I also felt a little proud of my street. In my opinion, this kind of activity must be short and easy. Most people work all week, so two hours on Saturday is enough. Also, the leader should invite people face to face. A post on Facebook is not enough for busy people. Finally, give people food and tea after the work. Then people talk, laugh and come back next time.

groups.question: Are you planning to travel anywhere unfamiliar soon? Tell me about it.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Getting lost in Sapa was completely my own fault. It was October, two years ago. I decided to walk from the town down to a village without a guide. I also never checked how long the route actually took. The path was clear for the first hour, and then it split in two. I chose the wrong one with great confidence. By four in the afternoon I was surrounded by rice terraces. My phone had eleven per cent battery and no signal at all. The fog was coming down the valley much faster than I expected. For the first half hour I was mainly annoyed with myself. Then the light started to go, and that annoyance turned into real fear. I kept walking quickly, which is exactly the wrong thing to do. It made me hot, thirsty and even more lost. In the end an old man with two buffalo pointed me towards a road. He refused the money I offered him. I am planning another trip like that in November, but I will be far less stupid. My brother and I are walking part of the old border road near Cao Bang over three days. I have already downloaded the offline maps and bought a power bank. More importantly, I have booked a local guide for the middle day, where the paths are least clear. I will also leave our route with the guesthouse owner.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I went to Da Lat and got lost there with my friend last year. We wanted to walk to a small waterfall near the town. We did not take a map, because the way looked easy. After one hour the path went in two directions. We chose the wrong one. Soon we were in a pine forest with tall trees. My phone had no signal at all. It was almost five o'clock and the sky was grey. At first I felt annoyed with myself. Then I felt really worried, because it was getting dark. My friend was quiet, but I know she was scared too. We walked for another thirty minutes and found nothing. We were very tired and thirsty. Finally we met a farmer with two dogs. He showed us the road back to the town. Next month I will travel to a new place again. My brother and I will go to Cao Bang for four days. This time I will prepare carefully. I will download an offline map and buy a power bank. We will also book a local guide for one day. I will tell my family our plan before we go. I do not want to be lost again.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I am usually quite an organised person, so one morning last March still embarrasses me. My alarm did not go off and I woke up at ten past five. My flight to Da Nang was at seven. I packed in about four minutes and threw things into the bag without folding anything. My brother drove me to the airport much faster than he should have. I checked in just as the desk was closing. If I had to do something important tomorrow with no time to prepare, a presentation to a client for example, I would feel exactly what I felt that morning. I would look calm on the outside and be a complete mess inside. My hands would shake while I smiled politely. My thinking gets very narrow under that kind of pressure. I can only see the next ten seconds instead of the whole problem. I would probably get through it, forget something obvious, and notice it only afterwards. Is it better to plan everything in advance or deal with things as they come? I lean towards planning. Almost every real disaster in my life came from thinking I would sort it out later. But there is a point where planning becomes a way of avoiding the work. People who need a perfect plan often never start at all. The best people I know plan whatever is expensive to get wrong and stay relaxed about the rest.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: One day at the office my manager gave me a report at four in the afternoon. The meeting was the next morning at nine o'clock. I had very little time, so I started at once. I called two teams and asked them for their numbers. Some people answered slowly, and that made me nervous. I made ten slides and checked them twice. I did not eat a real dinner, only bread and coffee. I stayed in the office until nine at night. In the end the report was fine, and my manager thanked me. If I had no time to prepare for something important, I would feel very nervous. My heart would beat fast and my hands would be cold. I'd say I am good at looking calm in front of other people. But inside I would think about only one thing at a time. After the meeting I would remember something small that I forgot. That always happens to me. For me, it is better to plan things in advance. When I plan, I sleep better and I make fewer mistakes. But we cannot plan everything, because life changes every day. So I plan the important things first. Then I stay relaxed about the small ones.

I can only see the next ten seconds instead of the whole problem. I would probably get through it, forget something obvious, and notice it only afterwards. Is it better to plan everything in advance or deal with things as they come? I lean towards planning. Almost every real disaster in my life came from thinking I would sort it out later. But there is a point where planning becomes a way of avoiding the work. People who need a perfect plan often never start at all. The best people I know plan whatever is expensive to get wrong and stay relaxed about the rest.

groups.question: What advice would you give to someone going to a music festival for the first time?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: My friend Duc rang me last July with two spare tickets to a music festival in Da Lat. I said yes before he had even finished the sentence. Honestly, I had never heard of half the bands on the poster. We took an overnight coach up on the Friday and arrived exhausted. Then we spent nine hours standing in a field with about six thousand other people. The headline act was a Vietnamese indie band my sister loves. When they played their final song, the whole crowd sang the chorus back at them. What I enjoyed most was not the music but the feeling around it. Complete strangers were sharing water bottles, and somebody's dad was dancing badly near the front. There was that odd feeling that everyone wants the same thing at the same moment. Nobody was checking their phone, which is quite unusual these days. If a friend were going for the first time, my advice would be fairly practical. Wear old shoes you do not care about, because the field turns to mud within an hour. Carry cash, since the signal disappears once the crowd arrives and card machines stop working. Agree on a meeting point with your friends before you go in. And do not try to see every band on the list. Pick three, arrive early for those, and wander for the rest of the day. The small stages are usually where the best moments happen.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I still remember a day in July two years ago. My best friend bought two concert tickets for my birthday. The show was in Ho Chi Minh City and started at eight. There were about five thousand people in the stadium. The singer was a young Vietnamese artist that we both love. We stood for three hours and sang every song. The lights and the noise were amazing. What I enjoyed most was the atmosphere, not the music. Everybody was happy at the same time. People shared water and helped each other in the crowd. A tall man let a short girl stand in front of him. Nobody looked at their phone for a long time. I felt like part of one big family. I still remember the last song very clearly. My friend and I talked about that night for days. For a first-time visitor, I have some simple advice. Wear old and comfortable shoes, because you will stand all day. Bring some cash, because the phone signal is often bad. Choose a meeting point with your friends before you go inside. Drink a lot of water, especially in hot weather. Finally, do not try to see every singer. Choose two or three and enjoy them slowly.

groups.question: Do you think travelling to new places changes people? Why?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Hanoi in January, three years ago, was the first city that really surprised me. I grew up in the south, so I expected something familiar. Then I stepped out of the station at seven in the morning. Within a minute I knew I did not understand the place at all. It was fifteen degrees, which felt freezing to me. My aunt met me in three layers and laughed at my thin jacket. When I first arrived I felt uncomfortable, and I am a bit ashamed of how fast I judged the city. The streets were narrow and crowded and the buildings leaned towards each other. Everything happened on the pavement, from breakfast to haircuts. People spoke more directly than I was used to. For two days I took that as rudeness and quietly wanted to go home. Then, somewhere in the middle of the week, that feeling turned into curiosity. I stopped comparing everything with the south and started enjoying it. On whether travelling changes people, I think it does, but less than travel companies like to say. One week away does not turn anybody into a different person. What it does is switch your attention back on. At home you notice nothing and could walk your own street with your eyes shut. In a new city even a bus ticket makes you think. It also shows you that your habits are local, not natural.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Early this year I visited Da Nang for the first time. I went there for a short training course. Two colleagues from my office came with me. We arrived by plane at eight in the evening. The city was clean and the roads were very wide. Our hotel was near the river. There was a big bridge with many coloured lights. We stayed there for four days in total. We ate seafood by the sea on the second night. When I first arrived, I felt excited but also a little lost. I did not know the streets at all. So I used a map on my phone all the time. The food was different from the food at home. People also spoke with another accent, and I listened carefully. On the second day I felt much more comfortable. We walked to the beach early in the morning. By the last day I did not want to go home. I think travelling to new places really changes people. When we travel, we see that people live in different ways. Then we understand that our own habits are not the only way. Travelling also makes us braver. We must solve small problems alone in a strange place.

groups.question: Why do you think the weather affects people's mood so much?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I got caught in a proper storm one October, riding home from work along Nguyen Trai street. The forecast had mentioned light rain, so I left my raincoat under my desk. I regretted that decision within about four minutes. The sky went dark at around half past five, and then the rain arrived sideways. Within ten minutes the road was under thirty centimetres of water and my motorbike stalled. I ended up pushing it two hundred metres to a petrol station. About twenty other soaked people were sheltering there. At first I was furious, mostly with myself. I remember standing there dripping and working out how much a new engine would cost. After half an hour, though, the mood changed completely. Somebody bought a bag of steamed corn, and an old man started telling stories about the floods of the eighties. I began to find the whole thing quite funny. Two of us pushed our bikes home together in the dark. I got home at nine, three hours late, and by then the rain had stopped completely. I think weather affects our mood partly for biological reasons, because light really does change our energy levels. Grey days make people slow. It also decides what we are able to do, and having your plans cancelled by something outside your control is frustrating. And there is the simple matter of discomfort. It is very hard to feel cheerful when you are wet, cold and still forty minutes from dry socks.

My motorbike stopped and I had to push it. I pushed it to a petrol station and waited there. My shoes and my bag were completely wet. At first I felt very angry with myself. I thought about the repair cost all evening. But after half an hour the mood changed. Other people were sheltering there and we started talking. One man bought hot corn for everybody. An old man told funny stories about the floods. I got home at nine, but I was not angry. To me, weather changes our mood a lot. Grey days give people less light and less energy. Bad weather also cancels our plans, and that is frustrating. Nobody feels happy when they are cold and wet. Now I always keep a raincoat under my seat. I also check the weather every morning.

groups.question: What did you learn from that experience?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The best phone call I have had in years came in June last year, while I was queuing in a supermarket. It was my younger brother telling me he had passed the entrance exam for the university he had wanted since he was fifteen. He had failed to get the marks the year before. Then he spent twelve months studying with a stubbornness that honestly worried the whole family. I actually shouted in the middle of the queue, and an elderly woman in front of me turned round. I had to apologise and then explain, after which she congratulated me too. What I enjoyed most was not the news itself but the sound of his voice. He was trying very hard to be casual about it and failing completely, and I could hear him grinning down the phone. I also loved the small ridiculous details of that afternoon. There was the stranger congratulating me, and the cake I bought on the way home without asking my mother. Then the four of us ate it standing up in the kitchen. What I learned from that year was about patience rather than success. Watching my brother fail and then work quietly for twelve months changed how I see good news. Behind one happy phone call there were twelve months that nobody noticed. I had privately doubted he would manage it, and I was wrong. Since then I am much slower to write anybody off after one bad result.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: A colleague of mine was sitting next to me when my sister called. It was last September, and I was still at work. She called me at about four o'clock. She told me she got a job at a big hospital in Hanoi. She had waited two months for the answer. I was very happy for her, because she studied hard for six years. That evening my family cooked a big dinner at home. We also bought a large cake. My mother cried a little at the table. My father opened a bottle of wine. I enjoyed the sound of my sister's voice the most. She tried to speak calmly, but I could hear that she was smiling. So I smiled too in the middle of the office. I also enjoyed telling my father the news. He never says much, but that day he called all our relatives. From this experience, I learned that good news often comes slowly. My sister failed one interview before this one. She was very sad for two weeks. I could not help her much at that time. But she did not stop, and she practised again. Now I am more patient with myself. After a bad result, I wait and then I try again.

groups.question: What are the benefits of answering difficult questions honestly?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: A student of mine asked me something two years ago that I still remember. I was teaching an evening English class in the city. During the break, a young woman of about twenty-two came up to me. She had just failed an exam for the third time. She asked me straight out if she was simply not clever enough to learn a language. The room was quiet and everyone else had gone outside. At that moment I felt a strange mix of panic and responsibility. I was very aware of the silence and of how long I was taking. If I said no too quickly, it would sound like an easy lie. If I waited, she would read that pause as the real answer. I was also annoyed with myself. I had watched her struggle for a whole term and had never asked her how she studied. In the end I told her the truth as I saw it. Her way of studying would not work for anybody, so we spent the rest of the break rebuilding it. She passed the exam the following term, and she told me straight away. The good thing about honest answers is that they give people something they can act on. Kind words alone leave them exactly where they were, only more confused. Honesty also protects the relationship. People can tell when they are being managed, and after that your encouragement means nothing to them.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: It started as a normal day, and then my nephew asked me a very hard question. He is fourteen years old. We were eating dinner together at my sister's house. He asked me why his father does not live with them now. His parents divorced two years ago. Everyone at the table stopped talking at the same time. For a few seconds I did not know what to say. I felt shocked and a little afraid. I did not want to say the wrong thing to him. I also felt sad, because he asked the question so quietly. In the end I told him the simple truth. I said that his parents were not happy together any more. But I also said that they both love him very much. Then I listened to him for a long time. He talked about his father for almost an hour. The way I see it, honest answers have real benefits. First, people trust you after that. Children always know when adults tell them lies. Then, an honest answer helps a person see the real situation. After that, they can slowly accept it and feel calmer. A kind and honest answer is better than a comfortable lie.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: There is a camera I still think about. It was a second-hand Fujifilm in a shop on Nguyen Trai Street, two winters ago. I had that exact model in my head, and there it was for about eight million dong. The problem was my motorbike. It had broken down the week before and the repair ate most of my savings. So I stood there for twenty minutes pretending to look at the lenses, and then I walked out. When I came back the next weekend with the money, it had gone. Oddly, the part I enjoyed most was the shopping itself. For weeks before that I read reviews late at night and compared prices. I watched videos of people photographing things I had no interest in. I even planned the pictures I would take. Standing in that shop holding the camera was the best part, and I think it usually is. Wanting something is a pleasure on its own, and often more fun than owning it. Does advertising have too much influence today? I think so, mainly because it does not look like advertising any more. Adverts never sell you the object. They sell you the person who owns it, the one who takes lovely photos and travels well. We now see hundreds of these images a day from people we think are just sharing their lives. It gets very hard to tell a real need from a borrowed one.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: One afternoon in March I saw a guitar in a music shop near my old school. It was brown and it had a beautiful sound. The price was four million dong, but I only had two million. I asked the shop to keep it for one month for me. I saved money from my part-time job every week. Sadly, another person bought it before me. I felt disappointed for about a week after that. What I enjoyed most was the time before I bought it. I read reviews on my phone at night and watched videos about guitars. I visited that shop three times and played the guitar a little. The staff were friendly and they never asked me to leave. That was the best part of the whole story. For me, wanting a thing is sometimes more fun than having it. I think advertising has too much influence on people today. We see adverts on our phones every few minutes. They do not really sell a product. They sell a happy and beautiful life. Many young people buy clothes and phones they do not need. Then they have no money at the end of the month. So my rule is simple now. I always wait one week before I buy anything expensive.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: There is a camera I still think about. It was a second-hand Fujifilm in a shop on Nguyen Trai Street, two winters ago. I had that exact model in my head, and there it was for about eight million dong. The problem was my motorbike. It had broken down the week before and the repair ate most of my savings. So I stood there for twenty minutes pretending to look at the lenses, and then I walked out. When I came back the next weekend with the money, it had gone. Oddly, the part I enjoyed most was the shopping itself. For weeks before that I read reviews late at night and compared prices. I watched videos of people photographing things I had no interest in. I even planned the pictures I would take. Standing in that shop holding the camera was the best part, and I think it usually is. Wanting something is a pleasure on its own, and often more fun than owning it. Does advertising have too much influence today? I think so, mainly because it does not look like advertising any more. Adverts never sell you the object. They sell you the person who owns it, the one who takes lovely photos and travels well. We now see hundreds of these images a day from people we think are just sharing their lives. It gets very hard to tell a real need from a borrowed one.

groups.question: Why do you think sport brings people together?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The match I always come back to is Vietnam against Thailand in the AFF Cup final. I watched it one December a few years ago at a coffee shop near my house. About thirty neighbours were squeezed onto plastic stools around one screen. My uncle had insisted we get there an hour early to claim a decent view. He was right, because by kick-off people were standing in the road outside. For the first half I was fairly relaxed. Once we scored, though, I was on my feet shouting with everybody else. The last fifteen minutes were honestly unbearable. I kept checking the clock, my heart was racing, and I could not sit still. When the whistle went, the street erupted. Somebody's grandmother was banging a saucepan, and half the city rode around with flags until midnight. Nobody in that street slept much that night. Looking back, what struck me was not the football. It was the fact that I was celebrating with people whose names I did not even know. I think sport brings people together because it is so simple. You do not need education, money or a shared background to understand who is winning. So a match creates an instant common language. It also gives people permission to show emotion in public, which many of us rarely do. And when a team represents a city or a country, supporting it becomes a small way of saying you belong somewhere.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: A few days before my birthday, Vietnam played Thailand in a big final. I watched the match in a small coffee shop near my house. About thirty neighbours sat there on plastic chairs. My father and I arrived one hour early for good seats. The owner put a big screen outside for everyone. In the first half I felt quite calm. Then our team scored, and everybody stood up and shouted. An old woman next to me hit a metal pot. The last ten minutes were very hard for me. My heart was beating fast and I could not sit down. When we won, people rode motorbikes with flags until midnight. I went out with them and shouted too. I think many people enjoy watching sport for simple reasons. First, you never know the result, so it is exciting until the last minute. Also, it is a cheap way to relax after work. You only need a screen and some friends. Finally, people like feeling part of a group. When your team wins, you share the happiness with thousands of other people. That is why my neighbours still meet at that coffee shop every weekend.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The match I always come back to is Vietnam against Thailand in the AFF Cup final. I watched it one December a few years ago at a coffee shop near my house. About thirty neighbours were squeezed onto plastic stools around one screen. My uncle had insisted we get there an hour early to claim a decent view. He was right, because by kick-off people were standing in the road outside. For the first half I was fairly relaxed. Once we scored, though, I was on my feet shouting with everybody else. The last fifteen minutes were honestly unbearable. I kept checking the clock, my heart was racing, and I could not sit still. When the whistle went, the street erupted. Somebody's grandmother was banging a saucepan, and half the city rode around with flags until midnight. Nobody in that street slept much that night. Looking back, what struck me was not the football. It was the fact that I was celebrating with people whose names I did not even know. I think people watch sport mainly because nobody knows how it will end. Films and novels are written in advance, but no one can tell you how a match will finish, and that uncertainty is addictive. Beyond that, it is an inexpensive escape: ninety minutes in which your own problems disappear. And it gives people a group to belong to, which matters more than we usually admit. My neighbours and I still meet at that same coffee shop, and the football is really just the excuse.

formalEmail.instruction: Write an email to the president of the club to apply for the race. Explain why you are suitable for these rules and how you feel about taking part. Write 120–150 words. Recommended time: 20 minutes.
formalEmail.sampleAnswer:
Dear President,
I am writing to apply for the club's two-week travel race across Europe and to explain why I am suitable for the rules.
First, public transport is already part of my daily life. I travel to work by bus every morning and rarely use a car, so timetables and connections do not worry me.
Second, I have experience of long journeys. Last year I travelled sixteen hours by train from Hanoi to Da Nang, and I have crossed my country by bus more than once.
Third, I stay calm when plans change. On one trip I missed a connection late at night and found another route myself without any help.
Regarding the broadcast, I would be happy to record short daily updates for the club channel.
I hope you will consider my application.
Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]

Best,
[Your Name]

question_text: Put the sentences in the correct order.
options: This is because they were all in black and white, and they had no sound.
In addition to these technical limitations, the film producers also had a limited budget.
Things have changed over time, and some of them now earn millions of dollars for appearing in films.
Films from that period were very different from films of today.
This lack of money mainly affected the actors, and they did not earn a lot of money.
During this education, he learned to be creative and to practise singing on stage.

explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
Dạng sắp xếp câu: tìm câu mở đầu (không trỏ ngược), rồi bám vào đại từ, từ chỉ định và từ nối để nối dần.

▸ Making films — thứ tự đúng:
  0. "In 1895, the Grand Café in France showed the first ever commercial film." → câu cho sẵn, nêu mốc thời gian và sự kiện đầu tiên.
  1. "Films from that period were very different from films of today." → "that period" trỏ thẳng về năm 1895 ở câu cho sẵn.
  2. "This is because they were all in black and white, and they had no sound." → "This is because" giải thích cho ý "very different" ở câu trước.
  3. "In addition to these technical limitations, the film producers also had a limited budget." → "these technical limitations" gom lại ý đen trắng và không có tiếng.
  4. "This lack of money mainly affected the actors, and they did not earn a lot of money." → "This lack of money" trỏ về "a limited budget".
  5. "Things have changed over time, and some of them now earn millions of dollars for appearing in films." → "some of them" trỏ về "the actors", chốt bằng tương phản quá khứ với hiện tại.

▸ The famous singer — thứ tự đúng:
  0. "Jade Nobelton is only 18 years old, and he is a famous singer." → câu cho sẵn, giới thiệu nhân vật.
  1. "Before becoming famous at this young age, he studied art and music at high school." → "this young age" trỏ về "18 years old".
  2. "During this education, he learned to be creative and to practise singing on stage." → "this education" trỏ về việc học ở high school.
  3. "In these performances, he liked to wear bright clothes and paint his face." → "these performances" trỏ về "singing on stage".
  4. "This strange way of dressing and his songs have attracted people's attention." → "This strange way of dressing" trỏ về quần áo sặc sỡ và vẽ mặt.
  5. "They started to follow him on social media, and now he is very popular." → "They" trỏ về "people" ở câu trước, chốt bằng kết quả hiện tại.

extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The first picture shows four friends pressed shoulder to shoulder on a rooftop, with one man in a black hoodie stretching out his arm to hold the phone. The three women around him are laughing, and everyone is wrapped up in thick coats, so it must be a cold but sunny day. Green hills and rooftops fill the background. The second picture could not be more different: a man in a bright orange jacket stands completely alone at the edge of a still lake, with a camera raised to his eye and bare brown mountains rising behind the water. Nothing else moves in the frame he has chosen. Both are photographs of a single moment, but the first one keeps the people and the second one keeps the place. The mood is completely different.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show people enjoying free time outside, but in different seasons. The first picture shows a wide sandy beach in summer. There are long rows of blue and white striped tents on the sand, and people in swimsuits are walking between the tents and the sea. Some of them are washing under outdoor showers. The sky is deep blue and there are houses on a green hill behind the beach. The second picture shows an outdoor ice rink in a city square in winter. Both show fun outdoor activities, but one crowd is dressed for heat and the other for cold.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Both pictures show people making the most of the weather, but at opposite ends of the year. The first picture is high summer on a wide, golden beach. Long rows of blue and white striped tents stretch along the sand, and people in swimsuits walk between the tents and the water, while a few rinse off under outdoor showers. Above them is a deep blue sky with thin clouds, and a green hill covered in houses rises behind the beach. The second picture shows an outdoor ice rink in a snowy city square. Skaters in cream and pink coats hold onto each other as they move across the ice, and strings of lights and a bright sign decorate the red roofs behind them. The sky is grey and heavy. Each season offers a different game, yet the pleasure looks the same in both.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The email I keep coming back to arrived about two years ago, from a company I had applied to and more or less written off. Three weeks of silence will do that. What it involved was a second interview, which I had convinced myself was never coming. This was a Tuesday morning, and I was still in bed with my phone in my hand, reading the same four lines over and over. The part that stuck with me was how badly my hands were shaking when I tried to type a reply that did not sound desperate. At the time I felt relief before anything else, which surprised me. Not long after, I rang my mother, and she cried, which she still denies. These days that email sits in a folder I never delete. As for how it felt, relief really was the honest answer. This is largely because I had told everybody I had applied, and the silence had started to feel like an answer in itself. On the last point, I would say a call wins whenever the news matters. One reason for this is that a voice carries hesitation and warmth, and a written message strips all of that out, which is why a perfectly kind text can land as cold. I have upset people by text without ever meaning to, and I doubt I am at all unusual in that. For anything difficult these days, I simply pick up the phone.

question_text: What is the speaker's opinion about security cameras at work?
options: People are unnecessarily worried about them
Most people don't even realize cameras are present.
Cameras should be placed to ensure complete coverage.
explanation:
Our workplace wellbeing session today begins with the topic that filled the suggestion box: the security cameras installed last month. I have read every note, and I want to respond honestly. Many of you wrote that you feel watched, even judged. My view, after sitting with the facts, is that people are worrying more than the situation deserves. Two claims from the notes need correcting. Somebody argued that most staff do not even realise the cameras exist — clearly untrue, given that they filled our suggestion box. Somebody else demanded the opposite: cameras extended into every corner of every room for what they called complete coverage. That would be excessive and will not happen. The cameras cover entrances, corridors and the equipment store. Nobody watches live feeds, and recordings are opened only when an incident requires them.
Let me offer a different frame for the anxious among us. When a package vanished from reception last year, we spent three unpleasant weeks in suspicion — a camera would have ended it in an hour. When the fire door was propped open all summer, nobody could say by whom. These little lenses answer questions that otherwise poison a workplace. I know they can feel intimidating, and I have heard the argument that they only matter after trouble has already struck. I would put it the other way: their presence should reassure us. The company is not doubting the people in this room. It is standing guard for them.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant camera #3 — bối cảnh buổi wellbeing.)
1. Đáp án: People are unnecessarily worried about them. Bẫy: "don't realize cameras are present" ("clearly untrue") và "complete coverage" ("excessive and will not happen").
2. Đáp án: People should feel reassured about their presence. Bẫy: "intimidating" và "only useful after incidents" đều được nhắc rồi lật lại.

question_text: Tell me about a time when you had to give a presentation.
explanation: The one I remember most clearly was last November. My manager asked me to present the results of a customer survey to about fifteen colleagues. I had never spoken to a group that size before. I had a week, which sounds generous until you try to turn four hundred responses into twelve slides. I cut the charts down twice, because my first version looked like a spreadsheet on a wall. My friend Nam sat through a rehearsal and told me, quite bluntly, that I was speaking far too fast. Beforehand I was worse than I expected. My hands were cold and I drank two glasses of water in the corridor. The first minute was rough, and I heard myself racing through the introduction. Then somebody in the second row started taking notes, and that small thing settled me down. By the middle I was actually enjoying it. Afterwards came a strange mix of pride and exhaustion, and I remember not wanting to talk to anybody for an hour. On the wider question, I think these skills matter enormously for young people here. Students spend years learning theory which they are never asked to explain out loud. Then they start a job where every meeting demands exactly that. Someone who can make a complicated idea simple gets noticed quickly, whereas a brilliant person who cannot be understood stays invisible. It is a skill you learn by doing it badly a few times.

I cut the charts down twice, because my first version looked like a spreadsheet on a wall. My friend Nam sat through a rehearsal and told me, quite bluntly, that I was speaking far too fast. Beforehand I was worse than I expected. My hands were cold and I drank two glasses of water in the corridor. The first minute was rough, and I heard myself racing through the introduction. Then somebody in the second row started taking notes, and that small thing settled me down. By the middle I was actually enjoying it. Afterwards came a strange mix of pride and exhaustion, and I remember not wanting to talk to anybody for an hour. On the wider question, I think these skills matter enormously for young people here. Students spend years learning theory which they are never asked to explain out loud. Then they start a job where every meeting demands exactly that. Someone who can make a complicated idea simple gets noticed quickly, whereas a brilliant person who cannot be understood stays invisible. It is a skill you learn by doing it badly a few times.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Last November I had to give a presentation at my company in Hanoi. My manager asked me to explain our new customer survey to about fifteen people. I had one week to prepare, and I made twelve slides with a lot of charts. I practised at home three times in front of a mirror. My friend Nam listened to me once and told me to speak more slowly. Before the presentation I was very nervous. My hands were cold and I drank two glasses of water. When I stood up, my voice was too fast for the first minute. But after a few slides I felt calmer, because people were nodding and taking notes. At the end my manager asked two questions and I answered both of them. I felt proud and very tired at the same time. My friends took me for coffee after work. I think presentation skills are important for every young person. In my country, students learn a lot of theory but they rarely speak in front of a group. When they start working, they suddenly need this skill in every meeting. A person who can explain an idea clearly gets more chances at work. It is not about talking loudly. It is about making other people understand you.

The second picture is all white and grey. A bearded man stands in a snow-covered forest, wrapped in a brown coat over a white hoodie, with a black woolly hat pulled down over his head. groups.question: Why do you think games are so entertaining for people?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: The game was Uno, which my cousins taught me the summer I turned twelve. We played it at my grandmother's house in Hai Duong, on the floor, because the only fan was down there. Games ran long, sometimes a whole hour, since nobody would accept losing quietly. My brother invented new rules whenever he was behind, which I am still bitter about. What I remember is not the winning but the noise. My heart went faster when I was down to two cards, and I would try to look calm, which never worked. There was a lot of shouting and some genuine arguing. Afterwards I slept immediately. My grandmother pretended to complain about the noise, though she never once asked us to stop. Those evenings are the clearest memories I have of that house, clearer than the meals or the garden. As for why games entertain us, I think it is because they are fair in a way that ordinary life is not. Everyone begins with the same cards and the rules apply to everybody. That is rare. A game also gives you a small problem that has an ending, whereas real problems drag on for years. And when you play with other people, you are allowed to be loud and slightly childish. Adults get very few chances to do that. Screens have taken over most of this, which I think is a small pity. A pack of cards asks nothing of you.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: The game I enjoyed most was a card game called Uno. My cousins taught me when I was about twelve years old. We played it every summer at my grandmother's house in Hai Duong. There was no air conditioning, so we sat on the floor near the fan. One game could last for an hour because nobody wanted to lose. I still remember the noise that we made. When I played, I felt excited and a little nervous. My heart beat faster when I had only two cards left. I laughed a lot, and sometimes I argued with my brother about the rules. After we finished, I felt tired but very happy. Those evenings are some of my best childhood memories. I think games are entertaining because they are simple and fair. Everyone starts equally, and anyone can win. Games also give us a small problem to solve, which keeps our mind busy. When we play with other people, we talk and laugh together, so we feel close. Modern life is stressful, and games let us forget our work for a short time. That is why people of every age still love playing them today. Some games are very old, but they never get boring.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: Of all the places I have been, the one that stayed with me is Phong Nha in Quang Binh. I visited it with my sister during a very wet week in October. We had booked it months earlier and the forecast ruined every plan we had made. So we ended up spending most of our time underground, in the caves. That was the only place the rain could not reach us. What I enjoyed most was not the size of the caves, impressive as they were. It was the guide who took us through them. He had grown up in a village two kilometres away and could name the year each passage was surveyed. He talked about the river that carved the whole system as though it were a difficult old relative. I have forgotten most of the photographs I took there. I still remember him explaining why the water runs clear in some months and brown in others. That trip taught me something I have used on every holiday since. The first lesson is that a ruined plan is not a ruined week. We would never have gone underground at all if the weather had behaved. That turned out to be the best part. The second is that a place is mostly its people. I now spend my money on a local guide rather than a better hotel. The hotel is forgotten within a month and the stories are not.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: One holiday in Phong Nha is still my favourite memory. I went there with my sister three years ago. We stayed for four days in a small homestay. The weather was terrible, because it rained every day. So we spent most of our time inside the caves. The caves were huge and very quiet. We walked inside them with small lights on our heads. The water in the river was cold and clear. What I enjoyed most was our local guide. He grew up in a village near the caves. He told us stories about the river and the rocks. He also knew the name of every small path. He answered all our questions with a big smile. He even showed us where to eat cheap noodles. I have forgotten my photos, but I remember his voice. That trip taught me two useful lessons. First, bad weather does not ruin a holiday. The rain changed our plan, and the caves were the best part. Also, the people make a place special. Now I spend my money on a good guide. A hotel room is forgotten after one month. That is why I always ask local people now. I want to go back next winter.

groups.question: How do you think people should make more time to see their friends?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: A couple of months ago I finally took up an invitation from my colleague Mai. I went to her family's house in Bac Ninh for the weekend, having postponed it about four times. She lives in an old house with a courtyard and a fish pond her father worries about constantly. Her grandmother decided within ten minutes that I was far too thin. I arrived at around eleven on the Saturday morning and left after lunch on Sunday. In that time I was fed what felt like nine separate meals. What I enjoyed most was how ordinary it all was. There was no plan and nowhere we had to be. My favourite hour was spent sitting on the step peeling vegetables with her mother. Mai and her brother argued cheerfully about football in the kitchen behind us. You cannot get that in a coffee shop with a two-hour parking ticket. On how people should make more time for their friends, my honest advice would be to stop waiting for a free weekend. It never appears. Put a date in the calendar the way you would a dentist's appointment, and treat it as hard to cancel. I would also suggest a fixed arrangement, like a meal on the first Sunday of every month. Then nobody has to organise anything and nobody has to send ten messages. And say yes the first time somebody invites you home. I postponed that trip four times, and I regret every one of them.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I met an old friend and visited her family home last month. Mai lives in Bac Ninh, about one hour from Hanoi. I arrived on Saturday morning and stayed one night. Her house is old and has a small garden. Her father keeps fish in a pond behind the kitchen. Her grandmother cooked a huge lunch for us. We ate fish, rice and vegetables from their garden. The grandmother also said that I was too thin. What I enjoyed most was the simple, quiet time. We had no plan and nowhere to go. I sat on the step and prepared vegetables with her mother. Mai and her brother argued about football in the kitchen. In the evening we drank tea in the garden. You cannot find that feeling in a coffee shop. I'd say people should plan time for their friends. Do not wait for a free weekend, because it never comes. Put a date in your calendar like a doctor's appointment. You can also choose a fixed day, for example the first Sunday. Then nobody has to organise it every month. And say yes the first time a friend invites you. A short visit is better than no visit. I will go back to Mai's house in September.

question_text: Would you prefer to work at a desk or to travel for work? Why?
explanation: I would prefer to travel, at least for part of the year. Sitting at a desk every day makes me tired, and I have noticed that my ideas get weaker after long hours indoors. Travelling gives me fresh air, new places and new people to talk to. However, I still need a steady income, so a job that mixes both would suit me best. A few weeks away, then quiet office work at home. That balance has worked well for two friends of mine, and I would copy it.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I would prefer to travel, at least for part of the year. Sitting at a desk every day makes me tired, and I have noticed that my ideas get weaker after long hours indoors. Travelling gives me fresh air, new places and new people to talk to. However, I still need a steady income, so a job that mixes both would suit me best. A few weeks away, then quiet office work at home. That balance has worked well for two friends of mine, and I would copy it.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Travel wins for me, though not the version people imagine. I have worked from cafes in other cities, and the internet is never as good as the photographs suggest. What strikes me is how much energy new surroundings give you. A desk job is safer, and the money arrives on the same day every month. Still, I get restless after a few months in one room. A job that sent me somewhere twice a year would be perfect. The rest of the year, honestly, I am happy at my desk.

Driving to a big supermarket is better once a month, when we buy heavy things like rice and water. My mother, who does not drive, shops on foot every single morning. So I use both, but walking suits my normal week much better than driving does. The small shops near me have also become part of my routine.

question_text: What do you think about street musicians?
explanation: I think street musicians make a city more interesting. When I walk past someone playing music, the street feels friendlier and less stressful. It is also a chance for musicians to practise and earn some money. However, some people say the music is too loud, especially near shops or offices. In my opinion, as long as they are not disturbing anyone, street musicians are a good thing. I always stop for a minute if the music is good.

question_text: Do you prefer writing by hand or typing on a device? Why?
explanation: I prefer writing by hand when I am studying. Words that I write slowly seem to stay in my memory longer, and I remember where they sat on the page. For long documents, though, a keyboard is much faster and easier to correct. I have used a tablet for university notes, and it was convenient, but I still keep a paper notebook for revision. So my honest answer depends on what I am writing. Speed matters at work, but memory matters more when I study.

question_text: In which kind of weather do you feel better? Why?
explanation: I feel better in cool weather than in heat. When the temperature rises above thirty-five degrees, I lose my appetite, sleep badly and get headaches. In cold weather I can put on more clothes and keep moving, and I have always slept better under a blanket. Of course, very cold air is bad for people who have chest problems. But for my own body, a cold morning feels much healthier than a burning afternoon. A thick jacket solves a problem that no fan can solve.

The obvious problem is that cold air is dangerous for older people and anyone who has a weak chest. So my preference is not a rule for everyone else.

question_text: What do you think about children learning to ride a bicycle?
