question_text: Where would you rather take a group of children? Why?
explanation: I would take them to the park first. Young children need to move, and after twenty minutes in a museum many of them stop listening. In a playground they run, share equipment and make friends quickly. Museums are valuable, but they work better for older students who can read the information. I have helped with a school trip before, and the children who enjoyed it most were over eleven. So age really decides my answer. A short walk in a park has never made a child unhappy.

extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The playground, if the children are small. So my answer is not about which place is better. It is about timing. Take the same class three years later, and the museum becomes the better choice.

question_text: Which of these two meals would you choose? Why?
explanation: Most days I would choose the healthy meal. I feel much better in the afternoon after fish and vegetables, and a heavy burger makes me sleepy at my desk. So I choose the healthy plate normally and the tray occasionally. The problem only starts when the exception has quietly turned into a daily routine.

Still, if I had one free afternoon, I would choose to sit and listen to someone. Trees can wait, but a lonely afternoon cannot wait at all.

question_text: Do you think it is important to do volunteer work? Why?
explanation: I would rather join a litter clean-up in the park. The change is immediate, and at the end of the morning you can look back and see a clean park. That feeling keeps people coming again. Planting trees is important too, but you have to wait a long time for any result. I have also noticed that clean-ups are easier to organise in a city, because you do not need any land. So I would start with the rubbish. A visible result is what keeps volunteers coming back.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Yes, I think volunteer work is very important, for two reasons. Firstly, it solves real problems that nobody is paid to solve. For example, the park near my house is only clean because a group of students collects the rubbish there every month. Secondly, it changes the volunteers themselves. When you give a few hours to help other people, you feel useful and you meet people from outside your normal life. I joined a tree-planting day last year, and I still talk to two friends I met that morning. So volunteer work is good for the community and good for the person who does it.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: I do, though not only for the reasons people usually give. The obvious argument is that volunteers fill gaps: the park near my flat is only clean because a student group turns up every month with bags and pickers. The less obvious benefit is what it does to the volunteer. Spending a Saturday planting trees with strangers pulls you out of your own routine and reminds you that the neighbourhood is shared. I have also noticed that people who volunteer complain less, probably because they have seen how much effort even a small improvement takes. So it matters, both for the place and for the person.

question_text: Why do some people prefer trains to other kinds of transport?
explanation: I think people prefer trains for several reasons. First, there is a lot of legroom, so long journeys feel less tiring. Second, you can move around, buy food, or sleep during the trip. Trains are also better for the environment than planes or cars. Many people also say the journey itself is part of the holiday, because you can sit back and watch the countryside pass by through the window.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think people prefer trains for several reasons. First, there is a lot of legroom, so long journeys feel less tiring. Second, you can move around, buy food, or sleep during the trip. Trains are also better for the environment than planes or cars. Many people also say the journey itself is part of the holiday, because you can sit back and watch the countryside pass by through the window.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Comfort is the first answer most people give, and it is a fair one, because you can get up and walk about whenever you like. Beyond that there is the environmental argument, which matters more to younger travellers than it used to. But I think the real reason is less practical than that. A train journey feels like part of the trip rather than dead time between two places, and people remember the window more than they remember the destination. Cheap flights, for all their speed, simply cannot compete with that feeling.

question_text: Why do some people find it hard to exercise regularly?
explanation: I think many people find it hard to exercise regularly because they are busy. After a long day at work, most people are too tired to go to the gym. The weather is also a problem, especially when it is very hot or raining. Some people start with a plan that is too difficult and then give up quickly. In my opinion, the main reason is that people expect results too soon.

In my opinion, the main reason is that people expect results too soon.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Time is the reason everybody gives, and it is partly true, but I think the real problem is how people start. They decide to run five kilometres four times a week, manage it for eight days and then stop for a month. Anything that ambitious collapses. Weather matters too, since almost nobody wants to run in Hanoi in July. And results arrive slowly, which is hard when you have rearranged your evenings and can see no difference in the mirror.

question_text: Why do so many young people eat fast food?
explanation: Fast food is popular with young people for simple reasons. It is quick, cheap, and available almost everywhere, including near schools and universities. Many students who live away from home cannot cook well, so ordering is easier than shopping. Fast-food restaurants are also social places where friends can sit for hours. Advertising and delivery apps make it even more tempting. Young people know it is not healthy, but convenience usually wins in the end. Habits that start at university often last for many more years.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Fast food is popular with young people for simple reasons. It is quick, cheap, and available almost everywhere, including near schools and universities. extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Speed and money explain most of it. A student between classes has twenty minutes and very little cash, and fast food fits both limits perfectly. Delivery apps have made the habit almost invisible, because nobody even leaves the room now. Young people are not ignorant about nutrition. They simply choose the option that asks the least of them. Time and money decide the plate, not knowledge.

question_text: Why do some people like sharing photos with their friends?

question_text: What does the expert say being professional is all about?
options: To maintain a positive attitude.
To create a good working environment.
To make a good impression.
explanation:
For the second half of our session, an expert takes the floor on professionalism — what it truly is, and where it is heading. People decorate this word with many meanings. Ask around the office and you will hear that being professional is about building a good working environment; ask the sales floor and you will hear it is about making a good impression on clients. Pleasant ideas, but they confuse the fruit with the tree. Professionalism is all about maintaining a positive attitude. Friendliness under pressure, openness to other views, the willingness to help without being asked — that attitude is what colleagues and clients actually experience. Impressions and environments are not built; they are grown, and positive attitude is the soil they grow from.
Now, the question of definition. There are veterans who insist professionalism means exactly what it meant forty years ago: the pressed suit, the formal letter, the unquestioned hierarchy. There are also younger colleagues hoping the modern definition is final, ready to be memorised once and used forever. Both are mistaken, and in the same way: our definition of professionalism is changing, and it has never stopped changing. Globalisation added cultural fluency to the job description; technology added digital competence; remote work is adding new rules as we speak. Treat professionalism as a moving target and you will always be aiming correctly. Treat it as a monument, and you will be photographing something that has already walked away.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant professionalism #3.)
1. Đáp án: To maintain a positive attitude. Bẫy: "working environment" và "good impression" — "confuse the fruit with the tree".
2. Đáp án: Our definition of it is changing. Bẫy: "same as 40 years ago" và "will not change anymore" — "Both are mistaken".

question_text: Do people in your country dress differently at work and at home?
explanation: Yes, most people in my country dress quite differently at work and at home. At work they wear shirts, trousers, or a uniform that the company provides. At home they change into shorts and a T-shirt because the weather is hot. Older people often wear very simple clothes at home. I think comfort matters more than style inside the house.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Yes, most people in my country dress quite differently at work and at home. At work they wear shirts, trousers, or a uniform that the company provides. At home they change into shorts and a T-shirt because the weather is hot. Older people often wear very simple clothes at home. I think comfort matters more than style inside the house.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Very differently, and the change usually happens within a minute of getting home. Offices here still expect shirts and closed shoes, even in June when it is far too hot for them. The moment people get through the door, everything becomes shorts and slippers. My father, who wore a tie for thirty years, has refused to own one since he retired.

question_text: Why do some people move to a country with a different climate?
explanation: I think people move to a different climate for several reasons. Many of them move for work or study, and the weather is simply part of the package. Others move because the climate at home makes them uncomfortable, for example people who cannot stand the cold. Some retired people move somewhere warm for their health. Family is also a common reason, because people follow their children or their partner.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think people move to a different climate for several reasons. Many of them move for work or study, and the weather is simply part of the package. Others move because the climate at home makes them uncomfortable, for example people who cannot stand the cold. Some retired people move somewhere warm for their health. Family is also a common reason, because people follow their children or their partner.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Work is the honest answer most of the time. Somebody takes a job in another country and the weather comes with it, welcome or not. Health matters too, particularly for older people, and there is a long tradition of retiring somewhere warmer. Then there are people who simply never adjusted to where they were born, and I have met a few. What surprises me is how quickly the weather stops being the interesting part and the language becomes the real difficulty.

question_text: Why do some people like working outdoors?
explanation: I think more people work outside the office now because technology makes it possible. With a laptop and a phone, you can work almost anywhere. Many companies also allow flexible working, so staff choose cafes, parks or their own homes. People say they feel less stressed and more creative outside. After the pandemic, a lot of businesses realised that staff can do good work without sitting in an office all day.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think some people like working outdoors for several reasons. The main reason is that fresh air and sunlight make them feel awake, and they feel free, not stuck between four walls. On top of that, a laptop and a phone are enough to work almost anywhere now, and a change of scene helps people be creative. For example, my friend writes her reports in the park every Friday. Having said that, not every job can be done outside, and the weather is not always good. So for many people, fresh air is worth more than a comfortable desk.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Some people like working outdoors because an office, however nice, is still a box. Fresh air and daylight keep you alert in a way that fluorescent light never does, and there is a sense of freedom in choosing your own spot — a park bench, a cafe terrace, a garden. Technology made it possible: a laptop and a phone signal are the whole office now. My uncle left a bank job to run a small farm and, exhausted as he is, he says he has never been happier. Of course, not every job can be taken outside, the weather has opinions of its own, and some people find birdsong more distracting than a colleague's phone call. Even so, for a lot of people, fresh air is worth more than a comfortable chair.

question_text: Which project is more beneficial to the environment? Why?
explanation: Local governments can do many practical things. They can put more bins and recycling points in public places, so people are not tempted to drop rubbish. They can also fine companies that pour waste into rivers. Improving buses and building cycle lanes reduces the number of cars in the centre. Schools can be given money for environment clubs, which teaches good habits early. Small local rules often work faster than big national promises. People usually follow the rules that make good behaviour easy and cheap for them.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think planting trees is more beneficial to the environment. A clean-up is useful, but the result does not last, because the same park is dirty again after a month. A tree, on the other hand, keeps working for many years. It gives shade, cleans the air and provides a home for birds and insects. For example, the trees along my old school were planted by students twenty years ago, and that street is still cooler than the roads around it. Of course, picking up litter is easier to organise and gives a quick result. But for a long-term benefit, planting trees wins.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Planting trees, I would say, even though the reward is slow. A clean-up treats the symptom: the park looks better for an afternoon, and a month later the same bottles are back, which I have seen with my own eyes. A tree changes a place permanently. It cools the street, holds the soil and gives birds somewhere to live for decades after the volunteers have gone home. I understand why groups prefer clean-ups, because the before-and-after photographs look dramatic and nobody needs land or permission. But if the question is real benefit to the environment, the row of trees outside my old school still proves the point.

question_text: Why do some people prefer meeting face to face?
explanation: I think some people prefer meeting face to face because it feels more natural. When you sit in the same room, you can see body language and understand the mood better. Conversations also flow more easily, because nobody has to wait for the sound. Meeting in person helps to build trust, especially with new clients or new colleagues. For important decisions, most people still want to be in the same room.

Conversations also flow more easily, because nobody has to wait for the sound. Meeting in person helps to build trust, especially with new clients or new colleagues. extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Because most of a conversation is not the words. In a room you can read the pause, the glance between two colleagues, the person who is clearly unhappy but has not said so. A screen flattens all of that. There is also the informal part, the five minutes before and after, which is where a surprising amount of real work actually happens. For a routine update a call is fine, but for anything difficult, or with someone you have never actually met before, people still want to be in the same room.

question_text: How do the seasons change the activities that families do together?
explanation: Seasons change family life a lot. In summer, families go to the beach, have picnics, or travel during the school holidays, and children play outside until late. In winter, activities move indoors, so families cook together, watch films, or visit relatives. In countries that have snow, winter brings skiing and skating instead. Festivals also follow the calendar, which gives each season its own routine. So the weather quietly decides how families spend their weekends. Children remember those routines long after they have forgotten the details.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Seasons change family life a lot. In summer, families go to the beach, have picnics, or travel during the school holidays, and children play outside until late. Festivals also follow the calendar, which gives each season its own routine. So the weather quietly decides how families spend their weekends. extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The calendar organises family life more than people admit. Summer means long holidays, so families travel, camp, or simply spend whole days outdoors together. Winter pushes everyone into the same room, which produces board games, cooking and long meals. In snowy countries the pattern flips, and the ski season becomes the busiest family time of the year. Festivals reinforce all of this. I have noticed that my clearest childhood memories are attached to a season rather than a place. Summer meant the sea, and December meant my grandmother's kitchen.

explanation: Yes, I think handwriting is still important for children. Writing by hand helps them control small movements and learn how letters are formed. Teachers who I have spoken to say children remember spelling better when they write words themselves. Of course, students need computer skills too, because most work today is done on screens. So schools should teach both, with handwriting in the early years and typing added later. Neither skill should replace the other completely. The two skills belong to different parts of a child's education.

My compromise would be simple. Teach handwriting properly for a few years, then let typing take over gradually. Nobody has to choose between a pen and a keyboard forever.

explanation: I think it depends on the situation. In a bank or a hospital, most people wait quietly and follow the numbers. But on the road, drivers are not patient at all. At a red light in Hanoi, people start pressing the horn after two seconds. Young people are also less patient than my parents, because they are used to fast apps. My father has waited an hour for a bowl of pho. I usually give up after twenty minutes and go home.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think it depends on the situation. In a bank or a hospital, most people wait quietly and follow the numbers. But on the road, drivers are not patient at all. extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: It really splits by place, in my experience. Inside a bank or a hospital people behave, because there is a number system which nobody argues with. On the road it collapses completely, and the horn starts about two seconds after the light turns green. Age matters a lot here too. My father has waited an hour for a bowl of pho without complaining once, whereas I check the app after ten minutes. Fast delivery has probably reset what my generation thinks a normal wait is.

question_text: How should schools balance classroom learning and outdoor activities?
explanation: Schools should treat outdoor time as part of learning, not as a reward. Children who move during the day concentrate better afterwards, so breaks and sport are not wasted hours. A good balance might be short breaks every hour, one sports lesson a week, and a few trips each term. Museums, farms and parks all teach different things. Exams are important, but a school that only sits children at desks will lose their attention. A day that mixes both kinds of learning usually produces the calmest classroom.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Schools should treat outdoor time as part of learning, not as a reward. Children who move during the day concentrate better afterwards, so breaks and sport are not wasted hours. A good balance might be short breaks every hour, one sports lesson a week, and a few trips each term. Museums, farms and parks all teach different things. Exams are important, but a school that only sits children at desks will lose their attention. A day that mixes both kinds of learning usually produces the calmest classroom.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: By treating the outdoors as a subject rather than a break. Studies have shown that children who exercise during the day concentrate better in the afternoon. Cutting sport to add revision is therefore a false economy. I would protect two things: daily physical activity and one trip each term to somewhere real. Exam pressure makes head teachers nervous, and I understand why. Still, a timetable of nothing but desks produces tired children and very ordinary results. The best schools I have seen protect both without any argument.

question_text: How does the weather affect people's mood and health?
explanation: Weather affects us more than we think. Sunlight helps the body produce vitamin D, and many people feel happier and more active on bright days. In long grey winters, some people become tired and sad, which doctors call seasonal depression. Extreme heat is also dangerous, because older people lose water quickly and their hearts suffer. Cold weather brings colds and flu. So both extremes affect health, and the mild days between them suit us best. Doctors say that the body works best in the middle range.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Weather affects us more than we think. Sunlight helps the body produce vitamin D, and many people feel happier and more active on bright days. In long grey winters, some people become tired and sad, which doctors call seasonal depression. Extreme heat is also dangerous, because older people lose water quickly and their hearts suffer. Cold weather brings colds and flu. So both extremes affect health, and the mild days between them suit us best. Doctors say that the body works best in the middle range.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The effect is real and measurable. Light influences sleep hormones, so grey months leave many people low, and doctors have recognised seasonal depression for decades. Heat is the more dangerous extreme, since hospitals fill up in very hot weeks with older patients whose hearts cannot manage. Cold brings its own problems, mainly infections and breathing trouble. What strikes me is how quickly mood follows the sky. One bright morning after a week of rain changes a whole street. People smile at strangers again, which nobody plans.

question_text: Why do fewer children play outside these days?
explanation: I think fewer children play outside now for several reasons. The main one is that they have phones and computers, so they can play games at home. Traffic is also much heavier than before, and parents do not feel safe letting children out alone. In many cities there are fewer parks and open spaces than there used to be. Children are also much busier with extra classes in the evening, so they simply have far less free time than before.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think fewer children play outside now for several reasons. The main one is that they have phones and computers, so they can play games at home. extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about my exam revision at the start of this year. I had a big English test in March, and for two whole weeks I could not start. Every evening I opened the book, read half a page, closed it and found an excuse: I was tired, the room was too noisy, or I would begin tomorrow. The worst part was the guilt, because I knew the time was running out. In the end I dealt with it by tricking myself. I set a timer for only ten minutes a day and promised to stop when it rang. Most days, once I started, I kept going for an hour, because starting was the hard part, not studying. I also told my sister my plan, so she asked me about it every day. I think people lose motivation when the goal feels too far away and the results come slowly, or when the task is so big that they do not know where to begin. What helps is small steps, small wins, and someone who checks on you. That experience taught me not to wait until I feel ready, because the feeling usually comes after the action, not before it.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I want to tell you about my exam revision at the start of this year. I had a big English test in March, and for two whole weeks I could not start. Every evening I opened the book, read half a page, closed it and found an excuse: I was tired, the room was too noisy, or I would begin tomorrow. The worst part was the guilt, because I knew the time was running out. In the end I dealt with it by tricking myself. I set a timer for only ten minutes a day and promised to stop when it rang. Most days, once I started, I kept going for an hour, because starting was the hard part, not studying. I also told my sister my plan, so she asked me about it every day. I think people lose motivation when the goal feels too far away and the results come slowly, or when the task is so big that they do not know where to begin. What helps is small steps, small wins, and someone who checks on you. That experience taught me not to wait until I feel ready, because the feeling usually comes after the action, not before it.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The clearest example was an online design course I abandoned exactly halfway through last year. For about a month I kept inventing very convincing excuses — work was busy, the next module looked dull, I would restart properly on Monday — and the strange thing is that the dread of studying was far heavier than the studying itself. When I finally returned, the remaining lessons took two quiet weekends. What broke the cycle was embarrassingly simple. I told my mother my exact plan, moved my laptop to the library where there was nothing else to do, and allowed myself to work for only ten minutes at a time. Once there was visible progress, a finished lesson and a certificate to chase, the energy came back on its own, and I did not need the timer any more. I have come to think motivation dies when goals are distant and results invisible: our brains need small, regular proof that effort actually works, and a task that feels enormous produces avoidance rather than action. What brings it back is the opposite — breaking the goal into pieces, making progress measurable, and adding a bit of social pressure so quitting has a cost. So rather than waiting to feel inspired, I now rely on tiny steps and fixed routines. Systems, in my experience, quietly beat motivation almost every time.

formalEmail.instruction: Write an email to the manager of the club. Write about your feelings and what you think the club should do about the situation. Write 120-150 words. Recommended time: 20 minutes.
formalEmail.sampleAnswer:
Dear Manager,
Thank you for asking members for their opinions about the two proposed activities.
In my view, the painting competition for local schools is the better choice this year. It would connect the club with the community, and students who submit paintings would bring their families and teachers to see the results. This means more visitors, more new members, and a stronger interest in art among young people, which matches your goal exactly.
However, I do not think we should completely drop the exhibition idea. We could combine the two: display the best competition entries in a small exhibition, and invite a local artist to give a short talk at the opening and present the prizes. This way, one event would serve both purposes at a reasonable cost.
I would be happy to help organize the event.
Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: This picture shows three young people sitting on a grey sofa in front of a pink wall. The girl in the middle, who has headphones around her neck and a laptop on her lap, is giving a high five to the young man in a black hoodie. extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The photo captures a happy little moment in what looks like a casual office or someone's living room. Three young people share a grey sofa against a bold pink wall: the woman in the middle, headphones slung around her neck and a laptop still open on her lap, is exchanging an enthusiastic high five with the curly-haired man in a black hoodie, while the bearded man on the left sits back, hand on chin, clearly still turning something over in his mind. The low wooden table in front of them is scattered with laptops, headphones and a paper cup — the debris of a long session. My guess is that two of them have just cracked a problem their colleague is still quietly checking.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: These two pictures both show people cooking, but in very different places. In the first picture, a woman with long dark hair is standing alone on a hillside. She is wearing a grey jumper and cooking in a small pot on a camping stove placed on a big rock. Next to it there is a metal flask and a cup. The second picture shows a man and a woman in a modern dark grey kitchen. They are both wearing black aprons. The woman is cutting a tomato on a wooden board, and the man is standing close behind her and smiling. On the counter there is a red pepper, some salad and dry pasta. So one person is cooking alone outdoors, and two people are cooking together indoors.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Both photographs show people preparing food, though the settings could hardly be more different. In the first, a woman with long dark hair and a grey jumper stands alone on an open hillside, stirring a small pot on a camping stove balanced on a flat rock. A metal flask and a white cup sit beside it, and low green scrub and hills stretch away behind her. The second photograph instead shows a couple in a sleek dark grey kitchen. Both wear white tops and black aprons, and the woman is slicing a tomato on a wooden board while the man stands close behind her, smiling as he watches. A whole red pepper, a plate of salad and a bundle of dried spaghetti wait on the counter. So one image is about solitude and simplicity, and the other about company and comfort.

2. Chọn "Natural barrier to resettlement" vì đoạn nhấn mạnh việc vượt biển rộng tới lục địa cô lập là "seemingly impossible" với công nghệ thời đó — biển là rào cản tự nhiên.
3. Chọn "Technology helps uncover the ocean's secret" vì đoạn nói remote sensing và GIS giúp phát hiện chuỗi đảo nối liền thành con đường di cư dưới biển.
4. Chọn "A Journey made by stages" vì đoạn mô tả hành trình island-hopping từng chặng, mỗi đảo là điểm nghỉ và nguồn thức ăn.
5. Chọn "No precise figures available" vì đoạn nói giới khoa học chỉ có thể phỏng đoán số người di cư, "the lack of exact statistics" — không có con số chính xác. Chữ "speculate" trong đoạn là bẫy kéo sang heading "New evidence to speculation".
6. Chọn "Lack of knowledge and skills" vì đoạn nêu ý kiến hoài nghi rằng người cổ không đủ năng lực trí tuệ, kiến thức và kỹ năng hàng hải để vượt đại dương.
7. Chọn "Determination of the explorers through the ages" vì đoạn nói về ý chí khám phá bền bỉ của con người xuyên suốt lịch sử, từ thám hiểm biển sâu tới du hành vũ trụ.
Heading thừa: "New evidence to speculation".

extra_data.title: The Early Australians

headings.text: Determination of the explorers through the ages
Technology helps uncover the ocean's secret

paragraphs.text: The history of early Australians stretches back much further than previously believed, with evidence suggesting human presence on the Australian continent dating back approximately 65,000 years. This timeline challenges traditional views held by historians regarding the first human settlers in Australia. Carbon analysis of archaeological sites has provided different results, leading to alternative hypotheses about the early inhabitants of the land Down Under. The findings shed new light on the ancient origins and rich cultural heritage of the Indigenous people who have inhabited the continent for millennia.

Recent discoveries have revealed that the settlement of Australia was not a singular event. In addition to the early settlers, scientists have uncovered traces of two other human groups that migrated to the continent. The presence of multiple groups suggests a complex history of human migration and interaction. However, reaching the isolated continent posed significant challenges for ancient humans, as they would have needed to traverse vast stretches of open sea, a feat seemingly impossible with the technology available to them at the time.

The aid of advanced equipment and techniques has allowed scientists to identify a series of small islands closely connected, forming a continuous pathway leading to Australia. Remote sensing technology has helped researchers identify and map small islands and potential migration routes. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have integrated various data sets to discover past and potential migration corridors. This discovery provides insight into the probable routes taken by ancient migrants as they ventured across the vast expanse of the sea, providing a deeper understanding of the complex migration patterns that shaped the early history of the continent.

The migration patterns of early Australians reveal a gradual journey to the continent. Archaeological evidence points to the likelihood of different tribes arriving in Australia through a series of island-hopping journeys. Each island served as a resting point and a source of food, allowing them to continue their voyage. This gradual movement indicates an adaptive and resourceful approach taken by these ancient tribes, who navigated the challenges of the terrain to ultimately settle in Australia.

Scientists can only speculate about the exact number of individuals required to undertake such a migration, which could have ranged from a small group to several thousand people. The uncertainty stems from various factors, including the limitations of available archaeological evidence and the complexities of ancient human migration. The lack of exact statistics makes it challenging to determine the scale and composition of these early human journeys accurately. However, ongoing research and technological advancements may offer more insights in the future.

Some skeptics argue that ancient humans didn't have enough intellectual capacity, knowledge, and skills needed to undertake such journeys. They question whether early humans possessed the navigational and maritime expertise to traverse vast stretches of ocean. Critics contend that without advanced tools or navigational aids, navigating through open seas would have been beyond the capabilities of ancient civilizations. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that human ingenuity and adaptability have proven remarkable throughout history, enabling our ancestors to overcome various challenges and achieve extraordinary feats.

History has demonstrated the unwavering determination and resilience of human explorers in the past. From deep-sea expeditions in ancient times to modern space travel, humans have showcased their resolve to explore and conquer the unknown. The same determination might have driven the early Australians to embark on journeys across treacherous waters. While the challenges they faced were undoubtedly immense, the spirit of human curiosity and the desire to discover new lands and opportunities likely motivated these ancient explorers, leaving a remarkable legacy in the annals of history.

groups.question: What factors help create a good conversation?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about a talk with a taxi driver last year. I took a taxi from the airport to my home, and the ride was only forty minutes. At first we talked about the traffic and the weather. Then he started to tell me about his family. He was an engineer for twenty years, but he left that job because he was always stressed. Now he drives a taxi, and he says he is happy with a simpler life. He sees his children every evening and he sleeps well. I listened to him for the whole ride, and I forgot to look at my phone. How did I feel after the conversation? I felt happy and thoughtful at the same time. This is mainly because he was so honest with a stranger, and his story made me think about my own job and my own family. I was still thinking about it on the way home, and I told my sister about it that evening. What factors help create a good conversation? I think the most important factor is real listening. People should ask questions and share their own ideas, and they should show interest in what the other person is saying. Being friendly and respectful also makes people feel comfortable. It helps to put the phone away, because a phone on the table breaks the connection. So good listening, interesting topics and respect are the key to a good conversation.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I want to tell you about a talk with a taxi driver last year. I took a taxi from the airport to my home, and the ride was only forty minutes. At first we talked about the traffic and the weather. Then he started to tell me about his family. He was an engineer for twenty years, but he left that job because he was always stressed. Now he drives a taxi, and he says he is happy with a simpler life. He sees his children every evening and he sleeps well. I listened to him for the whole ride, and I forgot to look at my phone. How did I feel after the conversation? I felt happy and thoughtful at the same time. This is mainly because he was so honest with a stranger, and his story made me think about my own job and my own family. I was still thinking about it on the way home, and I told my sister about it that evening. What factors help create a good conversation? I think the most important factor is real listening. People should ask questions and share their own ideas, and they should show interest in what the other person is saying. Being friendly and respectful also makes people feel comfortable. It helps to put the phone away, because a phone on the table breaks the connection. So good listening, interesting topics and respect are the key to a good conversation.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The conversation I always come back to happened on a night train two years ago, with a retired history teacher sitting opposite me. What began as small talk about the weather somehow turned into three hours on regret, career choices and what makes a life feel worthwhile. He spoke with a kind of honesty you rarely get from people you know; strangers have nothing to protect. Afterwards I felt lighter, and strangely awake, although it was past midnight. Partly it was the relief of having been listened to properly for once, and partly the sense that he had answered a question I had been carrying around for months without asking it. I wrote half of what he said in my notebook before I slept, and I still reread it. As for what makes a good conversation, I would put genuine listening first: people only open up when they feel heard, and a conversation dies the moment one person talks only about themselves. After that comes curiosity — asking real questions and offering something of yourself in return — and a basic respect that lets the other person disagree without fear. Practical things matter too: unhurried time, a quiet place, and a phone out of sight. That train had no wifi, and honestly, that was half the secret.

question_text: How much does the book cost?
explanation:
Welcome to the bookshop's morning announcements — well, it's just me talking to the shelves, but you're here now! You asked about the gardening book in the window. So: the big hardback edition next to it is seventeen pounds — beautiful, but heavy enough to press flowers with. The little pocket guide is seven, though honestly it's more pictures than advice. The one you want, the proper paperback everyone buys — that book costs eleven pounds. Eleven, and it includes the planting calendar. Shall I wrap it as a gift?

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – £11 (mười một bảng).
• Vì sao đúng: người bán nói về đúng cuốn khách hỏi "The one you want, the proper paperback everyone buys — that book costs eleven pounds. Eleven, and it includes the planting calendar".
• £17 sai: là giá bản bìa cứng khổ lớn "the big hardback edition next to it is seventeen pounds".
• £7 sai: là giá bản bỏ túi "The little pocket guide is seven, though honestly it's more pictures than advice".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi GIÁ SÁCH/MÓN HÀNG, một sản phẩm có nhiều phiên bản. Ghi nhanh cặp "phiên bản – giá" (hardback / pocket / paperback) rồi chọn giá của bản được nhắc bằng "the one you want".

question_text: Four people are talking about using the Internet. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: I'm not really a fan of talking to people online, so I usually prefer to communicate with my friends face to face, especially when we study together. However, most of my friends live quite far away from me, so I normally travel by bus when I want to meet them. When I'm on the bus, I often use the Internet to check transportation information, especially bus routes and directions. It's really useful because I can find the best route and make sure I don't get lost. I also check the estimated travel time before I leave home, so I know when I'm likely to arrive.
Speaker B: I have quite a lot of friends, and one of the most convenient ways for me to keep in touch with them is through the Internet. Some of my friends live in different countries, so meeting them in person isn't always possible. For example, one of my close friends lives in Sydney. She takes cookery classes there, and we often have online calls to talk about what she has learned. Sometimes, we exchange recipes and discuss different ways of preparing food. I really enjoy these conversations because social media and other online platforms make it easy for us to stay connected, even though we live far apart.
Speaker C: I use the Internet a lot for my schoolwork. At the moment, I'm working on a big assignment about different airlines. I have to collect information about several companies, including their services, prices and destinations. Without the Internet, I would have to ask lots of different people or visit different places to find all this information. Fortunately, I can search for most of what I need online. I can also compare information from different websites and find useful pictures and statistics for my assignment. It saves me a lot of time and makes doing a big project much easier.
Speaker D: I used to spend a lot of time playing computer games, but I think I've grown out of it now. These days, I mainly use the Internet for entertainment, especially for watching films. I don't really need a television because I can watch films on my computer whenever I want. If there's a film I really like, I can download it and watch it later when I have some free time. I usually watch films in the evening, especially at weekends. It's much more convenient for me because I can choose what I want to watch instead of waiting for something interesting to be shown on TV.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
LƯU Ý: Đây là bản ĐẢO SPEAKER của Đề 25 - The Internet (cùng 4 mục thông tin nhưng người nói khác nhau). Đề thi thật 25/8 ra bản này.
A = check transportation information (tra routes trên xe buýt). Bẫy: A nhắc "communication" nhưng là nói chuyện TRỰC TIẾP khi học nhóm, không phải qua mạng.
B = communicate with friends (gọi điện trao đổi công thức với bạn ở Sydney).
C = complete school assignments (bài tập lớn về airlines).
D = watch films (tải phim về máy tính). Bẫy: D nhắc games nhưng đã BỎ ("grown out of it").
"play online games" và "shop online" là 2 mục nhiễu — không ai dùng.

question_text: Listen to the announcement. What time will the train leave?
explanation:
Attention, passengers. The 8.45 train from King's Cross to Luton has been delayed. This means it will now depart at 9.30 instead, and we will reach Luton at 10.30. We apologize for the inconvenience.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – 9.30.
• Vì sao đúng: thông báo nói "it will now depart at 9.30 instead" — tàu bị hoãn nên giờ khởi hành MỚI là 9.30.
• 8.45 sai: là giờ khởi hành theo lịch cũ, đã bị hoãn "The 8.45 train from King's Cross to Luton has been delayed".
• 10.45 sai: không được nhắc tới trong bài; con số gần giống là 10.30 nhưng đó là giờ ĐẾN Luton "we will reach Luton at 10.30".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi GIỜ TÀU CHẠY, bài luôn có ba mốc: giờ cũ (tên chuyến), giờ mới (depart), giờ đến (reach/arrive). Chỉ lấy số đi sau động từ "depart/leave", đừng lấy số đi sau "reach/arrive".

question_text: Tell me about a time when you were responsible for something important.
explanation: I want to tell you about the time I was responsible for my class's charity sale at school. It turned out to be much harder than I expected. It was in my final year, about three years ago. My teacher asked me to plan the stalls, collect the money and keep it safe. Later, we gave everything to a children's hospital, and the total was higher than anyone expected. These days, I still think about that week whenever somebody gives me an important task. About the feeling, the honest answer is that I was nervous first and proud second. This is mainly because everyone was watching me, and one mistake would have spoiled the whole event. For example, I checked the numbers every night because I was afraid of losing money. On the other hand, that pressure taught me to be careful and organised. On the last question, I think responsibility is good for young people because it helps them grow up. One reason is that when something depends on you, you stop making excuses and start solving problems.

A good example would be that I rechecked the figures every night, terrified of losing money. That said, the pressure did exactly what pressure is supposed to do: it made me careful and honest. On the last point, I would argue responsibility is the fastest way for young people to grow up. One reason for this is that when something genuinely depends on you, excuses stop being available and problems have to be solved. People who learn that at fifteen find everything at twenty-five considerably less frightening.

The second photograph freezes a male athlete in mid-air, arching his back over the yellow high-jump bar with his arms trailing behind him. A thick blue landing mat waits below, and the stadium stands and a tent blur in the background. Nobody around can help him at that moment. So one picture celebrates a footballer in front of his supporters, and the other celebrates one person against gravity.

groups.question: Do you think comparing options carefully always leads to better choices? Why?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about choosing between two laptops before the new school year. One was cheaper, and one had better quality and a bigger battery, but online they looked almost the same. I could not decide, so I made a list of good and bad points for each one, read customer reviews for two evenings, and finally went to the shop to test both. In the shop the small details decided it. The cheaper one felt slow when I opened many pages, and it had no warranty, so I chose the more expensive one. I made the final decision by following my list, not my feelings. At first I wanted the cheap one because I did not like spending money, but the numbers showed that it could cost more later if it broke. I felt confused for a week, then very relieved when I paid. Do I think comparing carefully always leads to better choices? For big things like money, jobs or where to live, yes, because a list stops you from being pushed by advertising. But for small things, like which coffee to buy, comparing for days is a waste of time and makes people unhappy. So now I compare the big things carefully and relax about the small ones.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I want to tell you about choosing between two laptops before the new school year. One was cheaper, and one had better quality and a bigger battery, but online they looked almost the same. I could not decide, so I made a list of good and bad points for each one, read customer reviews for two evenings, and finally went to the shop to test both. In the shop the small details decided it. The cheaper one felt slow when I opened many pages, and it had no warranty, so I chose the more expensive one. I made the final decision by following my list, not my feelings. At first I wanted the cheap one because I did not like spending money, but the numbers showed that it could cost more later if it broke. I felt confused for a week, then very relieved when I paid. Do I think comparing carefully always leads to better choices? For big things like money, jobs or where to live, yes, because a list stops you from being pushed by advertising. But for small things, like which coffee to buy, comparing for days is a waste of time and makes people unhappy. So now I compare the big things carefully and relax about the small ones.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The clearest case was two job offers at the end of last year — one safe and close to home, the other more exciting but far less certain. For a week I did everything you are supposed to do: a proper pros-and-cons list, conversations with people who worked in both companies, even imagining an ordinary Tuesday in each life to see which one I could stand. What stayed with me is that the boring details ended up mattering most — commute time and the chance to learn something new — rather than the salary everyone asks about. I made the final call by trusting the list over my nerves, though I let instinct break the tie, and I accepted the riskier job. Six months later I still think it was right, mostly because I can explain why I chose it. Does careful comparing always produce better choices? For financial and career decisions, almost always: it forces you to name what you actually need and shields you from persuasion, from a friend's opinion or a clever salesperson. But some choices need courage more than analysis, and endless comparing becomes its own trap — people spend weeks choosing a phone and lose more in time than they ever save in money. There is also a point where two options are simply equal, and more research just delays the decision. So my rule is straightforward: compare the big things carefully, and release the small ones.

formalEmail.instruction: Write an email to the president of the club. Write about your feelings and what you think the club should do about the situation. Write 120-150 words. Recommended time: 20 minutes.
formalEmail.sampleAnswer:
Dear President,
I am writing to share my suggestions for the actor's talk at our annual meeting.
In my opinion, the actor should speak about his real experiences behind the camera: how a film is actually made, from reading the script for the first time to filming difficult scenes. This topic would be attractive to everyone. New members often join our club because they are curious about the film world, so hearing true stories from a professional would be the perfect welcome. Current members, who already know a lot about films, would still enjoy details that cannot be found on the internet.
I also suggest leaving fifteen minutes at the end for questions, because members will certainly want to interact with the guest. Perhaps we could collect questions in advance to save time.
I believe this event will attract many participants and make our club more popular.
Yours sincerely,
[Your Name]

explanation:
1. Chọn tiêu đề này vì đoạn văn nói thành tựu của phụ nữ trong toán học bị xóa khỏi sử sách hoặc bị gán cho đồng nghiệp nam — chính là "thành tựu bị làm mờ vì giới tính".
2. Đoạn nói Sophie Germain tự học, đóng góp lớn cho lý thuyết số và là người phụ nữ ĐẦU TIÊN nhận giải của Viện Hàn lâm Paris — đây là sự công nhận thành tựu của một người tiên phong.
3. Đoạn kể công trình của Maria Agnesi bị dịch sai tên và công lao bị gán cho các nhà toán học nam đi sau — đúng ý "người đàn ông được ghi công không công bằng".
4. Đoạn theo suốt cuộc đời Millicent Fawcett: diễn thuyết về Newton năm 19 tuổi rồi dành hàng chục năm vận động cho giáo dục và quyền bầu cử của phụ nữ — một sự nghiệp dài thể hiện năng lực xuất sắc.
5. Đoạn phân tích cách gọi "women geniuses" hay "female prodigies" khiến người ta nghĩ phụ nữ giỏi toán là chuyện hiếm — nhãn mác làm thay đổi cách nhìn về con người.
6. Đoạn liệt kê các chương trình outreach, học bổng riêng cho nữ và mentorship trong STEM — nỗ lực tạo cân bằng giới.
7. Đoạn nói tiêu chí đánh giá đồng nhất bỏ qua hoàn cảnh khác nhau của từng người, "one-size-fits-all" không tạo ra công bằng thật — sự đồng nhất là một bất lợi.

extra_data.title: Women Mathematicians

headings.text: Men use different languages than women
A long career showing exceptional ability
Attempting to create a gender balance
Labels can change perspective on people

paragraphs.text: In 2014, Iranian mathematician Maryam Mirzakhani received the prestigious Fields Prize, the highest honor in mathematics, and the first time in its 70 years that a woman has won it. For centuries, the achievements of women in mathematics were either omitted from historical records or attributed to male colleagues. Many of their contributions were later credited to male scholars. Such erasure has been a recurring theme in the history of women in this field.

Despite the many obstacles women faced in entering the field of mathematics, Sophie Germain stood out as a great female mathematician. Largely self-taught, she pursued her passion in a time when women were discouraged from academic pursuits. She made significant contributions to number theory and elasticity, and her work on Fermat's Last Theorem was particularly notable. In recognition of her groundbreaking efforts, she became the first woman to win a prize from the Paris Academy of Sciences in 1816 — an award originally proposed back in 1716. This long-standing prize had never before been awarded to a woman, highlighting the importance of Germain's achievements and marking a turning point in the acknowledgment of women in science.

Maria Agnesi, an 18th-century Italian mathematician, was one of the first women to write a comprehensive mathematics textbook. Her work, the Instituzioni Analitiche, was highly praised and became an important reference in the study of calculus. Despite her original contributions, one of the mathematical curves she described — the "Witch of Agnesi" — was mistranslated from Italian, giving it a mystical name that misrepresented her intent. Moreover, over time, credit for aspects of her work was sometimes attributed to male mathematicians who built upon her ideas. This reflects a broader pattern in history where women's intellectual achievements were overlooked or reassigned to men.

Millicent Fawcett demonstrated remarkable intellectual ability from a young age. At just 19, she delivered a public lecture on Sir Isaac Newton at a time when women rarely spoke in academic settings. Although she did not pursue a professional career in mathematics, her early accomplishments in the subject reflected a sharp analytical mind. Over the decades, Fawcett dedicated herself to advocating for women's education and suffrage, tirelessly working to open academic and political doors for future generations. Her lifelong commitment to intellectual and social progress stands as a testament to her exceptional capabilities and enduring influence.

Researchers sometimes talk about a "brilliance effect" in mathematics: fields believed to demand natural brilliance, with figures like Albert Einstein held up as the model of a genius, tend to make women's success look exceptional. When female mathematicians are described as "women geniuses" or "female prodigies", the gender label, while well-intended, often implies that excellence is rare among women. Such terms, though celebratory, can unintentionally reinforce the idea that women's success in mathematics is unusual, rather than simply the result of talent and hard work.

To address the gender imbalance in mathematics, many universities and organizations now run outreach programs, offer scholarships specifically for women, and encourage female mentorship in STEM fields. These efforts aim not to give unfair advantage, but to create equal opportunities in a domain where women have historically been underrepresented.

In efforts to level the playing field, some institutions have implemented standardized criteria for admissions or research evaluation. However, applying one uniform method to every case can be to the detriment of the very people it was designed to help, because it ignores the diverse paths and challenges faced by individuals, particularly women balancing academic and societal expectations. A one-size-fits-all approach may not always foster true equity.

groups.question: Why do people sometimes spend a lot of money on one single thing?

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about buying my first good laptop about a year ago. It cost almost three months of my savings, and I had compared models for weeks before I paid. I asked friends, watched videos, and visited two shops, because I did not want to make a mistake with so much money. At the counter my hands were almost shaking, and on the way home I could not stop smiling. After buying it I felt proud, because it was my own money, but also a little guilty, and I did not tell my parents the real price at first. That feeling passed quickly, because I used the laptop every day for study and work, and it solved a real problem: my old one was so slow that I lost an hour every day waiting. Why do people sometimes spend a lot of money on one single thing? I think quality is the main reason, because one good item can last for years and replace five cheap ones. Sometimes it is also a reward after hard work, or a way to feel successful. And for some people, an expensive thing gives them confidence, like a good suit before an interview. So I believe in buying less, but buying better, as long as you really use it.

extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The purchase I always think of is my camera, bought at the end of last summer after nearly two years of putting money aside. It cost noticeably more than a month's salary, and I remember the small ceremony of it: a hundred questions for the seller, the receipt checked five times, the manual read cover to cover that first night. Afterwards I felt an odd mixture — proud because every dong was mine, briefly guilty at the amount, then calm, because weeks of comparing had left no room for doubt. The guilt disappeared the first weekend I used it properly, when I realised I had stopped scrolling on my phone and started actually looking at things. Why do people pour money into one single thing? Partly quality, since cheap tools quietly cost more over the years through repairs and replacements. Partly status, if we are honest — some purchases are messages to other people about who we are. But mostly, I suspect, we are buying meaning: proof of our own work, a marker of a moment, a small daily joy that a cheaper version would not give. The danger is buying the feeling rather than the object, and then watching it gather dust. Spending big is fine when the use is real and the money is yours — save hard, choose slowly, then buy without regret.

question_text: Why is it important to celebrate small successes?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think celebrating small successes keeps people motivated. Big goals take a long time, so small wins remind us that we are moving forward. Celebrating together also makes a team feel closer, because everyone shares the good feeling. It does not need to be expensive; a coffee or a few kind words is enough. For example, my team claps for anyone who finishes a difficult task. So small celebrations keep energy high until the big goal arrives.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Small celebrations are the fuel that carries people to the big finish line. A long project is mostly invisible progress, so a moment of applause turns effort into something people can actually see. It also builds a habit of noticing each other, which is what separates a team from a group of strangers. The cost is almost nothing, because attention is the real gift. In my office we clap for whoever survives the hardest task of the week, and it works every time. So celebrating small things is not childish, it is how motivation stays alive.

question_text: What makes a good teacher, in your opinion?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: In my opinion, a good teacher explains things clearly and stays patient. Some students learn slowly, so the teacher has to try different ways to explain. A good teacher also makes students feel safe to ask questions and make mistakes. Enthusiasm matters too, because a bored teacher creates a bored class. For example, my English teacher used games and stories, and nobody wanted to miss her lesson. So knowledge is important, but patience and energy make the real difference.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: A good teacher is someone who makes the subject feel possible. Clear explanation is the minimum, but the real skill is finding the second and third way to explain the same idea. Patience matters even more, because most learning happens after a student has already failed once. The best teachers also protect the right to be wrong, so nobody stays silent out of fear. My English teacher taught grammar through stories, and I still remember them fifteen years later. So knowledge fills a lesson, but patience and warmth are what students carry away.

Hi, it's Rob. I'm really sorry, but a client has turned up unexpectedly, so I won't be able to make it to the meeting. • Vì sao đúng: Rob đề nghị "The best thing is to just go ahead and have the meeting without me, and update me afterwards".
• Delaying the meeting sai: chính Rob loại phương án này "Moving it to tomorrow won't work either, because the factory inspection is scheduled for then".
• Canceling the meeting sai: không được nhắc tới trong bài, chỉ là phương án gây nhiễu — Rob chỉ vắng mặt chứ không đề nghị hủy.

question_text: What are the benefits of playing a musical instrument?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Playing a musical instrument has many benefits for both the mind and the mood. It trains patience, because you have to practise the same part again and again. Music is also a good way to relax after a stressful day at work or school. Playing with other people builds confidence and creates new friendships. For example, my cousin joined a school band and became much more confident. So an instrument gives you a skill, a hobby and a way to calm down.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: An instrument gives you three things at once: discipline, a place to put your feelings, and company. Discipline comes first, because progress only arrives after weeks of repeating the same difficult bar. Then the instrument becomes a private room where a bad day can be turned into sound instead of words. Playing with others adds the social layer, and band friendships tend to last because they are built on shared effort. My cousin was painfully shy until a school band handed him a bass guitar. So music is a hobby that quietly rebuilds the person playing it.

question_text: How are these two activities different?
explanation: I think the two activities feel very different, although both are about food. A barbecue is a small outdoor event, with smoke, sunshine and neighbours who might join. The food is simple, and waiting around the grill is half the fun. Baking in the kitchen is slower and more careful, because a cake needs exact amounts. Children who help with baking learn to measure and follow steps. So the barbecue feels like a picnic, while baking feels like a small lesson.

Nobody measures anything, and that is exactly the charm. Baking is the opposite, because a cake punishes every careless gram, so the kitchen becomes a little classroom. The children who were laughing at the barbecue are suddenly concentrating over the scales. So one activity relaxes a family, and the other quietly trains it.

question_text: What are the benefits of doing exercise regularly?

Having said that, people should start slowly, because too much exercise at once causes injuries. So a little movement every day is worth more than one hard session a month.

question_text: Why are practical lessons important when learning science?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Practical lessons are important because science is easier to understand when you can see it. Reading about a reaction is abstract, but watching it happen makes the idea clear. Students also remember experiments much longer than pages from a book. Doing experiments teaches useful habits too, like measuring carefully and recording results. For example, I still remember a chemistry experiment from school, but not the chapter about it. So practical lessons turn theory into something students actually keep.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Science makes sense the moment it stops being words on a page. A reaction described in a textbook is just vocabulary, while the same reaction in front of you becomes a memory with colour and smell. Experiments also teach the quieter half of science: measuring honestly, writing down what happened rather than what you hoped. Failure is part of the lesson too, because a failed experiment forces real thinking. I have forgotten most of my chemistry chapters but not the day our test tube turned bright blue. So practical work is not decoration, it is where understanding actually forms.

question_text: Why do you think cooking with other people is becoming popular?
explanation: I think cooking together is becoming popular because people have less time to meet. Making a meal gives friends a reason to spend two or three hours together. It is also cheaper than going to a restaurant every week. For example, my friends and I have cooked at each other's houses once a month for years. Of course, a small kitchen can get crowded and noisy. Still, I think people enjoy making something with their hands together.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think cooking together is becoming popular because people have less time to meet. Making a meal gives friends a reason to spend two or three hours together. It is also cheaper than going to a restaurant every week. For example, my friends and I have cooked at each other's houses once a month for years. Of course, a small kitchen can get crowded and noisy. Still, I think people enjoy making something with their hands together.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: I think the main reason is that shared cooking solves two problems at once. People are busier than ever, so an activity that combines eating and seeing friends is efficient. It is also considerably cheaper than meeting in restaurants every week. A group of us have cooked at each other's flats once a month for about three years. Having said that, four people in a small kitchen quickly becomes chaotic. Even so, making something with your hands together is oddly satisfying.

question_text: What factors help create a good conversation?
What day should the listeners submit the report?
options: On Tuesday
On Thursday
On Friday
explanation:
Team, end-of-week voice memo — the report deadline, because three people have already asked me! I know the quarterly ones are usually due Fridays; not this time, the directors meet mid-week and need everything beforehand. And whoever wrote Thursday on the whiteboard — close, but still wrong, that's the printing day. Your reports must be submitted on Tuesday. Tuesday, by end of day, in the shared folder AND one printed copy on my desk. Tuesday, people! Now enjoy the weekend — after you start the report!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – On Tuesday (thứ Ba).
• Vì sao đúng: sếp chốt "Your reports must be submitted on Tuesday. Tuesday, by end of day, in the shared folder AND one printed copy on my desk".
• On Thursday sai: đó là ngày in ấn, không phải hạn nộp "whoever wrote Thursday on the whiteboard — close, but still wrong, that's the printing day".
• On Friday sai: là thông lệ mọi quý nhưng lần này khác "I know the quarterly ones are usually due Fridays; not this time".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi HẠN NỘP, cẩn thận ngày gắn với việc khác trong quy trình (ngày in, ngày họp, ngày tư vấn). Chỉ khoanh ngày đi kèm động từ "must be submitted", "is due".

question_text: Why do you think some people find it hard to make decisions?
explanation: I think some people find decisions hard because they are afraid of choosing wrongly. They worry about what will happen if the choice turns out badly. Having too many options also makes it more difficult. For example, I have a friend who spent a month choosing a phone and was still unsure. Some people also care too much about what others will think. In my opinion, it is often better to decide quickly and then adjust.

extra_data.imageDesc: A woman sits at a desk holding a phone to her ear with one hand and a pen in the other, with charts and papers spread in front of her and a computer screen to one side.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I think some people find decisions hard because they are afraid of choosing wrongly. They worry about what will happen if the choice turns out badly. Having too many options also makes it more difficult. For example, I have a friend who spent a month choosing a phone and was still unsure. Some people also care too much about what others will think. In my opinion, it is often better to decide quickly and then adjust.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: I think the main reason is simply fear of choosing wrongly. People imagine the version of their life that they will lose, which no list can measure. Having too many options makes it considerably worse, because every choice rules out ten others. A friend of mine spent a full month comparing phones and was no more certain at the end. There is also the pressure of what other people will say. Personally I think most decisions are easier to correct than we fear.

question_text: Listen to a tour guide talking about a writer. What was the writer's first job?
options: News reporter
Politician
Teacher
explanation:
If you look behind me, you'll see the house of William Roberts. He gave up his job as a news reporter for a local newspaper to start his writing career. At first, his work didn't attract much attention, and he even thought about going back to his earlier teaching job. But then his book about a politician became a best-seller, and he became famous around the world.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – News reporter (phóng viên báo).
• Vì sao đúng: hướng dẫn viên nói "He gave up his job as a news reporter for a local newspaper to start his writing career" — đây là công việc bài nêu ra làm điểm xuất phát trước khi ông theo nghiệp viết văn.
• Teacher sai: nghề dạy học chỉ được nhắc thoáng qua như một lối lui khi sự nghiệp viết chưa khởi sắc "he even thought about going back to his earlier teaching job", không phải nghề bài giới thiệu là khởi đầu.
• Politician sai: chính trị gia chỉ là NHÂN VẬT trong cuốn sách của ông "his book about a politician became a best-seller", không phải nghề của ông.
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi NGHỀ ĐẦU TIÊN, đừng chọn danh từ chỉ nghề nghe được cuối cùng — nhiều danh từ trong bài chỉ là chủ đề tác phẩm. Bám cấu trúc "He gave up his job as + nghề + to start...".

question_text: What will the student write about?
options: water
bikes
land
explanation:
Good evening, Professor, this is Milo from the environmental studies group, leaving the message you asked for — my project topic decision! I went back and forth all weekend. The cycling infrastructure idea — the bikes — felt exciting, but honestly, three classmates already took it. And the water quality study needs lab access I won't get until next term. So my final choice: I will write about the land. Land use around the town — how the farms became car parks in thirty years, with my grandfather's old field maps as sources. Hope that's approved! Thank you!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – land (đất đai/quy hoạch sử dụng đất).
• Vì sao đúng: Milo chốt "So my final choice: I will write about the land. Land use around the town — how the farms became car parks in thirty years".
• bikes sai: bị loại vì trùng đề tài "The cycling infrastructure idea — the bikes — felt exciting, but honestly, three classmates already took it".
• water sai: thiếu điều kiện làm "the water quality study needs lab access I won't get until next term".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi CHỌN ĐỀ TÀI, sinh viên luôn kể đủ 3 ý tưởng. Chỉ lấy ý sau "So my final choice is..." và loại ý bị chặn bởi "already taken", "needs... I won't get".

question_text: A student is calling his parents. How is he feeling?
options: Well
Warm
Sick
explanation:
Hi Mum and Dad, I left the university half an hour ago. My friend is driving me to the bus stop, but I'm afraid we won't make it, because the bus is moving faster than we are. And the next one isn't until 6.45. Could you come and pick me up? I hear it's really cold outside, and I'm not feeling very well.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – Sick (không khỏe).
• Vì sao đúng: cậu sinh viên nói cuối lời nhắn "I'm not feeling very well" — tức là đang mệt/ốm, nên mới nhờ bố mẹ ra đón.
• Well sai: từ "well" CÓ xuất hiện nhưng nằm trong câu phủ định "I'm NOT feeling very well".
• Warm sai: bài chỉ nói thời tiết bên ngoài lạnh "I hear it's really cold outside" — đó là nhiệt độ ngoài trời, không phải cảm giác của cậu.
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi CẢM THẤY THẾ NÀO, bẫy kinh điển là đặt đúng từ trong phương án vào một câu phủ định. Nghe trọn cụm "not feeling well" thay vì bắt mỗi chữ "well".

question_text: What bus number should the girl take?
options: ten
eight
nine
explanation:
Sweetheart, it's Grandma — your first trip to the swimming pool alone, so let's get the bus right! Now pay attention. The number ten stops near our street, yes, but it turns toward the industrial park — you'd end up among the warehouses, like your uncle did. The nine only runs on schooldays, and today's a holiday, so forget the nine completely. You need the number eight! The eight goes straight past the pool — ask the driver for the sports centre stop. Bus eight, sweetheart. Text Grandma when you arrive!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – eight (xe buýt số 8).
• Vì sao đúng: bà nói "You need the number eight! The eight goes straight past the pool — ask the driver for the sports centre stop".
• ten sai: dừng gần nhà nhưng đi sai hướng "it turns toward the industrial park — you'd end up among the warehouses".
• nine sai: hôm nay là ngày lễ nên không chạy "The nine only runs on schooldays, and today's a holiday, so forget the nine completely".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi ĐI XE BUÝT SỐ MẤY, mỗi số sai đều kèm một điều kiện chặn (sai hướng, không chạy hôm nay). Chọn số đi kèm "You need..." và có đích đến khớp với nơi cần tới.
