question_text: What time does the store open?
explanation:
Thank you for calling Fashion Corner — this is a recorded message with our opening hours, updated this week! Please note the changes carefully. Our old opening time of nine am ended last month — the staff now do restocking in that first half hour. And no, we do NOT open at half past ten — that rumour comes from the sale day queue confusion, we apologise again. The store opens at nine thirty. Nine thirty, Monday to Saturday, until eight in the evening. Sundays we rest — even mannequins need a day off! See you soon!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – At 9:30.
• Vì sao đúng: tin nhắn tự động nói "The store opens at nine thirty. Nine thirty, Monday to Saturday, until eight in the evening".
• At 9:00 sai: là giờ mở cửa cũ đã bỏ "Our old opening time of nine am ended last month — the staff now do restocking in that first half hour".
• At 10:30 sai: chỉ là tin đồn "we do NOT open at half past ten — that rumour comes from the sale day queue confusion".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi GIỜ MỞ CỬA, bài luôn cảnh báo "please note the changes". Bám cụm hiện tại "The store opens at..." và loại giờ đi kèm "old", "used to", "that rumour".

question_text: A mother is talking to her son. What subject does her son like studying?
options: Art
Science
Maths
explanation:
You really have to study harder, young man. Your teacher just called to tell me about your grades. Your marks in science and maths are very low. Anyway, he said you have a real talent for painting. I know you love drawing, but you still have to do well in all your subjects.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – Art (môn Mỹ thuật).
• Vì sao đúng: người mẹ nói "he said you have a real talent for painting. I know you love drawing" — vẽ chính là môn Art.
• Science sai: đó là môn cậu bị điểm kém "Your marks in science and maths are very low".
• Maths sai: cũng nằm trong nhóm điểm thấp cùng câu trên.
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi THÍCH MÔN NÀO, phương án đúng có thể không được gọi đúng tên môn mà mô tả bằng hoạt động (painting, drawing = Art). Đừng chỉ săn tên môn — nghe cả động từ chỉ sở thích "love", "talent for".

question_text: Listen to a man calling his friend. Why is he calling?
options: To suggest meeting for a drink
To say hello after a trip
To ask for directions
explanation:
Hey, I just heard you were in town last week. I had no idea, so I couldn't arrange to see you. Listen, I've heard there's a fantastic tea house here and the tea is really good. Next time you come, give me a call and we can meet up for some drinks.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – To suggest meeting for a drink (để rủ đi uống nước lần tới).
• Vì sao đúng: anh chốt lời nhắn bằng đúng đề nghị "Next time you come, give me a call and we can meet up for some drinks", kèm gợi ý địa điểm "there's a fantastic tea house here and the tea is really good".
• To say hello after a trip sai: anh có nhắc chuyện bạn ghé thành phố tuần trước nhưng chỉ để tiếc nuối "I had no idea, so I couldn't arrange to see you" — đó là phần dẫn, không phải mục đích.
• To ask for directions sai: không được nhắc tới trong bài, chỉ là phương án gây nhiễu.
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi GỌI ĐỂ LÀM GÌ, mục đích thật thường nằm ở CÂU CUỐI của lời nhắn, sau từ dẫn "Listen,...". Phần đầu chỉ là lời chào/bối cảnh.

question_text: Where is Gordon from?
options: Germany
France
England
explanation:
Let me introduce our new colleague Gordon properly, because the office rumour machine has him from three different countries already! Yes, he orders croissants every morning — that's just good taste, he is NOT French, stop telling clients that. And the surname sounds German, I agree, but that's his grandfather's side, four generations back. Gordon himself is from England — born in Manchester, raised in York, supports a football team he made us all promise never to mock. So: English, loves rain, hates our coffee. Make him welcome!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – England (nước Anh).
• Vì sao đúng: người nói khẳng định "Gordon himself is from England — born in Manchester, raised in York" và tổng kết "So: English, loves rain, hates our coffee".
• France sai: chỉ vì anh hay ăn bánh sừng bò "he orders croissants every morning — that's just good taste, he is NOT French".
• Germany sai: chỉ là gốc gác họ từ đời cụ "the surname sounds German, I agree, but that's his grandfather's side, four generations back".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi ĐẾN TỪ ĐÂU, hai quốc tịch nhiễu thường dựa vào thói quen ăn uống hoặc họ tên. Chỉ tin câu có "is from" kèm nơi sinh/nơi lớn lên cụ thể.

question_text: What time does the party start?
options: 3 o'clock
4 o'clock
5 o'clock
explanation:
Attention all cousins, aunties and honorary uncles — this is your party information hotline, also known as me! Grandpa's eightieth, this Saturday, final details. The invitation cards printed five o'clock — IGNORE them, that was before the hall double-booking drama. And the family chat voted for four, but the caterers laughed at us — the food simply can't be ready. So, carved in stone now: the party starts at three o'clock. Three pm sharp, surprise moment at quarter past, so do NOT be the person walking in behind Grandpa. Three o'clock! Bring tissues — Mum will cry!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – 3 o'clock (3 giờ chiều).
• Vì sao đúng: người thông báo nói "carved in stone now: the party starts at three o'clock. Three pm sharp, surprise moment at quarter past".
• 5 o'clock sai: là giờ in trên thiệp mời đã lỗi thời "The invitation cards printed five o'clock — IGNORE them, that was before the hall double-booking drama".
• 4 o'clock sai: là kết quả bình chọn trong nhóm chat nhưng bên phục vụ không kịp "the family chat voted for four, but the caterers laughed at us — the food simply can't be ready".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi TIỆC BẮT ĐẦU MẤY GIỜ, cảnh giác giờ in trên thiệp và giờ do nhóm tự bàn. Đáp án đi kèm cụm chốt "carved in stone", "final", "sharp".

question_text: A girl is calling her friend Emma. What did the girl lose?
options: A book
A phone
Paper
explanation:
Thanks, Emma. I'm almost ready for the presentation this afternoon. But there's one thing I need to ask you. I think I left my phone at your house. Could you check for me? I really hope I didn't drop it while I was walking to the car. Thank you so much.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – A phone (điện thoại).
• Vì sao đúng: cô gái nói "I think I left my phone at your house. Could you check for me?" và lo thêm "I really hope I didn't drop it while I was walking to the car".
• A book sai: không được nhắc tới trong bài, chỉ là phương án gây nhiễu.
• Paper sai: cũng không được nhắc tới trong bài, chỉ là phương án gây nhiễu.
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi ĐỂ QUÊN ĐỒ GÌ, bài rất ngắn nên đồ vật chỉ xuất hiện đúng một lần sau "I left my...". Nghe tập trung ngay khi có cụm "there's one thing I need to ask you" — thông tin quan trọng đến ngay sau đó.

question_text: Where is the entrance to the shopping center?
options: In front of the pharmacy
Near the station
Next to the cafe
explanation:
Welcome to the city information line — you asked about the new shopping centre entrance, an excellent question, since the building confuses everyone! The glass doors in front of the pharmacy look like an entrance, but they are actually the fire exit — pushing them triggers a very embarrassing alarm, ask anyone. The doors next to the café are for deliveries only, vans and crates all day. The real entrance is near the station — follow the covered walkway from platform one, and the big revolving doors are the way in. Near the station! Happy shopping!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – Near the station (gần nhà ga).
• Vì sao đúng: tổng đài nói "The real entrance is near the station — follow the covered walkway from platform one, and the big revolving doors are the way in".
• In front of the pharmacy sai: cửa kính đó là lối thoát hiểm "they are actually the fire exit — pushing them triggers a very embarrassing alarm".
• Next to the cafe sai: là cửa dành cho giao hàng "The doors next to the café are for deliveries only, vans and crates all day".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi LỐI VÀO Ở ĐÂU, bài gán cho mỗi vị trí một chức năng khác (fire exit, delivery). Nghe từ khóa "the real entrance", "the way in" rồi mới lấy vị trí đi kèm.

question_text: Stephanie is calling about a childcare job. How old is Stephanie?
explanation:
Hello, I saw the advertisement you posted online looking for someone to look after your children at weekends. I'm an English student, I'm 21 years old, and I speak good English. What's more, I really love children.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – 21 tuổi.
• Vì sao đúng: Stephanie tự giới thiệu "I'm an English student, I'm 21 years old, and I speak good English".
• 23 sai: không được nhắc tới trong bài, chỉ là phương án gây nhiễu.
• 19 sai: cũng không được nhắc tới trong bài, chỉ là phương án gây nhiễu.
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi BAO NHIÊU TUỔI trong bài giới thiệu bản thân, tuổi luôn nằm trong chuỗi thông tin cá nhân đọc liền mạch (nghề/ngành – tuổi – kỹ năng). Chuẩn bị sẵn bút, con số chỉ đọc một lần và không lặp lại.

question_text: What does the woman need?
options: A photo
A student card
An application form
explanation:
M: Good morning! Library services — you're here for the new membership?
W: Yes, finally! I brought everything your website listed... I hope.
M: Let's check together. Application form?
W: Filled in, printed, both pages — here you go.
M: Perfect. And you're a student, so... your student card?
W: Right here — it even survived the washing machine, as you can see.
M: Ha! Still readable, that's all we need. Now, the last item...
W: Don't say it. The thing I forgot?
M: I'm afraid so — a photo. Passport-sized, for the membership card. That's the one thing you still need.
W: I KNEW something was missing! Is there a photo booth nearby?
M: In the hall by the lifts, four pounds. I'll keep your forms right here — you'll be a member in ten minutes!
W: Running now. Don't give my membership away!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – A photo (một tấm ảnh thẻ).
• Vì sao đúng: nhân viên thư viện nói "a photo. Passport-sized, for the membership card. That's the one thing you still need" và chỉ chỗ chụp ngay trong sảnh.
• An application form sai: cô đã nộp rồi "Filled in, printed, both pages — here you go".
• A student card sai: cũng đã có "Right here — it even survived the washing machine".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi CÒN THIẾU GÌ, bài điểm danh từng giấy tờ theo checklist. Các món đã có đi kèm "here you go", "right here"; đáp án nằm ở món cuối cùng với cụm "the one thing you still need".

question_text: A woman is talking to her husband about a family trip. The woman's family decided to...
options: go camping
go cycling
see friends
explanation:
Honey, the kids are getting older now. We should go somewhere different this year. They want to spend time with their friends too. We go camping every single year. What do you think about going cycling this year instead? I think that's what we should do.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – go cycling (đi đạp xe).
• Vì sao đúng: người vợ đề xuất "What do you think about going cycling this year instead? I think that's what we should do".
• go camping sai: đó là hoạt động lặp lại mọi năm mà cô muốn đổi "We go camping every single year".
• see friends sai: chỉ là mong muốn của bọn trẻ, không phải kế hoạch chuyến đi "They want to spend time with their friends too".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi NĂM NAY QUYẾT ĐỊNH LÀM GÌ, chú ý từ "instead" và "this year" — chúng đánh dấu lựa chọn mới. Hoạt động đi kèm "every year", "as usual" luôn là cái bị thay thế.

question_text: Why does the man choose the jacket?
options: It's cheap
He likes the colour
It keeps him warm
explanation:
W: That's the third time you've circled back to that jacket. Verdict?
M: I'm deciding scientifically! Long winter, cold office.
W: The colour is very you — that forest green.
M: The colour's fine, but I already own two green jackets, as you remind me every winter. Colour is not the argument.
W: The price, then? Look at the tag — seventy per cent off.
M: It is a good price, but I'd never buy a coat just because it's cheap. Price isn't it either.
W: So what's left, professor?
M: The lining. Feel that — my old jacket lets the wind straight through, and I cycle to work at six every morning. This one will actually keep me warm all winter. That's the whole point.
W: Warmth wins, then.
M: Warmth wins. To the till!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – It keeps him warm (vì giữ ấm).
• Vì sao đúng: anh chốt "my old jacket lets the wind straight through, and I cycle to work at six every morning. This one will actually keep me warm all winter. That's the whole point" — lý do duy nhất anh giữ lại.
• He likes the colour sai: chính anh loại "The colour's fine, but I already own two green jackets... Colour is not the argument".
• It's cheap sai: giá rẻ được nhắc rõ (giảm 70%) nhưng anh gạt đi "I'd never buy a coat just because it's cheap. Price isn't it either".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi VÌ SAO CHỌN, người nói tự loại từng lý do bằng "X is not the argument", "X isn't it either". Đừng chọn cái được nói TO nhất (giảm 70%) — hãy chọn cái duy nhất KHÔNG bị phủ định.

question_text: A woman is doing a survey with a man. The man thinks that train travel is...
options: economical
practical
boring
explanation:
Woman: Hello, could I take a few minutes of your time for a short survey?
Man: Sure, go ahead.
Woman: How frequently do you travel by train?
Man: Every day, to work and back.
Woman: And how do you feel about travelling by train?
Man: Well, first there's the convenience. There are train stations almost everywhere in the city now, so you can catch a train from anywhere. And more importantly, taking the train saves a lot of money compared to flying.
Woman: And how do you avoid boredom on the train?
Man: I usually bring a book to read, but if there's someone to chat with on the train, that's even better.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án A – economical (tiết kiệm tiền).
• Vì sao đúng: người đàn ông nhấn mạnh ý quan trọng nhất "and more importantly, taking the train saves a lot of money compared to flying" — tức là đi tàu rẻ, kinh tế.
• practical sai: sự tiện lợi có được nhắc nhưng chỉ là ý phụ đứng trước "first there's the convenience. There are train stations almost everywhere" — và người nói tự xếp nó dưới ý về tiền.
• boring sai: ngược lại, anh còn kể cách để không chán "I usually bring a book to read, but if there's someone to chat with on the train, that's even better".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi Ý KIẾN/ĐÁNH GIÁ trong khảo sát, khi bài nêu nhiều ưu điểm hãy bám từ so sánh mức độ "more importantly", "above all", "the main thing" để chọn ý được nhấn mạnh nhất.

question_text: Jorge is calling his friend about the weekend. What time does the game start?

3 p.m.
1 p.m.
explanation:
Hi Jane, it's Jorge here. I'm so busy this week. On Sunday I'm going to watch a football game, which starts at 1 p.m. I think we can meet at 6 p.m. Would you like to see a film? There's a new one that's just come out at the cinema. Call me back.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – 1 p.m.
• Vì sao đúng: Jorge nói "a football game, which starts at 1 p.m.". 6 p.m. là giờ hẹn gặp bạn sau trận, không phải giờ trận đấu.

question_text: What does the man like about his new workplace?
options: It's a quiet place
He travels a shorter distance
It's less stressful
explanation:
W: Two months at the new company! Honest review — was the change worth it?
M: Completely. Though not for the reasons people guess.
W: Everyone says the new office park is so peaceful — all those trees?
M: Quiet, yes, until the construction crew arrived next door in week two. Drills from nine to five — so much for the peace!
W: Oh no! The stress levels, then? You always said the old place was a pressure cooker.
M: Truthfully, the deadlines here are just as brutal — same industry, same madness. That's not it either.
W: So what's the win?
M: The distance! I travel fifteen minutes now instead of an hour and a quarter. I get two extra hours of LIFE every single day — breakfast with the kids, the gym, actual dinners.
W: Two hours a day... that's a part-time life you got back!
M: Exactly. Shortest commute wins, every time. Best decision I've made in years.

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – He travels a shorter distance (quãng đường đi làm ngắn hơn).
• Vì sao đúng: anh nói "The distance! I travel fifteen minutes now instead of an hour and a quarter. I get two extra hours of LIFE every single day" và kết luận "Shortest commute wins, every time".
• It's a quiet place sai: sự yên tĩnh đã bị phá "Quiet, yes, until the construction crew arrived next door in week two. Drills from nine to five".
• It's less stressful sai: áp lực y hệt chỗ cũ "the deadlines here are just as brutal — same industry, same madness. That's not it either".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi THÍCH ĐIỀU GÌ Ở CHỖ LÀM MỚI, người hỏi nêu hai điều "ai cũng nghĩ" và đều bị bác. Đáp án đi kèm con số so sánh cụ thể (15 phút so với 1 tiếng 15).

question_text: Anna is calling her brother. What is Anna going to do?
options: Fix the computer
Pick up her kid
Stay late at work
explanation:
Woman: Hello? I need your help with something.
Man: What is it?
Woman: I've got so much work at the office today that I'll probably have to stay late. Could you pick up my daughter from school for me?
Man: Sure, I'm free anyway, so I'll play with her too. Do you want me to cook dinner as well?
Woman: That would be perfect. Thank you!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án C – Stay late at work (ở lại làm muộn).
• Vì sao đúng: Anna nói "I've got so much work at the office today that I'll probably have to stay late" — đó chính là việc CÔ sẽ làm.
• Pick up her kid sai: đó là việc cô NHỜ em trai làm hộ "Could you pick up my daughter from school for me?".
• Fix the computer sai: không được nhắc tới trong bài, chỉ là phương án gây nhiễu.
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi NGƯỜI X SẼ LÀM GÌ trong hội thoại nhờ vả, phải tách rõ việc của người nhờ và việc của người được nhờ. Câu "Could you..." luôn là việc của NGƯỜI KIA, không phải đáp án.

question_text: Where are they going to meet?
options: at the station
at the park
at the university
explanation:
M: Right, tomorrow's picnic with the study group — where do we all gather first?
W: Someone suggested the station, since half the group comes by train.
M: They did, but the station square is dug up this month — fences, mud, machines everywhere. Terrible meeting point.
W: True. The university steps then? Central, everyone knows them.
M: Locked on Sundays, remember? Whole campus is closed — we'd be sitting on the fence like pigeons.
W: Ha! So that leaves the obvious one...
M: The park! The main gate by the flower clock — five minutes from the station AND from the bus stops.
W: The park it is. Eleven o'clock, flower clock, blankets and snacks.
M: I'll message the group. Last one there carries the water bottles!

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – at the park (ở công viên).
• Vì sao đúng: hai người chốt "The park! The main gate by the flower clock — five minutes from the station AND from the bus stops" và "Eleven o'clock, flower clock, blankets and snacks".
• at the station sai: quảng trường nhà ga đang thi công "the station square is dug up this month — fences, mud, machines everywhere".
• at the university sai: khuôn viên đóng cửa Chủ nhật "Locked on Sundays, remember? Whole campus is closed".
👉 Mẹo: dạng hỏi HẸN GẶP Ở ĐÂU, hai địa điểm đầu bị loại vì lý do thực tế (thi công, đóng cửa). Đáp án luôn kèm mốc nhận diện nhỏ (cổng chính, đồng hồ hoa) và giờ hẹn.

The first captures a city at full speed: a dense crowd of commuters strides across a wide crossing, dressed for the office in coats and suits, weighed down with backpacks, handbags and coffee cups. Several walk with earphones in, eyes fixed on their phones, and low sunlight throws long shadows between the glass towers while traffic waits behind them. The second photograph empties the frame almost completely. A single hiker sits on a grassy mountainside, rucksack and metal flask beside him, gazing out over pine trees at a wide valley and a range of green peaks under a clear sky. One image is noise, movement and other people; the other is silence, stillness and space — and most of us seem to need a little of each.

question_text: Mountain (Version 5)
options: A disturbing revelation
Our changing perspective towards mountains
A more intimate relationship
The wrong priority
Publicising one's achievements
A unique sense of achievement
A focus on sustainability
explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. Chọn "Our changing perspective towards mountains" vì đoạn văn so sánh xưa – nay: người ta từng nghĩ leo núi là thú chơi hẹp, nhưng có bằng chứng leo núi đã là môn thể thao nghiêm túc từ lâu; điều KHÁC biệt bây giờ là định nghĩa "chinh phục" = đứng trên đỉnh, tự mình nhìn xuống thay vì nhờ ảnh và lời kể của người khác.
2. Chọn "A unique sense of achievement" vì đoạn văn nói về cảm giác thành tựu sâu sắc (profound sense of accomplishment): hình dáng núi tượng trưng cho chinh phục, vượt nỗi sợ, đẩy giới hạn, cộng thêm adrenaline khiến người leo quay lại mãi.
3. Chọn "Publicising one's achievements" vì đoạn văn nói selfie trên đỉnh gần như bắt buộc — bằng chứng và cách để mọi người biết; sự thoả mãn riêng tư giờ được đăng, gắn giờ, chia sẻ (posted, timestamped and shared).
4. Chọn "The wrong priority" vì đoạn văn chỉ ra người leo tập trung vào bức ảnh hơn ngọn núi, coi hành trình chỉ là chướng ngại, bỏ qua cảnh báo → tai nạn; "personal image ends up mattering more than safety or responsibility" = đặt sai ưu tiên.
5. Chọn "A disturbing revelation" vì đoạn văn mở bằng kỳ vọng Everest vắng vẻ rồi lật lại "The reality is startling": ảnh "traffic jam" trên death zone, rác mỗi mùa, thử thách cá nhân thành cuộc đua thương mại. Bẫy: đoạn 4 cũng nói tai nạn nhưng không "hé lộ" sự thật gây sốc.
6. Chọn "A focus on sustainability" vì đoạn văn nói về cách vận hành expedition đổi theo hướng bảo vệ môi trường: giới hạn permit, đặt cọc trả lại khi mang rác xuống, clean-up climbs, "a mountain should be left cleaner than it was found".
7. Chọn "A more intimate relationship" vì đoạn văn kể Nan Shepherd đi "into the hills rather than up them", biết núi như biết một người bạn — "one visits a friend with no intention but to be with him".
👉 Mẹo: đọc câu đầu + câu cuối mỗi đoạn; các cặp dễ nhầm là đoạn 3/4 (đăng ảnh vs ưu tiên sai) và đoạn 4/5 (tai nạn vs sự thật gây sốc ở Everest).

extra_data.title: Mountain (Version 5)

paragraphs.text: It's often thought that mountaineering has never attracted much serious attention - a niche pursuit that only became popular once modern equipment made the peaks accessible. There is clear evidence, however, that people were treating climbing as a demanding sport long before the era of social media. What is different in modern times is that many people now define conquering a mountain as standing on its summit - the particular thrill of being on top of the very thing you have just overcome, with the whole landscape spread out below, rather than relying on the photographs and accounts that other climbers have provided.

Climbing a mountain often leads to a profound sense of accomplishment. Because of their very shape, rising steeply to a single point, mountains stand for conquest and struggle, and reaching the top of one carries that meaning with it. But there is more to it than that: it represents not just reaching a physical summit but also conquering personal fears and pushing one's limits, creating memories that last a lifetime. There is also the adrenaline rush that comes with it - the same surge of excitement that draws people to other adventure sports, and one reason why so many climbers return to the mountains long after they have proved whatever they set out to prove.

Reaching the summit is no longer enough on its own. Taking a selfie at the top has become almost obligatory - the proof that the climb actually happened, and the means by which everyone else gets to hear about it. What was once a private satisfaction is now something to be posted, timestamped and shared within hours of the descent. This turns personal milestones into public spectacles that can inspire others, though it also raises awkward questions about authenticity: whether the climb was made for its own sake, or for the picture at the end of it.

In recent years, some climbers have become more focused on the photograph than on the mountain itself. Only the summit seems to count, as if there were nothing beautiful about the journey up, as if the hours of effort and the shifting landscape were merely an obstacle between the climber and the picture. Warnings go unheeded because nobody wants to turn back empty-handed, and in some cases this obsession with online fame has led to serious accidents. Reaching a major peak now also demands complicated organisation - permits, guides, bottled oxygen, a support team booked months in advance - and all of this can detract from the enjoyment of the climb. Personal image ends up mattering more than safety or responsibility.

You might expect the world's highest mountain to be an empty place - so hostile, so far beyond ordinary human endurance that hardly anyone would set foot there. The reality is startling. Photographs from recent seasons show a "traffic jam" of climbers on Everest, queuing along a single fixed rope in the death zone, waiting hours for their turn at the top. When a weather window opens, the ascent effectively becomes a race between them, the other climbers and the weather itself. Meanwhile the slopes carry the waste of every season, and what was once a personal challenge has become a commercial race measured in photographs and fame rather than respect for the mountain.

The pressure on high-altitude environments has forced a change in how expeditions are run. Authorities in several climbing regions now issue only a limited number of permits each season, and operators are required to lodge a deposit that is returned only once they bring their rubbish back down with them. Some teams organise clean-up climbs, whose purpose is not the summit at all but the removal of equipment and waste abandoned by earlier parties. Behind these measures lies a shift in what counts as a successful trip: protecting the slopes now matters as much as standing on top of them, and a mountain should be left cleaner than it was found.

For most people a mountain is something to be conquered - a summit to be reached, a target to be ticked off. The Scottish writer Nan Shepherd saw it differently. She grew up within sight of the Cairngorms and spent a lifetime walking the same range, setting down what she found there in The Living Mountain. She went into the hills rather than up them, returning to the same corries and burns until she knew them the way one comes to know a person rather than a place: to be with the mountain as “one visits a friend with no intention but to be with him”.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about a time I helped my neighbour. It was about two years ago, in the summer. My neighbour is an old man who lives alone, and one evening he fell ill and could not stand up. So I took him to the hospital on my motorbike and waited with him for three hours. The doctor said it was his heart, and he had to stay for two days. I also cooked for him for a few days after he came home. In the end, he recovered, and we became good friends. At that moment I felt really happy that I could do something useful. These days I still visit him every weekend. How did I feel about helping him? Honestly, I felt wonderful. This is mainly because I could see that my help really changed something for him. His smile when he came home told me it mattered. For example, I was smiling for the rest of that day. On the other hand, it took a lot of my time, and I was nervous at first because I did not know what to do. I think we should help other people because everyone needs help sometimes. When we help others, they help us later, and small acts of kindness can change someone's whole day. One reason is that many problems are easy for one person and impossible for another. My neighbour could not get to the hospital alone, but for me it was only thirty minutes. So I think everyone should help when they can, because a little kindness costs nothing but means a lot.

My neighbour could not get to the hospital alone, but for me it was only thirty minutes. So I think everyone should help when they can, because a little kindness costs nothing but means a lot.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Let me tell you about the time I helped my elderly neighbour, about two years ago in the middle of summer. He is a widower who lives alone across the corridor, and one evening I heard him call out; he had collapsed and could not get up. I took him to the hospital on my motorbike, waited three hours while they examined him, and learned it was his heart. He stayed two days, and for a week afterwards I cooked for him and picked up his medicine. He recovered fully, and the strange result is that we became genuine friends: I still drop in every weekend. As for how I felt, honestly, wonderful — though it was not a simple feeling. I was proud that I had not panicked, relieved that I had not simply gone back to bed, and moved by how sincerely he thanked me. Helping him also made my own worries look small for a while. On the other hand, it swallowed a lot of my time, and at first I was frightened of making things worse, because I had no idea what to do with a sick man. Why should we help other people? Partly because everyone needs help at some point, and kindness tends to come back to us. Partly because many problems are trivial for one person and impossible for another: a thirty-minute ride was nothing for me and everything for him. And partly because helping others gives our own lives a sense of meaning that very little else provides. So we should never simply walk past someone in trouble — a little kindness costs nothing but means a great deal.

question_text: What does she say about working at home?
options: There are no distractions
Not good as expected
Video calls are superior to face-to-face conversation
explanation:
Before I began working from home, I imagined paradise: no commute, no meetings that could have been emails, and above all, silence. I truly believed there would be no distractions once the chatting colleagues were gone. Reality re-educated me within a week. The distractions did not disappear; they changed uniform. The washing machine calls, the doorbell rings, the fridge whispers, and family members assume that being home means being available. As for video calls — useful, yes, but let nobody tell you they beat face-to-face conversation. Explaining a complicated problem through a frozen screen and a delayed microphone cured me of that idea permanently. So when friends ask for my honest verdict after a full year, I give them three words: not as expected. There are real advantages, but the dream and the reality live at different addresses.
Let me pass on what I have actually learned. First, forget the magazine photos — you do not need a big home office. My best work happens at a small desk in the corner of the bedroom. Second, do not believe anyone who says this lifestyle requires no self-motivation; with nobody watching, discipline is the entire game. And the biggest lesson: there is no universal answer. How well working from home goes depends on your situation and your personality. My neighbour thrives alone; I miss the noise of other humans. Learn which kind of worker you are — preferably before you sign anything.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
(Bản variant của Đề 02 bài 2.)
1. Đáp án: Not good as expected. Bẫy: "no distractions" ("changed uniform") và "video calls superior" ("cured me of that idea").
2. Đáp án: It depends on your situation and personality. Bẫy: "big home office" và "no self-motivation" đều bị phủ định.

I went there with my family two years ago and we stayed one night on a boat. It is famous because it is very beautiful and it is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The place most people know is Ha Long Bay, a few hours east of Hanoi, where thousands of limestone islands rise straight out of the sea. It is a UNESCO site, which explains the crowds, but seeing it from a small boat at sunrise still feels worth every tourist queue. I went with my parents two summers ago and my father, who dislikes travelling, has talked about it ever since.

He stands in the centre, silver-haired and wearing sunglasses, a pink shirt open over a white T-shirt and blue jeans, and the photographer has caught him just as he kicks a white football forward with his right foot. On the left, a boy in a yellow T-shirt and denim shorts stands with his feet apart, watching the ball closely. On the right, a girl with long dark hair, dressed in a denim jacket and green shorts, is also standing still and following the game. Behind them a thick wall of leafy trees closes off the garden, and warm sunlight spills across the grass. It has the feel of a relaxed weekend afternoon, with the grandfather showing the children that he still has some skills.

question_text: Laila is calling her mum. How much is the bus ticket?
options: Two pounds fifteen
Two pounds fifty
Five pounds
explanation:
Hi Mum, it's Laila. Can you lend me some money until Saturday? I'm going into town to buy my textbooks. I checked the price of the book already and I can pay for that on my card, but I don't have any cash for the bus. The ticket is two pounds fifty each way. I'll give it back on Saturday, I promise. What time will you be home?

--- GIẢI THÍCH: Đáp án B – Two pounds fifty.
• Vì sao đúng: "The ticket is two pounds fifty each way".
• Two pounds fifteen sai: bẫy âm fifty/fifteen — nghe trọng âm: FIF-ty (nhấn đầu) vs fif-TEEN (nhấn cuối).
• Five pounds sai: không được nhắc trong bài.
👉 Mẹo: số tiền có "-ty" và "-teen" luôn là bẫy phát âm, nghe kỹ âm cuối và trọng âm.

question_text: Write a short email (about 50 words) to your friend, and a longer email (120-150 words) to the manager of the club.
explanation:
Hi Lan,
Our social club is planning new activities for both young and old members, and they are asking whether events should be indoors or outdoors. I think we should combine the two, so everyone can join. I'm going to write to the manager tonight — want to come to the first event with me?
Best,
Phuong

Dear Manager,
Thank you for asking members about the new programme of activities. I am really pleased that the club wants to bring young and old people together, and I think this is a great chance to make the club more lively.
In my opinion, we should combine indoor and outdoor events rather than choosing only one. Outdoor activities such as walking in the park, picnics or a small sports day are perfect for younger members and for sunny weekends. However, older members may prefer indoor events such as board game evenings, cooking classes or talks, especially in cold or rainy weather.
I would suggest holding one outdoor and one indoor event each month, and choosing activities that need no special skills so that everyone can take part. I would be happy to help organise the first picnic.
Yours sincerely,
Phuong

question_text: What will this musician do in the near future?
options: He will probably retire from singing professionally
He plans to record another album with the Bats
He wants to go on another world tour
explanation:
At a press conference earlier this week, the musician launched his new album — and then surprised everyone in the room. He announced that this will be the last album of his career with the Bats, because he is leaving the band, and he added that he has no plans to sing professionally again. Now, his fans are hoping that this is just like last time. You may remember that a few years ago he walked out in the middle of a world tour, only to return to the stage a few months later. This time, however, he sounded very sure. There will be no new record with the band, and no more touring: he will probably retire from singing altogether.
Looking back, his story is remarkable. He recruited three amateur musicians to form the Bats, and the group was hitting the charts within a year of their first show. Fame came quickly after that. So what stopped him from becoming one of the greatest artists of all time? It wasn't the tour he abandoned, and it wasn't his songs, which fans always loved. The real reason is that he got married and had children, and he chose to spend most of his time with his family rather than in the studio. When he did return to the stage, the fans were excited, but he never made the same impact as before. Even so, we all hope that one day he will surprise us again and come back.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Đáp án: He will probably retire from singing professionally — "he has no plans to sing professionally again... he will probably retire from singing altogether". Bẫy: "another album" bị phủ định ("There will be no new record with the band"); "world tour" là chuyện QUÁ KHỨ và "no more touring".
2. Đáp án: He spent a lot of time with his family — câu hỏi "what does the speaker suggest" = người nói ngụ ý lý do gì; MC nói "he got married and had children, and he chose to spend most of his time with his family rather than in the studio". Bẫy: bỏ tour và bài hát đều bị loại trực tiếp — "It wasn't the tour he abandoned, and it wasn't his songs, which fans always loved".
👉 Mẹo: Part 4 hay dùng cấu trúc "It wasn't X, and it wasn't Y. The real reason is Z" — đáp án là Z.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show people doing exercise, but in different ways. In the first one, a young man in a light blue T-shirt and white shorts is doing yoga alone on a wooden terrace outside a dark wooden house. He is balancing his whole body on one hand and one foot, with his arms stretched out like wings, and he looks extremely concentrated. There are green plants and a striped mat around him. The second picture shows four people — three women and a man — warming up together in a gym with wooden walls. They are all stretching one arm across the chest and copying the same movement. So the first picture shows quiet training alone, and the second shows exercising together with shared energy.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Both photographs celebrate exercise, but they run on completely different fuel. In the first, a young man holds an advanced yoga balance on a sunlit wooden terrace — his entire body supported by one hand and one foot, arms spread like wings, eyes locked straight ahead. The dark wooden house, potted plants and striped mat make it clear his gym is simply his own backyard, and his only trainer is his own discipline. The second image swaps that silence for shared energy: four people in colourful sportswear stand in a loose line in a wood-panelled gym hall, each pulling an arm across the chest in the same warm-up stretch, clearly enjoying doing it together. One picture shows fitness as private concentration, the other as a social event — and both approaches obviously work.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about a very relaxing afternoon. It was an afternoon at my grandparents' house in the countryside. This was last summer, during my holiday. There was a hammock between two trees in the garden. After lunch, I lay in it with my hands behind my head and closed my eyes. The part I remember most is that I left my phone inside the house. At that moment I felt calm and completely free. Later, my grandmother brought me a glass of lemon juice. These days, I still think about that afternoon when I am stressed. Is it hard to feel relaxed? Yes, I think it is quite hard to feel relaxed these days. This is mainly because we are always busy with work and study. For example, I often check work emails even at the weekend. However, it becomes easier if you turn off your phone for a while. Why is it important to feel relaxed? I think feeling relaxed is important for two main reasons. First, it is good for our health, because stress makes us tired. Second, we can work and study better after a rest. So everyone should find a little time to relax every day.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I want to tell you about a very relaxing afternoon. It was an afternoon at my grandparents' house in the countryside. This was last summer, during my holiday. There was a hammock between two trees in the garden. After lunch, I lay in it with my hands behind my head and closed my eyes. The part I remember most is that I left my phone inside the house. At that moment I felt calm and completely free. Later, my grandmother brought me a glass of lemon juice. These days, I still think about that afternoon when I am stressed. Is it hard to feel relaxed? Yes, I think it is quite hard to feel relaxed these days. This is mainly because we are always busy with work and study. For example, I often check work emails even at the weekend. However, it becomes easier if you turn off your phone for a while. Why is it important to feel relaxed? I think feeling relaxed is important for two main reasons. First, it is good for our health, because stress makes us tired. Second, we can work and study better after a rest. So everyone should find a little time to relax every day.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: I'd like to describe one afternoon when I felt truly at peace. It was a lazy Sunday at my grandparents' farmhouse in the countryside. This was back in the summer of last year, just after a very stressful project at work. My grandfather had hung an old white hammock between two mango trees, so after lunch I climbed in, put my hands behind my head and closed my eyes. The part that stuck with me was that I had deliberately left my phone indoors. At the time I felt lighter than I had in months, and I fell asleep within minutes. Not long after, my grandmother woke me up with a glass of iced lemon juice. These days, I picture that garden whenever work gets on top of me. Is it hard to feel relaxed? To be honest, I find it surprisingly difficult to relax properly. This is mainly because our phones keep us permanently connected to work. To give an example, I often catch myself replying to emails late at night. That said, relaxing is a skill that gets easier with practice. So why does it matter? In my view, relaxing matters for both our health and our performance. The first reason is that constant stress gradually wears down the body and the mind. The second is that a rested brain thinks more clearly and creatively. So taking time to relax is not laziness but a smart investment.

extra_data.sampleAnswer: I want to tell you about the first foreigner I ever talked to. It was when I was still in secondary school, on an ordinary afternoon near my house. A tourist stopped me to ask for directions — he was standing with a map, looking completely lost. My English was broken, but I tried everything: hands, smiles and even my phone. In the end I walked with him all the way to the place. The part I remember most is that he actually understood my terrible English. At that moment I felt nervous at first, then strangely proud. Later, I started studying English seriously that same week. These days, I still count that chat as my real first English lesson.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: I want to tell you about the first foreigner I ever talked to. It was when I was still in secondary school, on an ordinary afternoon near my house. A tourist stopped me to ask for directions. He was standing with a map and he looked completely lost. My English was very simple, but I tried everything. I used my hands, I smiled, and I even showed him my phone. In the end I walked with him all the way to his hotel. It took about ten minutes. During that conversation I felt nervous at first. My heart beat fast and I forgot easy words. I was afraid that he would not understand me. But he was patient and he smiled a lot. After a few minutes I felt more relaxed. When he said thank you at the hotel, I felt strangely proud. He actually understood my terrible English. That same week I started studying English seriously. I think talking with people from other countries is very useful. First, it is the best way to practise a language. In class we learn rules, but with a real person we must speak quickly. Second, we learn about other cultures. That tourist told me about food and weather in his country, and I found it interesting. Third, it makes us more confident. After that day I was not afraid to speak English anymore. So I always say hello when I meet a foreigner in my city.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: I would like to tell you about the first real conversation I ever had with a foreigner, back when I was still a secondary school student. On a completely ordinary afternoon, a tourist stopped me near the old quarter. He was rooted to the pavement with a paper map, looking hopelessly lost. My English at the time was a patchwork of school phrases, but I threw every word I had at the problem, and what the words could not do, gestures and a phone screen did. I ended up walking him the whole way to his hotel, and somewhere along those ten minutes we covered food, weather and half my city's history. During the conversation my feelings changed almost minute by minute. For the first minute I was terrified, and I could hear my own voice shaking. Then I noticed that he was not correcting me or laughing at me; he was simply listening and nodding. That made me braver, and by the end I was making jokes, badly, and he actually laughed at one of them. When we said goodbye I felt a mixture of relief and a quiet pride that lasted for weeks. As for why talking with people from other countries is useful, I would say the obvious benefit is language. Ten minutes with a real person teaches you more than a month of grammar exercises, because you have to think and speak at the same time. Beyond that, it forces you to see your own habits from outside. That tourist asked me why everyone ate on the pavement, and I had honestly never thought about it. Finally, it builds confidence that spreads into other areas. That ten-minute rescue mission is the reason I take English seriously today, and probably the reason I am no longer afraid of strangers.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
1. "A way of life now out of date" → tuần 40 giờ "anchored in this industrial setting" của Henry Ford một thế kỷ trước, "no longer the norm among 21st-century workers".
2. "Benefits for employees" → "keep the workers away from stress", "more free time", "reduce gender inequality" — toàn lợi ích cho người lao động.
3. "Undesirable financial consequences" → "Employers are motivated by profit", "They fear staff producing 20% less for the same pay", và bài học Nhật 1988: "economic output was 20% lower", "a sharp rise in running costs". Cả đoạn nói về tiền của doanh nghiệp.

"Unforeseen challenges for employees" → "a theory called the hedonic treadmill: people will repeatedly return to their baseline of happiness"; công ty Pháp giảm giờ làm nhưng "failed to improve employee happiness"; làm nhanh hơn thì "Accidents may occur", "some people may be asked to leave the company". 5. "Difficult to change old habits" → "some employees went back to the factory floor of their own accord", "others picked up a second job" — được nghỉ vẫn quay về nếp cũ. Bẫy: hai câu đầu nhắc năng suất tăng trong sáu tháng và "the novelty of change", dễ kéo sang ý khác; trọng tâm đoạn nằm ở nửa sau.
6. "An unfair plan for some people" → "Is it even workable? What about schoolteachers?" — giáo viên không thể làm ít đi vì số học sinh và khối lượng phải dạy vẫn thế; "Hospitals take in the same number of patients... how can doctors and nurses work any less?"; "It is the same for the police and firefighters". extra_data.title: The Arrival of the Four-Day Work Week (Version 2)

headings.text: A way of life now out of date
Businesses preparing for a new policy
An unfair plan for some people

paragraphs.text: Proponents of the four-day week believe the time has come for change. They argue that working patterns have been modified throughout history. In the Western world, for example, industrialisation resulted in 48 hours of working per week. The idea of a two-day weekend was first introduced by car magnate Henry Ford about a century ago. The customary 40-hour workweek is still anchored in this industrial setting, where workers stayed outside of home, in the factories and other facilities. This is no longer the norm among 21st-century workers, as many jobs can be undertaken remotely using modern technology.

But why should a four-day workweek be considered? The advocates suggest that working one day less will keep the workers away from stress-inducing work for longer. By having more free time, workers can pursue pastimes or be with their friends and their loved ones. The supporters also argue that reducing work hours can reduce gender inequality in the workplace. Women mostly carry out the childcare duties, so they cannot pursue employment or careers. The proposal will go some way to negate this, although there are childcare facilities that can deal with the task.

Although the proposal for a four-day workweek sounds appealing, there are wider issues to consider. Employers are motivated by profit, and maintaining a high level of productivity is important to them. They fear staff producing 20% less for the same pay. The historical example of Japan, where the workweek was reduced from 44 to 30 hours in 1988, provides a cautionary tale. In the period between then and 1996, economic output was 20% lower than it would have been, and businesses saw a sharp rise in running costs as they hired and trained extra staff to cover the missing hours.

Supporters argue that shorter hours simply make people happier. Some question this notion, citing a theory called the hedonic treadmill: people will repeatedly return to their baseline of happiness, no matter what happened to them. There is evidence for it. Large French companies which reduced their working hours from 38 to 32 reported that they failed to improve employee happiness. Cramming the same amount of work into a shorter period of time may lead to work being done at a much faster rate. Accidents may occur. Workers who work faster cannot concentrate as well, and some people may be asked to leave the company.

The proposal of a shorter working week may be unfounded. However, some companies actually reported increased productivity over a six-month period, though the employees may be stimulated by the novelty of change. There is also the question of income. Fewer hours on the clock can mean a smaller income, and for workers on modest wages that difference matters. Others find the empty day harder to fill than they imagined, and boredom sets in when there is little to occupy them. Where shorter weeks have been tried on a national scale, the results have been telling: some employees went back to the factory floor of their own accord, while others picked up a second job to fill the hours they had just been given.

So, the utopian rhetoric around the virtues of a shorter working week may be unfounded. Is it even workable? What about schoolteachers? The number of students will stay the same, and the amount they have to learn will not diminish. There will not be a rapid rise in the number of this profession in a short period of time. Hospitals take in the same number of patients whether the week is four days or five, so how can doctors and nurses work any less? It is the same for the police and firefighters. The crime rate will not suddenly decrease, and the number of emergencies will stay the same. Employees' income will be reduced in line with their shorter working hours.

Many people remain unconvinced by the case for cutting working hours, and point instead to other ways of reaching the same goal. Raising the basic income would leave workers better able to meet their necessities without touching the timetable at all. There is also the idea of adding more national holidays and bank holidays, when companies are obliged to pay their staff, so that everyone gains extra rest without a single business having to restructure the way it operates. Whatever the outcome, the debate over working time looks unlikely to be settled any time soon.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show men who look worried. In the first one, I can see a middle-aged man in a smart camel coat standing next to the stone steps of a big old building. He is holding a black folder, but he is not reading it — he is staring into the distance with a very serious face. The second picture shows a much younger man in a dark red polo shirt, sitting outdoors on a low yellow wall. He is pressing one hand against his forehead and holding his glasses in the other hand, so he looks really upset. So the two pictures show the same feeling of worry at two very different ages.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Both photographs capture private moments of worry, but a generation apart. In the first, a middle-aged man in an elegant camel coat stands beside the sweeping stone steps of what looks like an official building. He clutches an open black folder without reading a word of it, gazing into the distance with a composed but unmistakably tense expression. The second picture strips away all that composure: a young man in a dark red polo sits alone on a low yellow ledge, one hand pressed hard against his forehead, his glasses dangling from the other. The sunlit trees and sandy ground around him only sharpen the sense that he is completely alone with his problem. Together, the images tell one story about pressure, told in two very different voices.

explanation:
--- GIẢI THÍCH ---
Dạng sắp xếp câu: tìm câu mở đầu (không trỏ ngược), rồi bám vào đại từ, từ chỉ định và từ nối để nối dần.

▸ Making films — thứ tự đúng:
  0. "In 1895, the Grand Café in France showed the first ever commercial film." → câu cho sẵn, nêu mốc thời gian và sự kiện đầu tiên.
  1. "Films from that period were very different from films of today." → "that period" trỏ thẳng về năm 1895 ở câu cho sẵn.
  2. "This is because they were all in black and white, and they had no sound." → "This is because" giải thích cho ý "very different" ở câu trước.
  3. "In addition to these technical limitations, the film producers also had a limited budget." → "these technical limitations" gom lại ý đen trắng và không có tiếng.
  4. "This lack of money mainly affected the actors, and they did not earn a lot of money." → "This lack of money" trỏ về "a limited budget".
  5. "Things have changed over time, and some of them now earn millions of dollars for appearing in films." → "some of them" trỏ về "the actors", chốt bằng tương phản quá khứ với hiện tại.

▸ A new coffee shop — thứ tự đúng:
  1. “When I arrived, the place was very crowded, and the staff were extremely busy on the first day.” → câu mở đầu, nêu bối cảnh.
  2. “Even though it was crowded, the staff still managed to find a table for me.” → “it was crowded” nối tiếp ý đông khách.
  3. “They handed me the menu, and when I looked through it, I saw quite a variety of dishes.” → “They” = the staff.
  4. “After checking them all, I decided to order the most expensive sandwich.” → “them all” = a variety of dishes.
  5. “It tasted really good with melted cheese on top, and I’ll definitely come back to this place again.” → “It” = the sandwich; câu kết.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show ways of keeping memories. In the first one, a woman is taking a photo of a family with her smartphone. The family — a father in a yellow T-shirt, a mother holding a small baby, and a little girl — are sitting close together on a green sofa and smiling, and I can see them again on the phone screen. In the second picture, which is black and white, someone is writing in a spiral notebook with a pen, and the page is already half full. So the first picture shows a modern, digital way to save a moment, while the second shows a quiet, personal way — writing it down.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Both photographs are about holding on to moments, but with completely different tools. In the first, a woman — very possibly the grandmother — is photographing a young family with her smartphone: a father in a mustard T-shirt, a mother cradling a baby in white, and a little girl leaning into her, all squeezed happily onto a green sofa under some party bunting. The same scene appears in miniature on the phone screen. The second picture could not feel more different: a black-and-white close-up of a hand with a beaded bracelet, moving a pen across a half-filled spiral notebook, probably a diary. One image captures a loud, shared celebration in a second; the other preserves a private moment slowly, word by word. Together they show the two great ways humans fight forgetting.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show people giving presentations, but in different situations. In the first one, a man with a beard and a grey T-shirt is standing on a small stage, holding a microphone and smiling while he talks to an audience. Behind him there is a large screen full of photos and articles, and next to the stage I can see big green plants and a colourful pillar. The second picture shows a small meeting in a bright office. A woman in a light blue shirt is pointing at a curve on a flipchart and explaining it to three colleagues, who are sitting around a table with laptops, phones and papers. So the first picture shows speaking to a big audience, and the second shows presenting to a small team.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Both photographs show the same skill — presenting — but at two very different volumes. In the first, a bearded speaker in a grey T-shirt commands a small stage at what looks like an evening company event, microphone close to his mouth, clearly enjoying himself. Behind him glows a huge screen collaged with photos and press clippings, while green plants and a pillar painted with a cartoon face give the venue a playful, modern feel. The second image shrinks the audience to three: in a bright office with a brick wall, a woman in a pale blue shirt points at a rising curve on a flipchart, guiding her colleagues through the numbers as laptops and papers cover the table between them. One is a performance for a crowd, the other a working conversation — and mastering both is what makes a truly complete speaker.

question_text: You are a member of the book club. You received this email from the club manager.

formalEmail.instruction: Write an email to the club manager. Write about your feelings and what you think the club should do. Write 120–150 words. Recommended time: 20 minutes.
formalEmail.sampleAnswer:
Dear Manager,
Thank you for your email about the special meeting. I was delighted to read that the club is planning to invite a guest speaker, and I would like to share my suggestions.
In my opinion, we should invite Nguyen Nhat Anh, a Vietnamese author whose stories about childhood and family are loved by readers of all ages. Many older members grew up with his books, while younger members study his work at school, so everyone would have something to ask him.

question_text: Singers can be good role models for young people.
options: Man
Woman
Both
explanation:
M: Did you watch that awards show for singers last night?
W: I did. My kids talk about it constantly. And honestly, a lot of those famous singers have become real role models for young people — they talk about staying in school, they give to charity, they seem to care.
M: I don't see it that way at all. Those people spend their time doing charity events and appearing on game shows instead of concentrating on their actual work. And can anyone today sing better than the singers of our generation? I doubt it.
W: You mean it's a question of taste, don't you? I know everyone's taste is different. Kids nowadays like modern music, and our generation liked something else. You, for example, only listen to classical music, so nothing else sounds good to you.
M: That's true, I suppose — taste is personal. But I still think music is a universal language. Whether a song has words or not makes no difference to how we experience it. Even music written in a language we don't understand can move us.
W: Hmm, I'm not sure I'd go that far. But then, I can't claim to know as much as you about this. You have a degree in music, don't you?
M: I do. But here's something I think you'll agree with: music can completely control people's emotions. Film directors and advertisers know exactly which chord to play to make you feel a certain way.
W: Oh, that I do agree with. I never know when I'm going to cry in a film, but the moment the music swells at the dramatic part, the tears just come — whether I want them to or not.
M: Exactly. That's a lot of power in a few notes.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
1. Singers can be good role models for young people → The woman: "a lot of those famous singers have become real role models for young people". Người đàn ông phản đối: "I don't see it that way at all".
2. Taste in music is a highly personal thing → Both: cô nói "I know everyone's taste is different"; anh đồng ý "That's true, I suppose — taste is personal".
3. Music is a universal language → The man: "I still think music is a universal language". Cô không đồng ý hẳn: "I'm not sure I'd go that far".
4. Music can be used to manipulate people's feelings → Both: anh nói "music can completely control people's emotions"; cô đồng ý "that I do agree with... the tears just come".
👉 Mẹo: Part 3 chọn Both khi có câu đồng thuận rõ ("That's true", "I do agree"). Chọn một người khi người kia phản đối hoặc lưỡng lự ("I'm not sure I'd go that far").

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show people working with plants, but in very different ways. In the first one, a woman in a light blue top and an older man with grey hair are standing in a vegetable garden, passing a head of red lettuce to each other and smiling. Around them I can see neat garden beds with onions, lettuce and orange flowers, a rope fence and wooden compost boxes. The second picture shows a young woman scientist in a white coat and safety glasses inside a greenhouse. She is wearing white gloves and writing notes about the plants, and behind her there are glass bottles with small plants hanging inside. So the first picture shows gardening as a relaxing hobby, while the second shows plants as a serious science.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Both photographs revolve around plants, but the spirit could hardly be more different. The first captures a sunny allotment where a blonde woman in a mint-blue top and an older grey-haired man are exchanging a freshly picked head of red lettuce, both laughing. Around them stretch tidy raised beds of onions, young lettuce and bright marigolds, framed by a rope fence and wooden compost boxes — gardening at its most social and rewarding. The second image moves indoors, into a greenhouse that doubles as a laboratory: a young researcher in a white coat, protective glasses and gloves is noting observations on a clipboard, surrounded by hanging glass spheres with tiny plants suspended inside, while a colleague works behind her. One picture grows dinner; the other grows knowledge — and both faces show the same quiet devotion.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show people relaxing, but in different ways. In the first one, a young woman in a yellow sweater and glasses is sitting in a cream armchair by a bright window, reading a book with a soft blanket over her legs. Next to her there is a small white table with a pile of books and a candle, and plants on the windowsill. The second picture shows a father watching TV with his two daughters in the evening. So the first picture shows quiet relaxing alone, and the second shows fun family time together.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The two photographs show the same goal — switching off — achieved in opposite ways. The first is pure silence: a young woman in a chunky yellow sweater curls up in a cream armchair beside a plant-filled window, glasses on, blanket over her knees, completely absorbed in her book. The stack of books, the candle and the coffee on the windowsill suggest this corner was built precisely for afternoons like this. The second photograph replaces silence with company: in a darkened evening room, a father aims the remote at the screen while his two daughters flank him on a leather sofa, all three orbiting a glass bowl of popcorn. One picture trains the imagination in solitude; the other trades depth for shared laughter — and honestly, a good week at home probably needs both.

groups.question: Why is sport important for people with disabilities?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Both pictures show people playing sport, but two very different sports. In the first picture, five men are playing basketball in wheelchairs on an indoor court. One player in a yellow shirt is holding the ball above his head, ready to shoot, and a player in blue has his arm up to block him. I can see numbers on their shirts, a wooden floor and people watching from blue seats. The second picture shows four women tennis players, all dressed in white, shaking hands over the net after a doubles match. They are smiling and holding their rackets, and there is a big crowd behind them in the sunshine. So one picture shows a game in action, and the other shows respect at the end of a game.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The two photographs catch sport at opposite moments. The first is pure action: five men in purpose-built wheelchairs contest a basketball match on a polished indoor court. The player in yellow, number 9, is at the very top of his shooting motion while a defender in blue stretches an arm up to block him, and two more players close in from the right. Squad numbers, angled wheels and rows of blue seats with scattered spectators complete the scene. The second photograph is the exact opposite — the moment after. Four female tennis players, dressed head to toe in traditional white, lean in to shake hands across the net, smiling and still holding their rackets while a packed crowd applauds in the sunshine. Together they show the two faces of sport: the fight, and the respect that follows it.

question_text: Four people are talking about outdoor activities. Match each person to the correct information.
explanation:
Speaker A: I like sport because it keeps me active, but I've had to be careful about which one. Years ago I fell off a horse and broke my arm, so I gave up riding for good. And climbing is out of the question — I'm terrified of heights. Luckily, there's a forest just behind my house with wide, flat paths, and lots of people jog there. So every morning before work I put on my trainers and run for about forty minutes. It's simple, it's free, and it clears my head.
Speaker B: I've loved horses since I was a little girl. Owning one is far too expensive, of course — the food and the vet bills would eat my whole salary. Many of my friends go skiing in winter, but I've never found snow sports very interesting; I hate the cold. What I'm lucky about is that there are several riding stables near my home, so I don't need a horse of my own. I still spend most weekends there, brushing the horses and riding out through the fields.
Speaker C: Where I live there's a very long beach, and hundreds of people jog along it every morning. I go in the opposite direction. There's a mountain behind the town with steep, rocky trails, and I love riding my bike up there. Pushing up to the top is hard work, but then you get the view — and the ride down is fast and exciting. It's a real challenge every time, and my legs certainly know about it the next day.
Speaker D: I'm getting on a bit now, so I can't do the things I used to. Climbing and cycling are far too much for my knees these days. Jogging isn't a bad idea, I suppose, but I need something slower. So what I do is go for a walk every day in the late afternoon. I follow the path by the river, enjoy the scenery, and by that time of day it's not too hot. It's gentle, but it keeps me fit and happy.

--- GIẢI THÍCH ĐÁP ÁN ---
A – going for a run: "every morning before work I put on my trainers and run for about forty minutes". Bẫy: ngựa (đã bỏ vì ngã), climbing (sợ độ cao).
B – horse riding: "there are several riding stables near my home... riding out through the fields". Bẫy: skiing/snow sports là sở thích của BẠN cô ấy.
C – mountain biking: "I love riding my bike up there... the ride down is fast and exciting". Bẫy: jogging là việc người khác làm trên bãi biển.
D – walking: "I go for a walk every day in the late afternoon". Bẫy: climbing, cycling (quá sức), jogging (cần chậm hơn).
Không ai chọn: snow sports, climbing — đều được nhắc như thứ KHÔNG làm.
👉 Mẹo: mỗi người nhắc 2–3 môn nhưng chỉ 1 môn đi với "I do / I go / I love"; các môn khác đi với "gave up", "out of the question", "my friends".

question_text: Do you prefer monkeys or dolphins?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: If I had to choose, I would prefer to be close to dolphins. The main reason is that dolphins are gentle and very intelligent, and being in the water with one sounds like a dream. On top of that, dolphins seem to enjoy playing with people, and they never try to steal your food like the monkeys in the first picture. For example, I once saw dolphins follow a boat in Nha Trang and I still remember it. Having said that, dolphins in a pool like the second picture are not really free. So dolphins are my choice, but from a boat, not a pool.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Dolphins, without much hesitation. They combine gentleness with real intelligence, and there are centuries of stories about dolphins guiding lost swimmers and fishermen — the relationship feels mutual rather than one-sided. Monkeys are undeniably entertaining, but the troop in the first picture is there for the food, and anyone who has lost sunglasses to a macaque in Da Nang knows how quickly that charm turns into a robbery. I once watched a pod of dolphins race a boat off Nha Trang for ten minutes, apparently for the fun of it, and I have never forgotten it. The caveat is the second picture: a dolphin in a pool performing hand signals is not the animal I mean. So my answer is dolphins — seen from a boat, on their terms, not ours.

question_text: Do you love spending time outside?

extra_data.imageDesc: Người bố da đen đội đầu trọc, mặc áo phông xanh rêu và quần short kaki, đeo ba lô, đang cõng con gái nhỏ trên vai đi trên con đường mòn trong rừng; bé gái mặc áo hồng, tết tóc, đang cười và nhìn ra xa; bố ngẩng lên nhìn con và cười; hai bên là cây cao, lá vàng xanh, ánh nắng xuyên qua tán cây.
extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Yes, I really love spending time outside. Usually I go for a walk in the park near my house, and at the weekend I ride my bike along the river with my friends. I often go early in the morning before it gets hot. I like it because fresh air makes me feel awake and happy, and it helps me forget my work and my phone. For example, when I was stressed last month, a walk by the lake helped me a lot. So I try to go outside as often as I can.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: I genuinely do, though I probably do not do it as much as I should. On weekdays I settle for a walk around the park near my flat, and at weekends I cycle along the Red River with two friends, usually early, before the heat sets in. What I love is the feeling of being out of four walls: my shoulders drop, my phone stays in my pocket, and problems that felt enormous at my desk shrink to their real size. Last month, in the middle of a stressful project, an hour by the lake did more for me than any advice. So time outdoors is never time wasted, as far as I am concerned.

question_text: Why do many people enjoy camping with friends?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Many people enjoy camping because it is a complete break from normal life. There is no traffic, no office and often no phone signal, so the mind slows down. Camping is also cheap compared with hotels, which makes travel possible for students. Doing simple things together, like cooking and building a tent, brings friends closer. For example, my friends and I still talk about a rainy camping trip from last year. So camping is popular because it is simple, cheap and full of shared memories.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Camping is popular because it removes almost everything people normally hide behind. No signal, no comfortable room, no menu to order from, so the group has to actually cooperate. That is exactly where the friendship grows, since cooking badly together creates better stories than a nice restaurant. It is also the cheapest way to travel, which matters enormously for students. My friends still bring up the night our tent flooded, and nobody remembers any perfect trip that clearly. So people go camping for nature, and come home with the group.

question_text: When was the last time you had a meal with your family?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: The last time I had a meal with my family was last Sunday. It was at my parents' house, and my grandparents came too. My mother cooked spring rolls, grilled fish and a big pot of soup, and as usual there was too much food. During the meal my father told his old jokes and we all laughed anyway, and my grandmother asked me about my exams. Everybody put their phones away for once. I felt really relaxed and close to everyone, because we are all so busy these days. So I hope we can do it again very soon.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The last proper family meal was last Sunday at my parents' house, with my grandparents joining us. My mother had cooked spring rolls, grilled fish and an enormous pot of soup — far more than seven people could finish, which is her way of showing affection. Over the meal my father recycled his oldest jokes, my grandmother interrogated me about my exams, and for once every phone stayed in another room. Nobody left the table for nearly two hours. I felt completely relaxed and unusually close to everyone, partly because our schedules rarely allow it. So that lunch remains my favourite memory of the month, and I am already hoping for a repeat.

Let's talk about friends. Please tell me about your best friend.

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: My best friend is Minh. We have known each other since primary school, so for more than fifteen years. He is funny and very honest, and he always tells me the truth even when I do not want to hear it. We like playing football and drinking coffee together at the weekend. I can talk to him about anything.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: My best friend is Minh, whom I have known since we sat next to each other in primary school. He is the honest one in my life: if I make a bad decision, he says so, kindly but clearly, which I have come to value more than compliments. We still play football most Sundays and argue about music afterwards. Fifteen years on, he is more like a brother.

question_text: How are these two ways of exercising different?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: Exercising alone and exercising with others feel very different. When you exercise alone you choose your own time, your own speed and your own music. Training with other people is more social, and the group pushes you to try harder. Alone is more flexible, but it is easier to give up when you feel lazy. For example, I run alone on weekdays but play football with friends at weekends. So one gives freedom and the other gives motivation.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: The difference is really freedom against accountability. Alone, everything is yours to control: the hour, the pace, the playlist, and the decision to stop early when nobody is watching. In a group the schedule stops being negotiable, because four people are already waiting and nobody wants to be the one who cancelled. Effort rises too, since we all quietly compete with whoever is next to us. My weekday runs are solitary and honestly quite slow; my weekend football is neither. So solo training fits your life, and group training rescues your discipline.

question_text: How are these two ways of relaxing different?

extra_data.sampleAnswerBasic: These two ways of relaxing are quite different. Relaxing indoors means staying at home with a book, a film or a phone, which is comfortable and cheap. Relaxing outdoors means going to a park or the countryside, so you get fresh air and exercise. Indoor relaxing is easier because the weather never matters. However, people usually feel more refreshed after being outside. For example, I watch films at home on rainy days but go to the park when it is sunny. So one is more convenient and the other is more refreshing.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Indoor rest is convenient, outdoor rest is restorative, and the two are not the same thing. Staying home costs nothing, needs no planning and ignores the weather completely, which is why most people default to it. The problem is that screens rest the body while keeping the mind busy, so you can finish an evening tired in a new way. Outdoors demands effort first, then returns something better: daylight, movement and a genuinely quieter head. I watch films when it rains, but the park is what fixes a bad week. So convenience explains what people choose, and quality explains what actually works.

question_text: How are these two places different?

question_text: Why do many people feel nervous when speaking in public?

Lack of practice is another reason, since most people rarely speak in front of a group. Some people also worry about their language or their voice shaking. For example, I was very nervous the first time I presented at university, but it improved with practice. So public speaking is frightening mainly because it is unfamiliar.
extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Public speaking frightens people because it combines exposure with the fear of judgement. In front of a group, a two-second pause feels like a minute, and one wrong word feels permanent. Most of us also do it rarely, and anything practised twice a year will always feel dangerous. There is a physical loop as well: nerves make the voice shake, the shaking is noticed, and the nerves grow. My first university presentation was genuinely painful, and the tenth was almost enjoyable. So the fear is normal, and repetition is the only real cure.

question_text: Why is sport important for people with disabilities?

extra_data.sampleAnswerAdvanced: Sport matters here for exactly the same reasons it matters for everyone, plus a few more. Physical strength protects independence, and independence is the thing disability threatens first. Confidence is the bigger prize, because achieving something demanding rewrites how a person is seen, including by themselves. Team sport then adds community, which is what isolation quietly removes. The Paralympics changed public attitudes far more effectively than any campaign, simply by showing what people can do. So sport is not therapy, it is participation, and that distinction is the whole point.
